headline: SUICIDE ATTEMPT.
text:
SENSATIONAL PRISON COM- POUND INCIDENT.

PERSONER$^{\text{®}}$ INJURIES.

An attempt at suicide on the part of a Chinese held in custody on a charge of the murder of a clansman was referred to at the Criminal Sessions this morning. The attempt, which had been made by throwing himself from the prison compound ramp, was said by Mr. T. M. Huzlerigg this morning to have necessitated the amputation of one leg above the knee and the amputation of the lower part of the other. According to the report of the medical officer, it appeared that the life of the man, who was now in the Government Civil Hospital, was still in considerable danger. Mr. Valentine's report stated that the prisoner would not in any event be able to stand his trial for at least two months.

Hau and the murder with which he is charged is that of Li Muk, a chinesan with whom it was stated at the Magistracy that he had had in quarrel the day previous. The murder took place at 4 Sun Street and it was stated at the Magistracy that the coolies of the house in fear of being implicated took the body and placed it on a heap of rubble in a side street. An admission of having stabbed his relative was made by prisoner at the Magistracy. The case this morning was adjourned for consideration at the June Sessions, the recognisances of witnesses being respected.

headline: Held To Runsom.
text:
When Lau Fong, alias Lau Ku pleaded guilty before Mr. Justified Wood at the Sessions this morning to having held Yeung Fat and Yeung Kwai to ransom, His Honour asked the two latter what their treatment at the hands of prisoners had been. Both said that they had been ill-treated, having been kept in a "small hole" on a boat, the opening to which had been kept covered up. They had no light and no rice. They had been kept there for eight days.

Prisoner was sentenced to 7 years hard labour on the charge of holding to ransom, two other charges of having stolen sums of money amounting to $430), on the same occasion being withdrawn, as prisoner pleaded not guilty to them.

The events in question occurred Leung Kiu Tan

ceita a year ago.

One case of hydrophobia (Chinese) and one of rabies have been reported for the twenty-four hours ended yesterday.

headline: A Bad Record.
text:
A record of convictions, for their extending over a period of six years was admitted by Lau Chi, who pleaded guilty to stealing a purse with $4 in it on March 25. He was sentenced to 2 years' hard labour.

This concluded the cases before Mr. Justice Wood and jurors were warned to attend in the Supreme Court on Wednesday when the charge of attempted fraud on the Wing On Bank will be heard.

headline: KOWLOON CASÉS
text:
A Chinese cook in the employment of Mr. Colbourne Little was fined $25 at the Newloon Magistracy this morning for possession of a small quantity of opium.

The cook's son, who had been previously employed in the house and was according to the evidence discharged owing to being untrustworthy, was fined $10 for trespassing on the premises, while on a similar charge another who went with him was fined $5.

For attempting to bring dogs across the harbour by the Shaukl-wan ferry, a Chinese coolie was fined $10.

Very little damage was done to the steam launch. "Vancouver" in a fire which broke out in the engine room yesterday afternoon while coaling at Mongkok. Prompt assistance was rendered by a police launch.

headline: CANTON FIRING.
text:
PICKENS ATTACK FISH COOLIES.

CARGOES FOR HONGKONG.

Either by ingenuity, or by force, coolies in change of fresh water fish for Hongkong," succeeded in evading the Canton boycott pickets on Saturday night when a number of volleys were fired from the shore.

Witherto the pickets had either rounded "up small craft or maintained a cordon from the shore. Only last week they prevented fish getting through for a few days. In the latter part of last week, supplies have again reached the Hongkong stemmers.

During the dark hours of Saturday night, prior to the "Lungshan's" departure at 8 a.m. yesterday (for Hongkong), a number of junks are believed to have put off for the boat. Before they had reached the "Lungshan" shots rang out and became more intense.

One who claims to have been near enough to have seen what was going on is of the opinion that the crowds of the junked took cover under the guagwhale and bulkhead and that they even returned the fire. The speaker remarked that there were too many of them to be rammed by the pickets' motor-boats, and the coolies eventually got out of range to complete their job. It is even said that they were armed for their own protection.

headline: FOG COLLISION.
text:
LOCAL STEAMER'S BOW DAMAGED

JARDINE BOAT ARRIVES

the Indo-China s.s. "Yatshing" (for which Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd.) are the general agents) arrived in Hongkong yesterday morning after being damaged in a collision with the

The "Yatshing" left Tsingtao on April 11 and Shanghai on April 15. The "Tacoma Maru" left Hongkong on Saturday for the North.

About 5.26 a.m. on Sunday, says the report of Captain J. S. Masson, the steamers collided in a thick fog at Jamgi Point. It is understood that this is near Chilang, about 90 miles or so from Hongkong.

The “Tacoma” subsequently proceeded and the “Yatshing” went alongside Jardine's wharf at West Point, on arrival here. The Jardine boat's stem is buckled and the bow plating has been damaged, these necessitating repairs in dock.

The "Tacoma Maru" is given as of 5,850 official tons and the "Yatshing" as 2,284.

headline: In Nick of Time.
text:
Captain Estevez is progressing, and desires to continue his flight.

He said that he was forced to land for lack of petrol after in-effectual endeavours to strike the Bagdad track.

Eight British machines engaged in the search. Before leaving here the Spaniards were warned by the Royal Air Force to take three days' supplies of food and water. It was thanks to this advice that Captain Estevez was alive after six days in a barren country. As it was, he and his mechanic were only rescued in the nick of time. Their trials were aggravated by a sand storm that lasted for two days.

King Alfonso has cabled to the Royal Air Force his appreciation of their admirable work and de-ploring the loss of two British airmen.

Comrades at Calcutta.

The other two Spanish aviators have arrived here from Agra.

headline: ROBRERIES
text:
Four Chinese, carrying between them two revolvers, entered a house at Wong Chuk Han village in the Aberdeen district at 10 p.m. yesterday. The inmates were tied up and a sum of $80 in money was stolen.

A ricasha coolie was the victim of a robbery at West Point last night; the thief having a long ride before he jumped off at Water Street, where he was joined by three others. They stole a sum of $2 of from the coolie.

Cargo to the value of $140 was taken by thieves from a boat at the Yaumati typhoon shelter last night.

The postponed inspection of the Hongkong Police by His Excellency the Governor will take place on Wednesday afternoon at the Central Police Station compound.

The new fro float built to the order of the Government and, which rendered assistance in a recent fire at the Kowloon Docks, will before being placed in commission, give a demonstration at the Queen's Pier at 5.30 p.m. on Wednesday.

headline: Closer Ties
text:
The steady increase in the volume of trade during the last quarter of a century between this Colony and Indo-China was created and nourished closer commercial ties, from which have sprung that spirit of mutual confidence, so necessary to beneficial trade, and I feel sure that it is this same spirit of confidence which has prompted those who guide the affairs of this Institution, to decide upon the wise step of acquiring even at heavy cost their own permanent premises in this important commercial centre of the British Empire in which one and all can meet in friendly commercial rivalry.

"This decision was arrived at shortly after the War and when Mr. Lecot's predecessor received instructions from his Head Office to study the question, the desirability of acquiring this site, which at the time was possible, naturally presented itself, with the result that after some very delicate negotiations on the part of our friend, the Bank became the happy owner of this valuable property."

The building was started just two years ago and in spite of all labour troubles brought on by the strike and boycott, the contractor, imbued with the spirit of energy and courage, imparted and sustained by our friend the manager, succeeded in overcoming every obstacle that arose in his path and we find ourselves to-day in this palatial building, finished to time. The work throughout, which, I am told, has been satisfactorily done, speaks highly for Hang On, the contractors, and Messrs. Clark & Iu, the architects.

headline: UNLIKE CLYDEBANK.
text:
POLICE "EVICT" LOCAL TENANTS.

300 YEAR INHABITANTS.

Three hundred years' association is claimed by some local Chinese, householders who were revicted by the Police yesterday after a long series of incidents starting from a deluge of a few wet seasons ago.

Early in the morning, divisional Inspector J. Ogg, of Wanchat station, took a posse comprising a European sergeant and ten Indians and Chinese down to Wong-nei-chong village. With the officers were representatives of the Public Works Department, for which several gangs of cookies had assembled to do the manual part of the job.

Verbal notice had been given on Saturday that the houses were to be demolished. As is characteristic of the Chinese masses, the inhabitants of the village delayed things till the very last minute. When the Police arrived they took matters stoically—after having hoped against hope for months on end, that they would be allowed to stay in tenements which nature had made both dangerous and insignificantly.

There was no "fun" similar to that when the Sheriff's officer went to evict the Clydebank workers who refused to pay rent. The only incident was when two women disputed ownership of a small board that was only worth a few cents. Knick-knacks and sundries that the foreigner was positive nobody could have any earthly use for were carried away with precision.

Each house was of only one floor and three ordinary office desks would have filled up the floor space up to the roof. The removal was a matter of only an hour or so and then the "pioneers" set to work with picks and shovels.

When the race-course was "mudded" a few years ago, the village was flooded out and a number of the hovels collapsed. With the deluges repeated, the place was deemed dangerous. Water stood several feet deep in the narrow lanes, and earth was piled up everywhere.

Negotiations are proceeding between the Government and respective owners for an interchange of lots. During the last months, a number of the small owners have been paid at Government expense to live away from their homes.

Yesterday the real work of pulling the village down began and modern houses will, it is hoped spring up very soon.

A number of the inhabitants are very hazy as to the conditions and they are afraid that they may be (in their opinion) unfairly treated. Their one obsession is to retain their present lots, but no one seems to be clear how he is going to keep the rickety house standing, or what he is going to live in. The Government has made a promise and a solution must come in time.

These people are of a clan which migrated to Hongkong long before it was seeded to Britain. Some have been there for not less than seven generations, whilst others maintain that their family has lived there for three hundred years.

In the property boom of three years back, a number were tempted to sell their “heirlooms.” But they did not leave the place. They went a little higher up the hill, “marked out a claim” on Crown land, put up matsheds, and are still living there to-day.

headline: RICE THEFTS / OFFENDERS SENT TO PRISON.
text:
Imprisonment without the option of a fine was meted out to offenders at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning in further thefts of rice.

Three women pleaded guilty to theft of 218 lbs. rice from the s.s. "Kwongtung" and were each given two months' hard labour. A boatman and a woman who were charged with receiving the rice, knowing same to have been stolen, admitted in answer to a question that they knew the rice was swept from the decks of the vessel. The man, having previous conviction, was sentenced to four months' hard labour and the woman to two months.

headline: RENTS ORDINANCE.
text:
PETITION TO CONTINUE RESTRICTION.

THE PROS AND CONS.

That a petition is to be prepared for presentation to the Government was the decision arrived at by the general meeting of the Hongkong Tenants' Protective Association.

Points mentioned by speakers were:—

Reasons advanced for resembling the Rents Restriction Ordinance (in the speakers' opinion): All effects of restrictions on owners of property; the increase of 15 per cent. on standard events (sanctioned last year) not being high enough in ratio to the rise in other costs of living; the number of vacant tenements in the Colony.

Arguments against the rescinding of the Ordinance were advanced, as follows: If no restriction is placed on the power to increase rentals, rents will be put up to such an extent that other costs will have to go up in proportion, thereby, tending to a high rate of living, demands for increased wages, etc., the statement that "if rents of restricted houses (i.e., those coming within the Ordinance) are put up, tenants can move" to houses at present vacant, is not true in fact, as the question of situation is of paramount importance to business, shops etc., bona fide landlords do not favour exploitation in rents, for which speculators and subsidiary landlords (i.e., "principal tenants") are responsible; the number of vacant tenements in the Colony, at present is not due to the presence of the Ordinance, but to the crisis.

As has been stated, the meeting was convened to discuss a proposal to petition the Government to continue the Ordinance (after June 30, 1926) or maintain some form of limited restriction.

The retiring officials were re- elected en bloc:

headline: DR. C.C. WU. / NOT YET ARRIVED IN THE COLONY.
text:
NO OFFICIAL NEWS?

Dr. C. C. Wu, the Mayor of Canton, who is reported to be likely to visit the Colony this week, did not arrive yesterday.

Up till tiffin time to-day there had been, as far as is known, no official intimation that he was coming down by the Steamboat Co.'s steamer this afternoon.

Vernacular papers indicate that if Dr. Wu does come down, his visit may only be in the nature of a complimentary return call to the Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp (Attorney-General) who went up to Canton some days ago and entered into unofficial conversations with Dr. Wu, relative to the projected conference to end the boycott.

headline: CAPTAIN FINED:
text:
CAUSING OBSTRUCTION IN HARBOUR.

RESULT OF "STRIKE:"

A fine of $40 (or, in default, one month's hard labour) was imposed on the captain of a local steamer, at the Marine Court this morning.

Defendant was Captain J. N. Catela, master of the m.s. "Wong Shek Kurig" who pleaded not guilty before Lentus Com. G. E. Hole, R.N. (Marine Magistrate), to a charge of anchoring in the harbour so as to obstruct the fairways at 3.30 p.m. on April 14.

Mr. W. R. Hillyer, boarding officer of the Harbour Office, testified that the steamer was three ships' lengths west of buoy No. B47, and that there was not enough room.

Replying to the bench, witness said that the ship was actually causing an obstruction to the s.s. "New Mathilde," whose captain he was going to call as a witness for the prosecution.

Captain E. G. Rapley, master of the s.s. "New Mathilde," said that he was taking his vessel from the mooring to Stonecutters Island and had to alter his course, thereby cutting through the line of buoys, because of the other steamer being in the way. Defendant stated that he left Canton, owing to the strike, and had only a crew of two. He was short of gasoline and his company had promised to have gasoline ready near Green Island. The fine was paid.

headline: CAPE FLIGHT. / ROYAL AIR FORCE SQUADRON RETURNING
text:
CORDIAL SEND OFF:

The Royal Air Force flyers have started on their return flight to Cairo.

They were seen off by a large crowd, including the Earl of Athlone, Governor-General of the Union of South Africa, and the various Cabinet Ministers.

headline: Mr. Alabaster's Point
text:
Before the charges were read out at this morning's proceedings, Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., made an application before the second prisoner (Lam Fuk-chiu) was called upon to plead.

Mr. Alabaster pointed out that the two prisoners had been charged on the same indictment where as from the particulars as set out by the prosecution it was clear that the second prisoner was not charged with perjury. He moved that either the indictment be quashed or with the alternatives that the two last counts referring to the alleged perjury be struck out or that the prosecution be called on to elect which counts they would proceed with. Mr. Alabaster pointed out the anomalies of prisoner being called upon to plead on a count on which he was not charged.

Mr. Jenkin pointed out that the same facts in the conspiracy charge stood for the perjury charge and after cases had been quoted and some legal argument, His Lordship held that he did not see any ground for alleging that the second prisoner would be aeriously embarrassed by the inclusion in the indictment of those two counts. He did not, at any rate, propose at that moment to exercise his discretion in favour of striking out the counts or hearing the case separately, although if, as the case proceeded, he should see reason, he might exercise his discretion. Mr. F. C. Jenkin (together with Mr. Sheldon) was for the prosecution; Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K. C. for one prisoner and Mr. Elaley Zettlyn for the other. The case is proceeding

headline: MISSION GOODS.
text:
CLERGYMAN'S KEROSINE

As the commodity is under a Canton Government monopoly, a quantity of kerosine oil for a foreign up-puntry mission formed the subject of a "seizure" on April 17 which, however, did not result in any complication.

For about a year, kerosine oil has been sold under the control of the Canton Government, this phase of what has been an extensive foreign trade having been reviewed in the last annual report of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce.

As the tow-boat for Shekki was about to leave the Bund at Canton on the night of April 17, a party of plain-clothes searchers from the "Merchants' Protection Preventive Committee," accompanied by police, executed a search-warrant and detained 45 cases of kerosine oil on board without the revenue stamps attached.

A foreign clergyman who claimed to be associated with a mission at Shekkf (the vernacular report does not give any other detail as to the gentleman's identity) then came forward and explained that the oil was purchased in Canton for the poor in his district.

During the discussion a Chinese is alleged to have interceded on the clergyman's behalf. This man is described as the chief commissariat officer of General Li Fook-lam's army but his name is not given in the report.

When the chief of the Preventive Committee arrived on the scene, a permit was shown to him, issued by Mr. T. V. Soong, who is head of the Government monopoly. The mit was accepted and the oil was allowed to be shipped away. The so-called military officer is said to have tendered an apology for unwarranted interference, this being accepted.

People's Mass Protest. From Ko. In comes news of a demonstration, which practically amounted to a riot, against the existence of the monopoly. On April 15, over 10,000 people are said to have organised a parade. In spite of heavy rain, they marched to the local Government oil depot to protest, forcing an entrance.

The authorities, however, were prepared, police and military having assembled there. A number alleged to be leaders of the demonstrators were arrested. The crowd then surrounded the depot until those detained had been released. One of the conditions of release was the setting off of firecrackers, this being a Chinese custom of restoration of "face."

headline: CANTON LABOUR.
text:
MERCHANTS FLOUTED.

Canton merchants are now reported to be in communication with the Provincial Government in regard to the suggested removal of all "strikers" to Whampoa.

Last week specific instances were mentioned in which so-called armed labour pickets marched into business premises and took possession whilst the Police remained inactive.

This interference, alleged to have originated in disputes between masters and their employees' guilds, is regarded very seriously. To-day the vernacular papers record another case of workmen taking the law into their own hands, ignoring the representatives of law and order. The proposal that all strikers be accommodated at Whampoa in matsheds is mentioned as having been disfavoured by the labour leaders. On the other hand, the Canton merchants are said to have put forward statements that the labourers should not be allowed in the city, their presence being looked upon in the same light as the unruly military elements of the past.

headline: CAUGHT REDHANDEI
text:
THEFT FROM "EMPRESS"

BAKER CONVICTED.

A Chinese employed as a baker on the s.a. "Empress of Asia" was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with the theft of certain articles of bedding from the cabin of Mr. C. Rimmer, second mate of the vessel.

The arrest of the accused while he was getting away with the property was stated in evidence and he was sentenced to six weeks hard labour.

headline: “FOR VALOUR.”
text:
MEDALS' PRIZIES, ETC.

As announced in Tuesday's "China Mail," the annual inspection of the Hongkong Police by E. E. the Governor, has been postponed till next Wednesday.

This change is of course, due to the weather. As a matter of fact, the refreshments for the subsequent entertainment were being laid out and arrangements completed, when one of the "Mail" reporters was informed of the postponement.

The awards gained during the preceding year are officially distributed at the annual inspection. This year's list comprises:—

King's Police Medal: — Asst. Supt. of Police, Mr. W. G. Gerrard; for prolonged service distinguished by very exceptional ability and merit.

For conspicuous and valuable services rendered during the General Strike 1925:—2nd class, Chief Det. Inspector J. Grand; 3rd class, Det. Inspector Chu Huang; 4th class, Lee-Sgt. (B 126) Khan Mohamed, Lee-Sgt. (C 303) Kwong Yi, Lee-Sgt. (C 296) Wong Sò, P. C. (C 14) Wong Xiao-shing

text:

headline: KARAKHAN TO GO.
text:
CHANG TSO-LINS GRAVE WARNING.

DRAMATIC EXPOSURE

A Mukden (correspondent publishes a report that Chang Tso-lin has requested the Soviet Consul-General here to warn the Moscow Government of the necessity of replacing M. Karakhan, the Soviet Ambassador, Peking, on the ground that "since his arrival in China he has employed bribery to cause student riots and assisted Feng Yu-hsiang with arms in order to create internal strife in China, which actions constituted a misuse of his Ambassadorial position and a violation of international usages."

The Consul-General was further informed that when Peking was occupied by the allied troops M. Karakhan no longer would be considered entitled to the protection of international law.

headline: CHINA'S WARS.
text:
PROTECTION OF FOREIGNERS IN PEKING.

ELIMINATING BOLSHEVISM.

The Superintendent of Police visited the Senior Minister to-day and gave an assurance that, although Tuan Chijul's Government had suddenly been dissolved, the Police authorities would take all necessary measures to protect foreign life and property. It is reported from Hankow that Wu Pei-fu at a conference of his lieutenants, expressed the opinion that Bolshevist influence in China should be eliminated and that the Tariff Conference should proceed in compliance with the people's will.

headline: PASSING THROUGH / CHINESE FOUND WITH DAGGERS.
text:
Defending two Chinese young men charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession of three daggers. Mr. C. A. S. Russ tendered a plea of guilty and pointed out that the daggers (or knives) were in common use in Java for peeling fruit and opening coconuts. He said the men were labourers returning from Java and passing through here on their way to Foochow. He asked for a small penalty as there had been no unlawful intent. To a question by the Magistrate (Mr. R. E. Lindsell), Sergeant Flaherty said the police had no reason to doubt that the men were merely passing through the Colony. Each of the accused was fined

headline: CITY FIRE. / BLAZE AT WELLINGTON
text:
A MORNING CALL

The third floor of No. 162, Wellington Street, used as an enting house, was gutted in a fire which broke out on this part of the building this morning. The flames had secured a good hold when the alarm was received at the Central Fire Station, but the efforts of the fire-fighters to quell the outbreak proved successful after considerable labour.

The inmates of all the floors look to the street on the alarm being given and there were no asualties.

Besides the third floor, which was left with the bare walls standing, the flames worked into a part of the second floor used as a restaurant. The contents of the floors below were damaged by water.

The extent of the damage has not been assessed: It is understood that the building was insured for $4,000.

headline: ACCIDENTS / TWO MOTOR CASES AND A DEATH.
text:
Driving a motor car at Coronation Road yesterday afternoon, Mrs. Geldart, of Torres Building, Kowloon, ran into a Chinese girl who came from the rear of a bus. The girl received injuries to the face and was taken by Mr. Geldart in her car to the Kowloon Hospital and later to the Kwong Wah Hospital. On inquiries being made by the police after a report was made, it was found that the girl had been removed by her people after receiving attention.

At 2.30 this morning a motor bus ran into two ricsha coolies at Gascoigne Road, necessitating the removal of the men to the Kwong Wah Hospital. The driver of the bus has been detained.

While sitting over the edge of a Taikoo Sugar Refinery lighter lying alongside the wharf at North Point, a member of the crew dropped into the water at 7 o'clock this morning.

The coxswain heard the call "man overboard" and promptly threw a rope. An attempt was made by the unfortunate man to reach the rope, but failing in this he was carried away by the strong current flowing at the time and lost.

headline: PROTEST "STRIKE."
text:
HOIHOW MERCHANTS AGAINST PICKETS

BOYCOTT BOYCOTTED

A boycott has been declared by the merchants of Hoihow against the pickets, who are maintaining the anti-foreign boycott at that port.

As a matter of fact, the commercial interests have suspended operations against what they consider to be the high-handed action of the local boycott committee.

This Monday, a foreign steamer (said to be the "Mingsang") was in port. A junk, loaded with poultry for export, was making for the ship when pickets—vigil

ance having been increased on the steamer's arrival—gave chase. Rather than let the goods fall into the hands of the pickets, the shippers' fokis threw most of it overboard. As the birds were in baskets in crates, some of the

abandoned poultry was retrieved. At any rate, one foki was arrested. He was sentenced by a "committee of cargo, investigation-tion" to be marched, in shame, around the town, as a lesson to others.

The mercantile bodies considered the punishment too harsh. Business organisations decided that doors should be closed in protest.

Several hundred men are also reported to have marched to local government offices to petition redress.

A subsequent incident was the capture of one of several lecturers (or street speakers) sent out by semi-official authorities. He fell into the hands of a crowd but was rescued by the action of boycott pickets, who took into custody a bad character.

headline: RICSHA MISHAP. / WHEEL AND AXLE PART.
text:
COOLIE INJURED

A peculiar accident occurred at Bonham Road yesterday as Dr. W. B. A. Moore, of the Victoria Hospital, was riding in a ricsha. One wheel of the vehicle dropped out and the coolie was knocked down to the ground by receiving a prod on his side with a portion of the shaft.

Dr. Moore was not hurt and escaped with a mere shaking. The coolie was struck in the region of his spleen and also received abrasions to the right ankle.

headline: BUNGALOW THEFT.
text:

Mr. Takeuchi, who is the manager of the Osaka Shosen Kaisha reports that the money and jewellery were left in a box, which is also missing. The theft occurred between 11 p.m. on Wednesday and 6 o'clock the next morning.

With the detection of the theft a chair coolie in the house was found to have disappeared. Suspicion rests on this man.

text:
That he is believed to have acted under orders by the Canton Government in coming to Hongkong, in connection with the negotiations to end the present boycott, is stated by the local vernacular papers regarding the visit of Dr. Giri Tzafling.

Dr. Lam is described in the Chinese report as the Deputy Superintendent of Customs (Canton). headline: PASSENGERS HELD TO RANSOM? / OVER 80% CAPTURED
text:
Over eighty passengers are alleged, in the "Kung Sheung Yat Fo," to have fallen into the hands of boycott pickets in Chinese territory near Macao, for whom ransoms were demanded.

After a running duel in waters near Chin Shan, a native boat was captured. Several kinds of weapons were used in the fight, it is stated, including machine-guns and cannon. The boat was ultimately boarded by pickets who took all the passengers to their depot. There, the report continues, they were made to communicate with their relatives, making that sums of money, varying from $80 to $120, should be paid to bring about their release.

headline: REFORMATORY FOR STREET
text:
With a number of Clubs in the place, why not a Hongkong Street Urchins Club?

The idea has been furnished by the receipt of a report from the Ceylon Police who have instituted such a movement in Colombo with satisfactory results. "As an experiment a Club on similar lines has been started by the Hongkong Police and barely two weeks old; it promises to be a permanent one in making useful citizens of the waifs and strays in the Colony.

Well might the boys say "We are Seven", for that is the present membership of the Club. Details gathered show that their ages vary from 14 to 16 years, while residence in Hongkong since leaving the various Chinese districts from which they had all count from one to seven years. All but one lad who states he has a father in the country are without parents. During this period they have lived in the streets and carries on a miserable existence on the proceeds of pilfering and hawking.

Clad in navy blue suits provided by the Poor Box funds in place of the rags in which they were found in the streets, the boys attract considerable attention while engaged in their new occupation of selling Chinese newspapers. With the confidence born of their new environment, they are happy and keen on their work. At present the boys are provided with a room above the Central Magistracy. They are supplied with soap and towels and one of the stipulations is that they have a bath every day. Facilities are given to take part in games while otherwise free from their work of selling newspapers in the mornings and afternoons. Already a football has been supplied and the boys often engage in a little game on the compound. Arrangements have also been made with a school at Cochrane Street to teach them English and Chinese during their leisure hours at moderate fees to be borne by the boys themselves. Although the wages earned at present make the boys self-supporting, it is hoped to find more remunerative employment for them later. They provide their own meals and pay 25 cents each a month as rent, this sum being placed to a fund for their benefit. Two have already started to save money, their savings bank books shewing sums of $1 and 40 cents. Membership is secured on expressing a desire to join, but candidates must be physically fit and prove that they are bona fide waifors strays. Sergeant Nolloth, in charge of the hawkers' department, presides over the Club and when more roomy quarters have been secured for the members they will be looked after by a responsible officer who would reside in the place. The main idea is to eliminate petty crime among juveniles and this seems to be gradually achieved by the formation of the Club.

headline: COURT NEWS: / AN ASSORTED LIST OF

Several cases engaged the attention of the Kowloon Magistrate this morning, the majority of them being prosecutions under the muzzling law which in the case of several Chinese were met by fines of $2

headline: 100 TON BOULDER
text:
CRASH FOLLOWS BLASTING FATALITY.

A serious accident occurred on Saturday afternoon during blasting operations on the hillside behind the market at Tai Hang in the Causeway Bay district.

Six charges had been put in and when five of these had exploded, a piece of rock loosened by the vibration from the spot where the sixth charge was placed rolled down the hill. The coolies took this as a sign that all the explosions were over and came out of their hiding places. In the explosion which followed one coolie was killed on the spot and two others severely injured by flying fragments.

Sub-Inspector Field immediately ordered the cessation of work as it was seen that a large boulder threatened to come down any moment. The contractors' coolies occupying the matshed at the foot of the hill were also advised not "stay there overnight, and about 40 of them quickly gathered their be- longings and spent the night elsewhere. This was fortunate as the expected crash came at 7:30 yesterday morning. The boulder, weighing about 100 tons, took a part of the matshed away and completely demolished two new buildings under construction, the property of Mr. Cham Kai of the "South China Morning Post."

headline: GENERAL STRIKE CERTAIN.
text:
The usual Sunday calm was varied by a succession of meetings of political and labour leaders striving to effect a settlement of the coal crisis.

In the morning a ninety-minute meeting of the Cabinet Council was held.

Meanwhile the General Council of the Trade Union Congress was sitting at Headquarters.

The significant announcement is made that the Miners' Executive has been telegraphically recalled from the district.

headline: Basis of Negotiation?
text:
The Cabinet set from five to seven o'clock when it summoned the Trades Union Congress Negotiating Committee This development is held to indicate that a basis of negotation has been found.

The ponderous machinery in connection with the strike is gradually gaining momentum. The Food Commissioners have arrived at their posts. The National Union of Railwaymen has formulated regulations for the running of milk trains.

The Railway Companies have received notices terminating employment to-morrow.

headline: Germans Pleased.
text:
The developments in the British coal mine dispute are being watched most interestedly in Germany.

German mine owners, who were recently suffering from British competition, are pleased at the prospect regarding their share of the world's coal trade wrested from them by British mines.

The leaders of the Socialists and Communist Parties are urging the German miners to do their utmost to help their British colleagues. They think that they will be able to prevent the direct transport of coal from the Ruhr to Great Britain; and are negotiating with the Dutch Labour Unions with a view to preventing German coal reaching Great Britain via Holland.

headline: Not Too Late.
text:
The General Council of the Trade Union Congress has issued a manifesto declaring, inter alia, that even now an honourable settlement can be reached but the Government's demand to the miners' leaders to consent in advance of the negotiations to a reduction in wages must be withdrawn. The notices also must be withdrawn to allow the negotiations to proceed without the issue being prejudiced.

The manifesto concludes: There is no shadow of reason why the miners should be locked out or the grave decision of a stoppage allowed to take effect. If it does, then the responsibility will lie with the Government and the owners.

"Daily Mail Suspended." London May 2. The "Daily Mail" is not publishing on Monday owing to a strike of printers, who objected to a leader condemning a general strike. The Editor of the "Daily Mail" refused to alter the article.

What is regarded as a hopeful development in the labour crisis took place late last night when the Negotiating Committee of the Trades Union Congress visited the Prime Minister. Mr Baldwin was accompanied by several members of the Cabinet. It is understood that, in the course of the meeting, a statement was made by the representatives of the Trades Union Congress to the effect that the conclusion of the negotiations was in immediate prospect when a general strike was due to begin at midnight. On Monday the general strike would not be carried out. The meeting, which lasted five hours, adjourned at 120 this morning.

headline: COAL WAR. / FINAL RAY OF HOPE IN THE COMMONS.
text:
General Strike Formally Proclaimed at Midnight.

(1)

In the House of Commons an animated discussion took place on the coal crisis.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer significantly hinted that the Government was prepared to resume the negotiations if the challenge of a general strike was withdrawn.

Mr. J. H. Thomas asked if this meant that the employers notices would likewise be withdrawn, but he did not press for an immediate answer.

A meeting was arranged subsequently between the member of the Cabinet and the Trades Union Congress.

It was announced at 11.30 p.m. that the negotiations had failed. A general strike was proclaimed at midnight.

Notwithstanding numerous conversations between the members of the Cubine and the Trade Unionists in the House of Commons it was announced at 11:30 p.m. that the negotiations had failed. A general strike was proclaimed at midnight.

headline: Majority 200
text:
Com. the Rt. Hon. B. M. Eyres-Monsell (Conservative, Evesham), moved the adjournment of the House, whereupon Mr. Baldwin, who received an ovation from the Ministerinlists, made a statement. He declared that the occasion was one of the gravest on which the House had ever met. He reviewed the difficulties of the coal industry, which were largely due to its own extraordinary machinery for the adjustment of wages. That machinery required radical overhauling, which would be one of the first things that must be tackled when the atmosphere was calmer. The owners and miners must find, or have found for them, some way of managing their own business independently of a Government intervention just like other great industries.

The Risk He Ran Mr. Baldwin dwelt on the risk he ran in negotiating up to the last minute under the threat of a general strike. (Ministerial cheers).

The situation had changed materially on Sunday. Certain overt acts in anticipation of a general strike and involving interference with the freedom of the Press, occurred between 2 and 3:30 o'clock on Sunday (Labourite laughter). That made the continuance of the negotiations impossible. The Government found itself challenged with an alternative Government. Despite Power. He (Mr. Baldwin) did not believe that there had been a thorough-going consultation with the rank and file before this despotic power was put into the hands of a small Executive in London. (Ministerial cheers) This was a gross travesty of every democratic principle. The Labour leaders did not seem to realise that they were threatening the basis of ordered Government

and going nearer to proclaiming civil war than we had been for centuries.

The only light hearts in the country to-day were those which either envied or hated us because they saw our whole democratic freedom entering on a course which, if successful, could be the only substitute for tyranny.

It was not wages but the very freedom of our Constitution that was impelled. Everything for which he had worked and cared for during the past two years had been smashed to bits, but that did not shake his faith or the courage of his aims. (Ministerial cheers).

headline: LABOUR VIEW.
text:
Mr. J. H. Thomas (Labourite, Derby) said that whatever might be the result of the strike anybody was a blind idiot who did not see that the economic facts of the coal position would remain. He did not believe that two per cent. of the population would support a revolution but people involved in the strike might be driven to circumstances that might have all the effects of a revolution with entirely different objects.

"This is not a revolution, but a plain economic industrial dispute." Parliament could force an honourable settlement, and he would make a contribution to that where ever the opportunity offered.

headline: AN APPEAL
text:
Will Government Make One More Effort?

Mr. D. Lloyd George (Liberal), Carnarvon), begged the Government be make one more effort for peace. He said that the members of the Trade Unions Congress who ordered the strike were as little revolutionary as anyone there, and the Government could continue the negotiations without any loss of its rights or position.

He proposed that the miners be asked to open the negotiations and discuss wages, but not to pledge themselves to a reduction in advance.

He added that in the event of the resumption of the negotiations the House would agree to a limited continuation of the subsidy.

headline: NO HOT HEADS.
text:
See Reconstruction Programme

Mr. J. Ramsay MacDonald (Labourite, Aberavon) solemnly asked the members of the House in their hour of trial to raise themselves to a great triumph. He declared that they were faced with a situation the development and end of which none could visualise. If the miners were going to accept a reduction of wages on the programme of reconstruction they must see the programme of reconstruction first.

He respected the Constitution as much as the Conservatives, and whatever their differences they ought not to enter on the dispute with hot hands, but with a determination to do justice.

headline: PARTNERS? / CHANGE
text:
Although "confirmation is lacking, there is no reason to doubt a report, from Canton, that Mr. Wong Ching-wai (erstwhile chairman of the Political Council) has left for Shanghai on a Russian vessel, the declared object of his trip being to go to Mostow to recuperate (after his recent reported illness).

Mr. Wong's departure, if correct, synchronises with the return from Moscow of Mr. Hu Han-min. Before the first big coup of last summer, Mr. Hu had been governor of Kwangtung. When the system of government by commission was set up, Mr. Wong became chief civil politician by reason of his post. It is no secret that Mr. Hu then fell into disfavour with General Chang Kai-shek, who had just reached the head of affairs as the soldier of the hour. About a month or so ago, Mr. Wong was reported to have sought privacy on account of his ill health. Since then he has taken little part, in public at least, in the administration. One of his last acts, it believed, led to the letter to Hongkong, asking for the appointment of three official delegates to meet three Canton officials in strike negotiations.

Rumours have been current that Mr. Wong has not seen eye to eye with General Chang (who is best known as commandant of the Whampoa Cadets).

A gentleman who is well touch with the position would not go so far as to say that General Chang had made overtures to Mr. Hu Han-min to cooperate with him. In his opinion that would be a natural inference as there is no denying that General Chang has the biggest say, directly or indirectly. He did not express any definite view regarding this latest report of political movements. There might be, he said, other reasons for Mr. Wong's departure than disagreement with General Chang and he thought that Mr. Wong's going to Moscow was unlikely to have been influenced by the General's attitude.

It is interesting to note that although an ardent revolutionary and republican long before the fall of the Manchu dynasty in 1911, Mr. Wong Ching-wai has hardly, if ever, been in office, until the death of Dr. Sun Yat-sen, when his leadership (as "President" or "Generalissimo") was succeeded by the form of government by commission.

RAN INTO A WALL

Marine Lake was driving the cycle and Marine Jones occupied the billion seat. On taking a curve in the road, the machine suddenly swerved into a granite wall. The riders were both unsentenced and received severe injuries to the head, hands and neck by striking against the wall.

The cyclists were lying on the road in a helpless condition for some considerable time when a Chinese driving a motor cycle and side-car happened to come along. He promptly attended to the removal of the injured men to the Naval Hospital.

headline: GENERAL STRIKE. / NATIONAL FOOD SUPPLIES REGULAR
text:
YESTERDAY'S POSITION.

Nasty Scenes Reported In Dock Land.

A review of the events of the first full day of the general strike at Home shows that milk and fish trains are arriving in London on scheduled time. The London underground railway and omnibuses are being run by volunteer workers. In the provinces railway services are at a standstill.

Nasty scenes were witnessed in dock, land, East London. hooligans coming into contact with the Police, who were reinforced and made several truncheon charges.

To counter-act the dislocation of the Press the Government has issued a penny paper—the British Gazette—to keep the public fully and correctly informed of all developments and to guide them in their action.

The “Gazette’s” circulation will be raised by means of the unlimited resources of the State until it provides a sure and sufficient means of information and a guide for the action of all British citizens.

The “Guzette” urges the nation to “Be strong; quit yourselves like men.”

The first strike time edition of a regular newspapers to reach Reuter's office was a diminutive copy of the Times consisting of a single sheet of foolscap with typescript on both sides, at the price of two-pence, containing the briefest possible digest of yesterday's developments.

An official broadcast message states that the London milk transport service is working according to scheme, and that long-distance milk and fish truins have arrived according to schedule.

The London Underground Railway and Omnibus Combine notify that they are endeavouring to operate their services with voluntary labour. The extent of working will depend on the number of volunteers.

The trunk railway companies hope to run passenger trains during the day.

Menntiane reports from the provinces show that the services are practically non-existent. The principal stations in Manchester are picketed, but one or two trains managed to leave London termin.

Hundreds of railway clerks and employees in supervisory grades resumed their ordinary duties in Hull after telegraphing to the Executive disapproving...of the strike action.

News from the provinces shows that the strike is being observed in the industries embraced in the Trade Union Congress order, but work is proceeding in others, including the Clyde and Sunderland shipyards, the Northampton boot factories and the Leicester hosiery factories.

A number of potteries have stopped owing to the lack of coal. In Belfast business is being carried on as usual.

H. R. H. the Prince of Wales is proceeding to London by aeroplane to-night.

The Prince of Wales arrived by aeroplane at Croydon from Paris and quietly motored to London.

headline: A Firebrand.
text:
Saklutvala, the Communist M.P., was remanded at Bow Street Police Court till Thursday on a charge of making an inflammatory speech at a May Day demonstration in Hyde Park, in the course of which, according to a detective shorthand writer, he incited the Army to revolt and refuse to fight. He spoke contemptuously of the Union Jack. Sir Travers Humphreys, prosecuting, said that this being the first case in the present situation, the prosecution only required accused to enter into recognisances to be of good behaviour.

Saklatvala was released on bail in two sureties of £100 each. British Gazette.

The Government is publishing a penny newspaper called the “British Gazette.”

The first issue to-morrow will be distributed in the whole London area.

Number one of the “British Gazette,” not exceeding 700,000 copies, published by His Majesty's Stationary Office, consists of four sheets, the inside pages being blank.

It explains its objects as a reply to the strike makers' plan to paralyse public opinion. "Nearly all the newspapers have been silenced by a violent and concerted action, and this great nation is momentarily reduced in this respect to the level of African natives, dependent only on rumours carried from place to place. It adds that in a few days, if this is allowed to continue, rumours will poison the air, and raise panics and disorders, and "carry us to depths to which no sane man of any party or class would care even to contemplate."

headline: ASSAULT ON GIRL.
text:
SEQUEL TO A MOTOR ACCIDENT

EUROPEAN SUMMONED:

Mr. F. P. R. James, of the P.W.D., was summoned before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning for falling to report an accident and with assaulting a ten-year old Chinese girl living at No. 5, Prince's Terrace.

The complainant in the assault summons was represented by Mr. McCallum and Mr. A. O'Donoghue defended in both charges.

Prosecuting in the tram case Sub-Inspector Alexander said the accident took place at Caine Road at 2:30 p.m. on Thursday, but a letter reporting it was only received the following morning. The accused explained from the witness box that he wrote the letter at 4 o'clock the same afternoon and gave it to the chief clerk to send to the traffic office, but the coolie had instead made calls on the way and did not deliver the letter until the following morning. Mr. O'Donoghue said that he was supplied with a copy of the letter shortly after it was written. Under these circumstances His Worship held that the charge could not be maintained and the summons was dismissed.

In the assault case Mr. McCallum said that the accused was riding a motor cycle and there was an accident. A little girl was badly hurt and ran into a shop. Accused followed her there and smacked her on the face for laughing at him. He thought it was unfortunate that, acting probably in anger, accused should have assaulted the little girl who was already suffering from the reaction of the accident.

After the evidence of the girl, accused, made a statement from the witness box. He said that he was proceeding at about ten miles an hour when the girl suddenly rushed across the road. He tried to avoid the accident by swerving, but she was hit by the front wheel. The girl got up and ran into a shop and he also went there to make inquiries. She then grinned at him and he merely flicked his fingers saying she had done nothing clever. He said that his fingers merely touched the girl's head.

Under cross-examination by Mr. McCallum, accused admitted that he wrote a letter to the girl's guardian claiming damages and that he also received a reply, followed shortly after by the summons. Answering another question he said he would have been justified even if he had assaulted the girl, as the accident was caused by her neglect. He had hurt himself, torn his clothing and damaged his machine.

Mr. O'Donoghue submitted that the case was very trivial and there was no evidence for a conviction. He thought the summons was an attempt to extort money by a mild form of black-mail.

Mr. McCallum strongly resented this suggestion and said that the accused did not cut a good figure in the box.

His Worship held he was satisfied that the accused deliberately smacked the girl and fined him

headline: CONDITIONS DIFFERENT.
text:
Second Day's Impressions in London.

Although it was the second day of the strike all the roads to the city were crowded with traffic, chiefly an endless procession of private cars and food lorries, yet the conditions were most different. A twelve mile run yesterday took two hours and to-day one hour.

A number of omnibuses are working on the principal routes, including the London and General, besides independent buses manned by volunteers, even the stairways of these being packed.

There were distinct evidences of regular, although attenuated, train services, both long distance and suburban.

The tubes are partially working. Queues are waiting outside the stations, which yesterday were closed.

People coming to the City by long routes from the suburbs are most good-humoured in spite of the very dismal weather, drizzle, and mist. A novel feature is the posting in windows of broadcast news bulletins, which are surrounded by eager crowds.

headline: Both Sides Satisfied
text:
Both sides are satisfied with the position.

The Government Spokesman today broadcast that the position throughout the country was satisfactory. There was no sign of panic or even of great excitement, and no serious disturbance anywhere. Food supplies were normal, and 12,450 volunteers had so far been enrolled in London. Volunteers are flowing in all over the country.

An announcement is made by the Trade Unions Congress that the response of the workers to the strike call has surpassed expectations. The difficulty of the General Council has been to keep men at work in trades which are “the second line of defence.” Everywhere there is order and good temper. The Council is confident of securing an honourable settlement.

text:
Blue Summer skies on the third morning of the strike found vast crowds going to business in London in a gaymood. "Vehicles were more numerous than ever. But traffic jams were fewer, partly due to the drivers following the back streets hitherto unexplored.

headline: EMERGENCY SERVICES
text:

The London tubes are reopening to-day.

Government reports state that, speaking generally, there is no shortage of food. Apparently there has been little effort to raise prices. In to-day's issue of the strike newspaper, the "British Worker," which is published by the General Council, a reply is made to the statement of the Prime Minister that the Government was prepared to resume negotiations immediately the general strike is called off. The reply states that at this stage, with no knowledge of the subsequent line of policy that the Government intends to pursue, the General Council cannot comply with the Prime Minister's request for the unconditional withdrawal of strike notices. headline: GERMAN AIR CRAFT.
text:
NEGOTIATIONS WITH ALLIED AMBASSADORS

AN AGREEMENT REACHED.

Rugby: May 7.

Negotiations which have been taking place for several months between representatives of the Conference of Ambassadors and the German Government regarding German air craft, resulted in an agreement to-day.

It takes the form of an exchange of Notes with annexes between the Ambassadors' Conference and the German Ambassador in Paris. Texts of the various documents have been initialled, and they will be signed when they are approved by the Governments concerned.

headline: $4,000 GONE?
text:
HAS HE VANISHED?

Entrusted with $4,000 to pay into his firm's account, a shop coolie has been "posted missing" since yesterday afternoon, and the money has not reached its destination.

The accountant of a Chinese firm at No. 105, Queen's Road Central says that he handed the money over at 1:30 p.m. Instructions were given to the foki to pay it to the Wui Loong Bank, also of Queen's Road Central. As he did not return by 3 p.m., inquiries were made, and the police were communicated with. The cash had not been paid in.

headline: Rising From Sea.
text:
Three 60 ton cranes are used for the removal of the blocks to trucks of tremendous strength, their transfer to barges and eventual placement on the scene of the work in the sea. The exact alignment of the wall here is somewhat of a wonder to any but the experts. It rises out of the sea just as if it had been built with all the conveniances of surface construction. Divers have, of course, worked in conjunction with surface workers in this connection.

Prior to the construction of the wall itself, some 200,000 cubic yards of sea surface had to be dredged, a sand trench made and the rubble mound foundation built, finer material gunged to an exact level providing the final top on which the concrete blocks rest. In the dredging, what is believed to be the second biggest dredger in the world was engaged, its ladder still being alongside the reclamation and giving an idea of its enormous capacity. Dredging was carried out over some portions to a depth of 90 feet.

headline: RUSSIA'S HELP.
text:
Further evidence—if such be needed—it Russia's help in Canton agitation is forthcoming from the following "Taps" message, dated MoscoW April 14:

"In response to the appeal for aid issued by the Hongkong-Canton Strike Committee, the Red International of Labour Unions and the Central Council of Trade Unions each made a grant of 10,000 roubles."

The report also gives a list of donations varying from 250 to 5,000 roubles by various workers' unions, "making a total granted by the Russian Unions" of 47,750 roubles.

headline: Aeroplanes on Way.
text: A report from Canton details alleged plans to assist the Canton Government Aeronautical Bureau. Inter alia, the intelligence is that there are nine "fighting 'planes, fitted with bomb devices, machine guns, &c. which will be shipped down from 'ladivostok, on instructions from Moscow." The report also says that there are sixteen expert Russian airmen in the Canton air service at present, the "crack" flying-men getting Gold $200 pay a month each. headline: POSITION UNCHANGED.
text:
OVERCOMING OBSTRUCTION BY PICKETS.

Prime Minister's Message to the Nation.

“Unchanged” is the description in an official communique of the general strike on the sixth day. Obstruction by pickets is being more effectually overcome, and order is being maintained in the inflammable Docks area of London.

In a message to the nation the Prime Minister makes overtures for the resumption of negotiations, a condition of which is that the general strike must be called off. In replying, the Trades Union Congress assert that the coal owners' lock-out notices must also be withdrawn.

Earl Balfour utters a warning against dispossessing the people of their Parliamentary liberties to a minority of extremists who regard the Trade Unions as a political instrument for destroying the industrial system.

headline: Riot at Hull
text:
Hull, May 9. Two constables and 17 civilians were admitted to hospital and 16 arrests made in Hull yesterday when the rioters damaged the trams and buses. Police charges against the mob continued until midnight.

The greatest asonishment and enthusiasm were aroused everywhere along the route yesterday by a convoy of 104 lorries laden with flour, with an escort of sixteen armoured cars, cavalry, and mounted police extending about two miles, which marched from the London Docks to Hyde Park whence the contents of the lorries were distributed to the district where the supplies were very short. Two battalions of guards and 500 volunteers were sent down to the docks on Friday and helped to load the lorries yesterday morning. Large crowds cheered the convoy, the sight being as popular as the Lord Mayor's procession. A Good Spirit. The spirit prevailing throughout the country was exemplified at Plymouth yesterday when a football match was played between a team of strikers and a team of police, the former winning by two goals to 1. The wife of the Chief Constable kicked off. No Acceptance Yet. London, May 9. headline: WELL MAINTAINED.
text:
STRIKERS' ANXIETY.

A Union Secretary Sent to Prison.

"Well maintained" is the Government's description of the situation. The vast machinery set in motion to safeguard the people's supplies of foods and necessaries of life is working marvelously.

Many strikers are betraying anxiety lest they acted unconstituitionally in coming out, and there is now a keen desire to reestablish the dispute on a purely industrial basis.

headline: TRANSPORT IMPROVES.
text:

Motor buses are running on most of the routes, and their capacity is in no way overtaxed. Volunteers are arriving every

Three hundred Cambridge undergraduates went to Hull yesterday to assist in unloading at the docks.

headline: MERCHANTS BANK
text:
Little has been heard of the Chinese Merchants Bank, Ltd., which suddenly closed its doors some time ago. It is now stated that order has been evolved and a first dividend may be paid. So much has been intimated as creditors have been asked to register their claims by the end of this month.

According to rumours in business circles, about 20 per cent. is expected in the first dividend. Anything further will depend on the results of recovery from the Bank's alleged debtors.

It will be recalled that the Bank was interested mainly in the rice trade, with offices at Shanghai, Canton, Saigon and Singapore.

The Canton accounts have not been handed over to the liquidator, it is stated. Representatives of depositors (or creditors), of that branch, together with leading merchants are said to have been recognised—it is not known by what process or authority—as a committee to wind up the affairs at Canton. Therefore, that branch will not come into the general scheme of liquidation.

Popular opinion is that about $800,000 owing to Hongkong creditors—or rather by the Hongkong office—will rank for dividend.

headline: "FRONT UNBROKEN."
text:

It quotes a message from the National Union of Railwaymen declaring that reports that some men have returned to work at different centres has been proved to be entirely without foundation.

It also quotes a message from the Transport Workers Union that all are solid and their spirit wonderful.

The communique adds that the Trades Union Congress has received a message from the Master of Balliol and the Master of Oxford University (sic1) earnestly hoping for the future peace and unity of the country and that nothing may be allowed to stand in the way of an attempt to resume the negotiations. headline: SIGNIFICANT
text:
There was an important development to-night concerning the earlier reports that tentative peace moves were progressing.

A special meeting of the General Council of the Trade Union Congress was hurriedly held this evening.

It was officially stated that the meeting had been held with a view to exploring the position still further in order, if possible, to open the door for resumed negotiations and to keep it open.

Essentially Preliminary

Great excitement prevailed in Eccleston Square this evening. The news of a possible peace move spread rapidly and a considerable crowd collected

The General Council of the Trades Union Congress assembled again at eight o'clock in the evening and was joined by the full Executive of the Miners' federation.

The Executive of the Labour Party were also sitting in an ad joining building.

It is stated unofficially that a definite change in the situation is not likely to occur to-night, and whatever moves are being made are essentially of a preliminary character.

headline: SPECIAL CABINET MEETING.
text:
Following a special Cabinet meeting in the House of Commons, lasting for ninety minutes, Mr. S. Baldwin, Mr. Winston Churchill, the Earl of Birkenhead, and other members of the Cabinet conferred till past midnight at No. 10 Downing Street.

Meantime the General Council of the Trades Union Congress with the Miners' Executive had been sitting for two hours. Then the latter met the Executive of the Labour Party with whom they conferred for over an hour.

It is believed that strong efforts are being made to induce the miners to agree to a basis on which negotiations might be re-opened.

It is even possible that the Cabinet and the Trades Union Congress Council will meet to night. [Note: The foregoing cables arrived after the receipt of those published below.]

headline: CREW REMOVED. / BOYCOTT COMMITTEE INTERFERES.
text:
COAL STEAMER'S PLIGHT.

Because the Canton Boycott committee decided that a foreign ship should carry a crew of their selection, an ocean-going steamer has had to make its way here with only seven officers.

The Norwegian s.s. "Marosa" arrived here at 9 a.m. to day, from Canton. Captain J. Jorgensen reported that his crew had been taken off by the Seamen's Union.

For some time past, the "Marosa" has been on the southern coal trade, plying to such ports as Bangkok and Singapore. She has made two trips to Canton, apparently with coal. Nothing occurred the first time. On this second occasion, the Union crew were not accepted, but the old crew had to leave. Accordingly the steamer made its way down here, there being on board only the captain and six other European officers—both deck and engine room.

headline: ANOTHER SHUFFLE.
text:
LATEST PHASE OF CANTON POLITICS

INVASION FROM NORTH?

Militarists Looking to Land of Promise.

Beyond a persistent rumour, as yet uncontradicted, that Mr. Hu Han-min has left Canton (and may have come down to Hongkong), there is no telling what the latest political developments in South China will be.

Hitherto it has been a struggle for power between the Leftists and Rightists, or rather, the so-called Communists and anti-Communists. A new phase is appearing on the horizon and that is the danger of invasion from the North.

For some time at any rate mystery will enshroud the movements behind the scenes of the Canton political stage. Why Hu Han-min (formerly Civil Governor and leading politician) returned from exile and why he left again so suddenly is not known perhaps but to a few.

This week vernacular papers have published ominous forebodings about what is going to happen in Canton on the fifteenth of this month. This being Saturday of the current week. Why this date should be selected for any outbreak, and how secrecy was not established are other mysteries which baffle the layman.

General Chang Kai-shek is independently the strong man of Canton today. On the one hand he is said to have brought about the expulsion of so many Russians from the Government. Not long afterwards there is talk of Borodin returning, and promises of further material help. Mr. Hu Han-min is alleged to have quarrelled with the soldier of the hour over General Hsu Shung-chi, that broken repd of the Kuomintang Cantonese army, who is now seeking his fortunes elsewhere. Apparently, Hu wished Hsu to return and Chang did not. Danger From Wu Pelfu General Hsu is reported to be seeking a command in the army of Marshal Wu Pelfu, but it is not definite that he has taken the oath of allegiance. headline: PLOT IN GERMANY. / SCHEME TO OVERTHROW REPUBLIC.
text:
BERLIN TO BE ATTACKED.

Plans to Create a National Dictatorship.

Germany is excited over the discovery of a comprehensive plot to overthrow the Republic and the Government and to establish a National Dictatorship.

All Federal and State Parliaments and political parties were to be dissolved; the Capital was to be attacked; von Hindenburg was to retire voluntarily; the Constitution was to be abolished; and the Republican leaders were to be banished.

Ex-Colonel, von Luck, President of the Olympia Club, has been arrested.

GOOD POLICE WORK. (Reuter's Service.)

Dr. Neumann, Burgomaster of Luebeck, was to be Chancellor; Herr Hugenberg, Germany's newspaper king, was to be Finance Minister; and General von Moehl was to be Minister of Defence. The death penalty was to be imposed for every offence against the new regime, and martial law was to be declared all over the country.

The Nationalist journals ridicule the alleged plot.

“WAR” WITH NORTH

Two of Canton's civil officials are now definitely reported to have come to Hongkong together but the very fact of their acting in conjunction renders the situation the more difficult to understand.

It is stated emphatically that Mr. Wong Ching-wai (chairman of the Political Council of Government) and Mr. Hu Han-min (former Governor and another member of the National Government) came down together by the same steamboat in adjoining cabins, with great secrecy.

To day it is almost impossible to say which of these two, or General Chang Kai-shek, favoured Communistic ideas, brought about the previous departure of Russian officials, or their recent return to Canton. headline: POLISH REVOLT.
text:
(Havas Agency.)

Börin, May 12.

It is reported from Warsaw that a military revolt is reported to have broken out in Poland. Officers supporting ex-President Pilsudski are marching to the capital with troops to overthrow the new Government under M. Witos.

Martial law has been proclaimed, and the Government is taking energetic measures of defence.

As the result of a recent agitation some detachments of troops from the region of Rembertow refused to obey the Government's orders. The latter has taken measures to protect the capital and called on the insurgents to submit. The Government claims to be master of the situation.

Precaution of all kinds are being The Cabinet continuously. The Government buildings, bridges, telephone stations, etc., are being guarded with troops with machine-guns.

headline: THREATENED BURST.
text:
Ugly rumours point to impending serious trouble on Saturday. Semi-official sources state that a real attempt will be made to put Communism into force. According to an official who came down yesterday, a number of politicians are expected to leave, possibly for Hongkong, before the week-end, so as to avoid being involved in any outbreak. The story goes that the principal Russian helpers strongly advocate the "nationalisation" of the rice stocks, and native banks in the city, to provide the sinews of the war, for the proposed expedition against the North.

General Chang Kai-shek is said to disfavour such an action at least till the conquest of Kiangsi and Hunan provinces has been accomplished.

The labourers and the farmers—who are enrolled in their own so-called volunteer corps are alleged to be contemplating a monster parade, if not actually a march on Canton, to put Communistic ideas to the test. To prevent disorder, General Chang is reported to have brought thousands of his Whampoa Cadets to the pricnots of the city.

headline: Sir H. Samuel's Intervention.
text:
The cancellation of the strike was largely due to the intervention of Sir Herbert Samuel, who, following conversations with the Trades Union Congress, wrote a letter to-day formulating the conclusions reached and emphasizing that he was acting entirely on his own initiative. He had not received authority from the Government and was unable to give assurances on its behalf.

He expressed the opinion that the proposals embodied in the memorandum were suitable for adoption and likely to promote a settlement of the differences in the 2016 industry.

He promised strongly to be commend Government acceptance when the negotiations were renewed.

Mr. Arthur Pugh replied, 'concurring that the memorandum offered a basis for the renewal of negotiations. He stated that the necessary measures were being taken to terminate the general strike, relying on the Prime Minister's published assurances regarding the steps that would follow, and assuming that during the resumed negotiations the subsidy would be renewed and the lock-out notices to the miners immediately withdrawn.

headline: Mr. Baldwin's Statement.
text:
Mr. Baldwin said that the Trades Union Congress had called at Downing Street and told him that they had decided to call off the strike forthwith. He (Mr. Baldwin) replied to them that it would be the immediate effort of himself and his colleagues to secure the resumption of the negotiations on the mining industry with a view to the earliest possible settlement. He (Mr. Baldwin) would only add to the House that he believed that peace had come and that the victory that had been won was a victory for common sense not for any one part of the country but for the best part of the whole of the United Kingdom. Mr. Baldwin added that it was of the utmost importance that the British people should look not backward but forward. "We should resume the work in a spirit of co-operation, putting behind us all malice and vindictiveness. Discussion Desired. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald said that he was anxious not to commit a breach of the good feeling for which Mr. Baldwin had appealed, but many practical details had to be considered. This necessitated a discussion and he hoped that Mr. Baldwin would make a fuller statement.

Mr. Baldwin replied that he recognised the necessity for a fuller statement as soon as possible, but it was impossible that day. He would keep in touch with Mr. MacDonald.

There was no demonstration on Mr. MacDonald's question and Mr. Baldwin's statement, and after Mr. Baldwin, Mr. MacDonald, and other leaders departed the House proceeded to debate the Merchandise Marks Bill.

headline: OUTBURST AVERTED?
text:
Canton may avert, at the last moment, the threatened outburst which current gossip says is due to-morrow.

Although many things point to opposing sides doing all they can to pit their strength against each other on that fateful day—May 15—it seems that the forces of law and order will prevail.

Supporters of General Chang Kai-shek claim to have unravelled a plot which had as its main objectives—not only the initiation of Communistic creed—but also the overthrow of the present Government and its substitution by reversion to the old form of "Generalissimo headquarters"-cum-Civil Governor, as was the case before the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen left for the North.

Alleged to have been abetted by their Russian “advisers,” the principal agitators are stated to have aroused the wrath of General Chang Kai-shek. The soldier of the hour has issued a stern warning that all attempts to interfere with the fabric of government will be suppressed.

Strikers' Power Disputed. On the Communist side are the so-called labourers and agricultural. But even these are divided. Bodies which have succumbed to "Red" temptation are working for the agitators. Those which have not responded to the overtures, or rather, were not satisfied with the terms, are siding with the "Nationalist" party.

A document has been brought to light, upsetting the equilibrium of the self-styled workers. Whether it is genuine or not remaining to be seen. Briefly, it purports to be a questionnaire by the General Labour Union of all Guilds, sent to the Boycott Committee, and imputing alleged ulterior motives. In plain words, it is—unless it is a forgery—an open challenge to the authority of the boycott chiefs.

In the fourth and fifth police districts, near the Strikers' Headquarters, the police are maintaining special vigilance and searching all pickets for illegal arms.

Cadets March On City General Chang's Whampoa Cadets have already concentrated on the city precincts. It is the presence of these troops which, it is surmised, will have a salutary effect. From what meagre news has filtered through it appears that those who planned the great parade to start Communism will fold their tents and steal away like the Arabs by night. Should it come to open strife, the rabble will be no match for the well-trained and soundly-equipped Cadets. Because of their presence the sponsors may yet forego the pleasure of taking over private property and stocks for the common weal.

Mr. Hu Han-min and Mr. Wong Ching-wai, who are said to have left Canton for Hongkong to avoid being involved in any outbreak, are not now in the Colony. Mr. Hu is reported to have sailed for Shanghai and Mr. Wong is believed to have embarked on a tour of France.

General Chang Kai-shek has warned the leaders of the Communist party that they should on no account plot to the detriment of the Government. He will use all available strength to protect Canton city.

Martial law is very strictly observed in Canton. The military and police have sent out armed patrols. In connection with the threat anent Communism, many rumours are going around the city.

"Workmen in the city are planning for a (general) strike and employees are leaving shops."

The Government has transferred two aeroplanes to the city, to protect traffic on the Yueh-Han Railway (from Canton to Shiu-kwan).—“Wah Tsz Yat Po.”

headline: Attacks on Trade Unions Denounce
text:
Naturally, after the industrial upheaval, Great Britain is taking time to settle down. The Trade Unions are apprehensive lest the employers make harsh conditions on the men resuming, and have given instructions not to resume work till the position has been made quite clear. In a great speech in the House of Commons the Prime Minister revealed how close the country had been to anarchy. He declared that he would not countenance wage reductions or attacks on Trade Unions, although it was inevitable that there should be less employment owing to the derangement of industry caused by the general strike.
