headline: BOYCOTT MUST END.
text:
NORMAL TRADE BEFORE END OF JULY?

"COMPROMISE WITH HONOUR."

In official and unofficial circles in Canton the feeling is growing that the Hongkong boycott not only must be brought to an end, but that the present situation will have been changed back to a basis for normal trade before the end of July—possibly sooner than that. Canton, with a serious northern military venture on her hands, realises the necessity for putting her house in order. She wants to resume normal relations with the rest of the world, and to have, so far as possible, the sympathy and some measure of co-operation of the outside world. This, as much as a change of heart, accounts for the recent overturn against the Communists, for it was realised that the Hongkong trouble could not be settled, and that outside sympathy could not be hoped for, so long as the Nationalist Government could, with any justice, be termed "Red."

"Compromise, with honour," is the way one prominent official defined the terms upon which the Hongkong situation can be ended. More specific terms could not be elicited.

The military campaign is gradually taking shape, and if the Cantonese plans can be pushed to a successful conclusion, the Southern Government will control about one-third of China before winter. Besides the large bodies of soldiers being sent daily from Canton to Sui-kwan, Kwangsi province is sending armies northward, and Kweichau province, though not under this Government, is cooperating with men and supplies. Hunan is to be taken first, then Fukien and then Chekiang provinces. This will leave Kiangsi no choice, but to come in with Canton. The Cantonese officials are also looking confidently for help from Yunnan, all local differences being forgotten in face of the peril of an advance by Wu Pei-fu. Officials here say: Frankly that they had hoped to defer a test of arms with Wu Pei-fu until next year. They wanted another twelve months in which to consolidate their positions here, and in which to raise money, but Wu Pei-fu's declared policies, they say, have

Communists Aggrieved: Meanwhile the Communists and Russians here are not accepting the Kuomintang's new policies with either meekness or satisfaction. They declare that General Chang Kai-shek is developing into another War Lord like Wu Pei-fu, that his "resolutions" against Communism were forced upon the Central Executive Committee by the presence of his soldiers, and that the Kuomintang is now merely a mask for Chang Kai-shek's personal tyranny.

For a day, or two the now famous "eight resolutions" were regarded in some quarters as merely a blind to win back the alienated sympathy of the Chinese living abroad who have done so much to help finance the Canton Government, but now it is realised that Chang Kai-shek means business, and that the Kuomintang must be purged of Bolshevikism.

A Surprise Order.

Last night General Chang Kai-shek sprung in surprise by issuing a military order forbidding the sale of liquor in the cafes along the East Bund, and in the Flower Boat section of the city. This section, usually the refuge of criminals or the politically wary, is to say being combed by soldiers. Many arrests are being made, and virtual martial law is in effect. These measures are being taken because it is said that many discontented Communists took refuge there, and tried to use that section to foment trouble against the Government.

To every one's surprise, Sun was not elected permanent chairman of the Central Executive Committee. That plum fell to Chang Ching-Kiang, a man little known in Canton, but long a zealous Kuomintang worker in other provinces. He hails from Chekiang, General Chang Kai-shek's own province, and his selection is taken as only another evidence of General Chang's present power.

headline: READY FOR WAR.
text:
CANTON AEROPLANES FOR NORTH.

HUNNAN OFFENSIVE

decided to form a military base at Shiukwan (on the North River) Four aeroplanes are being sent there to reconnotre on the boundary with Hunan province. Because General Chang Kai-shek and Dr. C. C. Wu have disfavoured the project, the rertmours of a fantan monopoly have died out.

The delegates of General Tang Sang-che (the militarist who is being pressed south by Wu Pei-fu) have again been sent to confer with Canton on the offensive against Hunan—"Wah Tsz Yat Po."

An engagement is announced in London between Hubert F. Phillips, of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, and Nmid M. Powell, daughter of Dr. Llewellyn Powell, of 10. Duke-street-mansions, W.1.

Now it is the Hospital For The Blind which is in trouble with the strikers. That institution refused to accede to a demand from picketers and Union leaders that the Union be paid $2 per month for every $10 in salaries paid to help though the Union did succeed in making most of the employees' pay tribute of $1 per month for every $10 of pay. Threats are being made of cutting off supplies and boycotting the institution.

It is now a practical certainty that the oil monopoly will be abandoned at an early date. Day after day various Unions and merchants' organisations pass resolutions declaring the monopoly an oppressive policy, and urging its discontinuance

Meanwhile the seizure by pickets of $11,000 worth of Texas Oil Company oil at Kongmoon has brought about a new problem. The oil, which was American property, has been brought to Canton, and urgent representations are being made for its return or for an immediate cash settlement.

Ten more organisations have also passed resolutions "to settle the strike and boycott" against Hong Kong by co-operative effort of workers, merchants and government. These organisations are the Peasant, Labour, Merchant and Student Co-Operative Association, the Canton City Merchants' Association; the Canton Chamber of Commerce, the Merchants' Union Federation, the Canton Merchants Federation, the Kwangtung All-Province Educational Association, All-China Central Labour Union, the Kwangtung All-Province Peasant Union, and the Worker-Peasant-Merchant-Student Union. No Offices For Communists.

Great interest is manifested here as to the official and army heads that will fall as a result of General Chang's resolutions to the effect that members of the Communist Party cannot hold office as heads of bureaus, and can no longer rank even as captains in the army—a lieutenantacy being the highest army rank open to a Communist here in future.

This resolution, it was announced, will be retroactive, which means great changes in the Government offices and in the army, or immediate and wholesale resignations from the Communist Party on the part of present office holders and army officials. It is certain that the “house cleaning” will be thorough, and in the opinion of outsiders who are careful observers, it came none too soon, for the defeat of the “Christian General’s” army at Peking recently was followed by a large influx of Russians and Chinese Communists to Canton, where they had expected a warm welcome.

It now develops that Wu Hon-man, Minister of Foreign Affairs, who "disappeared" from Canton ten days ago just after his return from Russia, is not hiding in Hongkong, as had been reported, but is actually in Shanghai on a secret mission of great importance to the Canton Government. It is thought to have to do with finances, and with the hope that Kangsu and Anwei provinces will help the south against Wu Pei-fu.

headline: CINEMA INCIDENTS.
text:
WITNESS WHO QUARRELLED. WITH UNCLE.

A WORDED APOLOGY.

There was a continued hearing at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday of summonses and crosssummonses in respect of "incidents in the "Star" theatre in which Mr. and Mrs. J. S. Gill, Miss M. T. de Jesus Sequeira, Mesars A. A. Barros, M. Prata, F. Prata and the Misses Beatriz and Celeste Gill are involved.

Mr. M. K. Lo, for Mr. and Mrs. Gill, put it to Miss Sequeira, the original complainant, that she had brought the case in order to get Mr. Gill into trouble and that she had told her friends that as a Government servant he would get into trouble for being in a police court case.

This Miss Sequeira denied and said that she issued the summons because she was assaulted. She had no idea of revenge on Mr. Gill.

Mr. Lo questioned witness as to an apology which Mrs. Gill had made when she had called on Miss Sequeira. Witness admitted that Mrs. Gill made an apology and asked her (Miss Sequeira) not to worry her husband. Witness, however, wanted an apology in black and white and this had not been forthcoming.

Evidence was given by Miss Beatrice Gill bearing on incidents which led up to the alleged striking of Miss Sequeira by Mr. Gill. She admitted that she and Miss Sequeira laughed in the course of the picture presentation but denied that they were laughing at Mr. and Mrs. Gill or that they were kicking the seats.

Witness stated in answer to the Magistrate, Mr. J. H. B. N'hill, that Mr. Gill was her uncle but they had not been on friendly terms for some time owing to trouble. They had not spoken to each other since 1919. The proceedings were adjourned.

headline: UNFAVOURABLE
dateline: London, May 21. Railway Agreement. London, May 21.
text:
COAL MINERS REJECT NEW PROPOSALS.

MINERS' DELEGATES DISPERSE.

The coal miners have sent a reply to Mr. S. Baldwin, Prime Minister, unfavourable to the acceptance of the latter's proposals, at the conclusion of a meeting at which an objection was raised to the suggested legislation providing for a permanent Wages Board, compulsory arbitration, and the assessment of the industry's capacity to pay wages on the basis of the full proceeds of the industry in the March quarter.

Bare Acknowledgment. Meantime the miners' delegates have dispersed and will remain at home until they are recalled. Up to now the miners have received from the Prime Minister only a bare acknowledgment to yesterday's resolution rejecting his new proposals.

Owners' Arguments. London: May 21.

The owners' reply declares that Mr. Baldwin's proposals will not be helpful toward increasing the efficiency of the industry. On the other hand, it is impossible to continue to conduct the industry as a private enterprise unless it is accorded the same freedom from political interference as is enjoyed by other industries. The owners demand a period of freedom from industrial unrest and political interference, when they guarantee that throughout the industry there will be a systematic effort toward development and progressive improvement.

The owners urge the restoration of the eight-hour day to reduce production costs, declaring that if this is accepted the reduction in wages will not exceed ten per cent.

At a meeting of the Railway Companies and the Railway Unions arrangements were arrived at for the suspension of the guaranteed week, thus enabling the Companies to spread out the work and remove the post-strike difficulties.

headline: LOOKING AHEAD.
text:
CANNONS PLANS TOWARDS PROGRESS

BORO DIN SPEAKS OUT.

Notabilities & Their Latest Proposals

From Our Own Correspondent.)

After eight consecutive days of long sessions, the extraordinary session of the Central Executive of the Kuomintang came to an end today with a session which lasted from 9:30 a.m. until nearly 3 p.m. The surprise of the last day's meeting was the announcement that Mr. Wu Han-min said to begin Shanghai on an important mission, is in reality on a "long leave of absence," and that Mr. Eugene Chen has been given a temporary appointment to his office of Secretary of Foreign Affairs. Mr. Chen, formerly editor of the "Canton Times," which has been suspended by the "Canton Gazette," is known as a forceful writer, but in his earlier journalistic days here was always markedly anti-British in sentiment. He has recently returned from the North having left after Peking had fallen into the hands of Wu Peifei and

The next session of the Central Executive Committee of the Ku-mintang will be held in mid-August. Normally that body meets only twice each year, but the meeting just closed was a special session to consider the status of the Communists.

headline: C. C. Wul's Suggestions.
text:
To-day's closing session of the Central Executive Committee of the Kuomintang was marked by the introduction of two resolutions by Dr. C. C. Wu, both of which were passed.

The first declares that a definite policy and method must be found for the future development and standing for both the Peasant and Labour movements, and recommendations that such policy and method be worked out by the Standing Committee of the Kuomintang. This committee has nine members, and is almost continuously in session between meetings of the Central Executive Committee.

The other resolution sponsored by Dr. Wursays that there are "certain theoretical and controversial points concerning which the Kuomintang has as yet reached no decision, and that these should be referred to a special committee for study and for reporting upon to the next National Congress of the Kuomintang."

This National Congress, which will be held in November, probably in Canton, will attract delegates from all over China, from America, and from every other place where the Kuomintang has members in good standing. The committee will meanwhile study abstract questions like the "Class Struggle," and will hew out party platform planks or planks for submission to the National Congress for adoption, amendment or rejection.

headline: STORE BURGLARY.
text:
POLICE SEARCH FOR "SWAG" FROM

NOT "PIONEER" PEARLS.

Clues in the recent silk store burglaries in the centre of the city are still being followed up by the Criminal Intelligence Department, but a raid for pearls, during the week-end, proved unsuccessful.

Jude ornaments and other jewellery were included in the "swag" taken by the robbers from the two firms in China Building, viz., the Popular Silk Store and the Pioneer Silk Store.

During the week-end, detectives visited a Chinese flat in Lyndhurst Terrace, where a pearl necklace and another set of pearls worked out in the design of a flower, were found. It was suspected that these might be connected with the recent burglary at the Pioneer Store.

Explanations were given by the Chinese couple in whose possession the pearls were found. A sister of the husband, living at Yaumatti, bore out the man's statement that she had loaned them to him. Bona fides were established and the "clue" proved to be false alarm.

As far as is known, there has been no trace of any of the “swag” having found its way into the open market.

"Mr. James Younge Mackintosh, who rode "Wild Man From Borneo," the winner of the Aintree Race in 1995, is on a visit to Hongkong and hopes to be present at Fanling Hunt Steeplechases this afternoon. It is unlikely that he will be seen in the saddle as he has done little riding on the flat or across country since the victor of "Wild Man From Borneo," 21 years ago.

Borodin's approval of the Kuomintang's new policy of conciliation and of settling as quickly and advantageously as may be outstanding vexatious problems, such as the Hongkong boycott, the oil monopoly dispute, and other pressing problems which must be adjusted so that the government can give undivided time and effort to the Northern campaign.

headline: A General's Opium
text:
War preparations go on apace, the last two days having seen the shipment of 1,100,000 cases of ammunition to Shiukwan. The Government has also announced that for this campaign no coolies will be conscripted. Coolies, of whom 1,500 are needed at once, will be paid $1 per day, with a food allowance of 60 cents per day. This new policy is proving very popular with the coolie class here.

The School for the Blind is still operating, in spite of threats by strikers to close the institution, but to-day it was placarded with notices that "action" will be taken if servants are engaged further without permission of the union. To-day the home of General Chu Pui-tak, commandant of the third Yunnanese Army, was searched by police and soldiers, who report finding three casks of opium, which the official version says were seized. The general is absent.

headline: Trouble Over Sports.
text:
Threats of the students and pupils of many schools and colleges to quit the big annual inter-schools field meeting here, if the Canton Christian College was permitted to enter athletes, have come to nothing. To-day the Canton Christian College had all of its competitors there, and won many events.

Yesterday it was reported that if the prescribed team entered the grounds they would be stoned, and then eight large schools sympathising with the College threatened withdrawal from the meeting if conciliation were not effected. Such a withdrawal would have cut the attendance so seriously that the gate receipts would not have paid expenses, so the Canton Christian College, which usually wins the meeting, was permitted to enter its team under an assumed name. Opposition to the College entry was because of the recent expulsion of three radical students.

The meeting, which will continue until Wednesday, is the largest ever held in South China, 91 schools and organisations being represented by more than 1,100 young athletes, of whom about 400 are girls.

headline: STRIKE PICKETS
text:
PATROL BOATS COME NEAR

INCREASED ACTIVITY.

Several boats used by the Canton boycott picRets for patrol, are reported to have come close down to Hongkong during the week end.

They are stated to have left Canton and called at the Chinese Maritime Customs station at Tai Chaam, a landmark at the mouth of the "River which is close to Hongkong waters.

From Tai Chaam, this fleet of fast boats is said to have turned towards Macao, to scour the waters of Heungshan district. The report also says that the pickets in the boats delivered a formal message (?) to somebody at the Customs station. On nearing Macao, the boats took up various stations where

headline: Caught a Tartar.
text: Eight pickets: who "caught a tartar" and fell into the Macao police hands have now been released. They were connected with the seizure of the Hong Kong steam-launch "Wikins." This launch was towing a cargo junk to Macao when interfered with. Both the "Wikin" and the junk have since been restored, thanks to timely intervention by the Macao water police. Of the eight pickets arrested, four were released and the other four handled over to the Chinese authorities, it is stated.

headline: EMPIRE DAY. / OFFICIAL OBSERVANCES TO-MORROW / SPECIAL SERVICES
text:
There are no official observances of Empire Day to-day but to-morrow a united services at which local schools will be represented will be held at St. John's Cathedral at 9 a.m., the Bishop, the Rev. C. R. Duppuy, being the speaker.

A commemoration service for the Catholic schools of Hongkong will be held at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception' at 9 a.m. to-morrow.

The Very Rev. Fr. G. M. Spada, Pro-Vicar Apostolic will officiate, assisted by the clergy and the students of the Cathedral Seminary.

The order of service will be:

(Pupils of the Italian Convent). 2.—“Mile volte benedetta”

headline: DRAMATIC ESCAPE.
text:
SENTENCED SOLDIERS' 24 HOURS' LIBERTY.

ARRESTED IN KOWLOON

After over twenty-four hours of liberty, two Surreys' private who escaped from Murray Barracks guard room at midday on Saturday under somewhat dramatic circumstances were recognised yesterday afternoon in Kowloon by a police officer who arrested them. They were later handed over to the military authorities. From the rather meagre details that have leaked out it appears that the three men had been duly tried by court-martial—one (Private Kebble) on a charge of alleged attempted suicide, whose sentence was six months, and the other two, (Privates Arnold and Barker) on charges alleging disobedience and striking their superior officer, they being sentenced to twenty-eight days' detention.

headline: "To Seek To Find"
parent_headline: EMPIRE DAY. / SPECIAL SERVICES AT THE CHURCHES.
text:
All this feels us, continued the Bishop, of the height to which man's spirit can rise. The stones which had been placed in memory of those who did not return cried out to us to set ourselves a hard task just as the memorial to Capt. Oates, of Southern expedition fame, bade us "to seek, to strive, to find and not to yield."

As one stood by the tomb of the Unknown Warrier and noticed nearby the memorial to David Livingstone, one read "Here rests David Livingstone, missionary, traveller and philanthropist. For 30 years his life was spent in unwearied effort to evangelise the native races, to explore the undiscovered secrets, to abolish the devastating slave traffic in Central Africa." His memorial was not only a sign of the unconquerable spirit of this Scottish hero but the words "brought by faithful hands over land and sea" were a sign of the brotherhood of brave men throughout the world as shown by the action of the faithful African carriers who had borne his embalmed body through jungle and over river on a nine months journey, leaving his heart buried in the land to which he had given his labours.

Similar records of hard tasks undertaken for the benefit of humanity were to be got from the lives of the Northumbrian boy, George Stephenson, who persevered for 30 years in the face of unbelief and eventually bestowed on man the steam engine; Wilberforce, who set himself to abolish the slave traffic; Shaftesbury who worked for the improvement of factory conditions; and, more than anyone else, that little boy who used to wander among the ships at Taraus, Paul the dauntless, missionary of Jesus Christ. His motto was "run to win."

In conclusion, he would remind his hearers, said the Bishop, that the lesson to-set oneself a hard task was but incompletely learned unless one combined with a determination to work together in team work. Bruce did not only ask himself "is this man a good climber?" when he chose his men for the Everest climb. He had to ask himself "is this a good team worker who will get on with the other." The result of his choice was that everyone of the party was out to help the other man, not to grab what he could for himself. Odel might very well have asked himself why to him had been assigned the support work when he might have had a chance to participate in the supreme effort but he had carried

a brave effort to rescue those to whom had fallen the lot he would gladly have undertaken.

You have heard the story of brave men, said the Bishop in conclusion. You have seen them shoulder heavy. burdens and face countless difficulties. You are on the threshold of life and I ask you to bear in mind that even the best men cannot get near their best ideals without the love of Christ. It is this which is going to take away strife and discord amongst nations. You must play the game here and fight to win. All of you be players in God's name.

Roman Catholic Service.

At the Roman Catholic Cathedral, the attendance of school children filled the church to overflowing. The Cathedral was decorated with drapery and fresh flowers. The Rev. Father Spada gave the address, the celebrant being Father L. Banchlo assisted by Father Rossi, Father Granelli and Seminarlans. Father Riganti and the choir. The Rev. Father Spada said: As he customary on this day we have come together into this sacred office to give us only meet and fitting's religious significance to this annual civil festival.

headline: GOING HOME / TWO POLICE OFFICERS LEAVING.
text:
ONE ON RETIREMENT.

Two police officers are booked to leave the Colony by the P. and O. "Melwa" on Saturday. Acting Chief Inspector W. Kent, who was in charge of transport during the recent strike, leaves on a well-earned furlough which he has curtailed to one of six months. He is accompanied by his family and will be back in November.

headline: A Distinguished Record.
parent_headline: GOING HOME / TWO POLICE OFFICERS LEAVING.
text:
Sub-Inspector C. McNab Wilson, the other officer leaving this week on furlough prior to retirement, has a distinguished record of local and war service.

Leaving the Royal Garrison Artillery, Mr. McNab Wilson joined the Hongkong Police in January. 1910 as a constable. He was a lance-sergeant at the time he volunteered for war service, and after his return he received a promotion in February 1920, being made Sub-Inspeet or in June of the following year.

In December of the same year, Mr. McNab Wilson was commended by His Excellency the Governor for courageous performance of his duty on the occasion of an attack by a hostile mob in which he arrested one man. He was further commended in March 1912 for saving the life of a Chinese woman who missed her footing and fell into the harbour.

Whilst on war service, Mr. McNab Wilson was mentioned in despatches in August 1916. In October 1917 he was granted a commission as 2nd-Lieutenant in the R.G.A., and on September 28, 1918 he reached his crowning achievement, being awarded the Military Cross for conspicuous gallantry and devotion to duty. Mr. McNab Wilson received the decoration from His Majesty the King at Buckingham Palace on May 29, 1919.

The departing officer also held the position of musketry instructor for a short time and was a reputed rifle shot in the force. He has also represented the Colony in interport rifle meetings.

Mr. R. B. Salisbury arrived in the Colony to-day from Manila by the "Empress of Russia."

headline: BOYCOTT PICKETS. / PERSECUTE MISSION UP. COUNTRY.
text:
GODOWN BROKEN INTO

(Krom Our Own Correspondent.) Pakkal, Kongmoon, May 15

Canton boycott pickets are still interfering with the local Presbyterian Mission. The employees of the hospital have been persecuted and the preacher at the church has come in for unwelcome attention.

Chiu Yan-po, head of the Merchants (Protective). Preventive Bureau, together with a number of pickets, broke into the Texas Oil Co.'s godown at Kongmoon, taking away 5,000 cases of kerosine and some personal effects. A foki of the Co.'s native agent was arrested, on a charge of alleged smuggling of kerosine (in contravention of the Canton Government's oil monopoly) and other stuff (said to be of an explosive nature), which the pickets maintain were found in the godown. The native agent has appealed to the local Chamber of Commerce for assistance. But without result.

headline: The Accounts
text:
Turning to the accounts for the year 1925 you will observe that the balance of Working Account amounted to $1,139,176.19 being a decrease of $242,761.18 compared with the preceding year. The balance of Profit and Loss Account (notwithstanding the fact that the amount brought forward was $34,000 greater in 1925 than in 1924) shews a decrease of $420,969.73. The main items of increased expenditure in the Profit and Loss Account are as follows:—

Maintenance and Repairs by..... 48,000 Depreciation by..... 40,000 and Rents, Rates and

The increase in Bank interest is naturally accounted for by the fact that due to the financial stringency in the third quarter of 1925, our capital issue, in common with that of other concerns, did not meet with the support that under normal conditions would have been forthcoming. Therefore we had perforce to resort to other means in order to finance our commitments and it is due to the facilities granted by our Bankers that we were enabled to pursue, without interruption on account of finance, the constructional programme upon which we had embarked in connection with the Peninsula Hotel.

Turning to the Balance Sheet you will observe that the items "Land" and "Buildings" have increased by $2,820,000 which is in the main accounted for by the acquisition by the Company on favourable terms of the reversionary interest in the Palace Hotel, Shanghai (to which reference was made in the speech from this Chair last year). As a result, the item "Leasehold Properties" has been eliminated from our Balance Sheet and in pursuance of our policy we are now the owners of freehold property in respect of all the establishments we operate.

The year which has passed since our last General Meeting has been, as you are probably only too well aware, one presenting unprecedented difficulties to practically every business concern of this Colony and it would be superfluous, therefore, for me to labour this point. The unsettled situation created by the disturbances of the month of May resulted in a serious set-back in our turnover in the Northern port but Shanghai recovered quickly, as reflected by our revenue figures which, I am pleased to say, she won an appreciable increase in most departments; and, whilst on this point, it appears to me opportunity to emphasise that the action of your Company in acquiring the Hotels in Shanghai has proved a source of very considerable strength to the Company and is more than justified by the results, for since the amalgamation effected with The Shanghai Hotels, Ltd. at the end of 1923, the Company has been placed in a position where- under it is not nearly so vulnerable as would be the case if its interests were concentrated in one place. In Hongkong, as the employer of a large staff, the Company was naturally seriously affected by the strike which occurred towards the end of the second quarter of last year, nevertheless, I am pleased to state that we were enabled to carry on the essential services of our establishments; and in fact the Hongkong Hotel, due to its central position, was called upon to supply more meals per day than would have been the case in normal times — although I must add, en passant, that little or no profit accrued to the Company in this respect, our primary object, as a semi-public utility undertaking having been to meet the needs of the community at rates as reasonable as possible in the exceptional circumstances then obtaining. Towards the end of the year the new native staff which had been secured had to some extent been trained in the requirements of our various departments, and generally speaking, the business of our hotels in Hongkong was running smoothly. Our new Garage at Happy Valley, Hongkong, was completed and put into service in June 1923.

headline: CANTON DOINGS.
text:
ANOTHER RED OFFICIAL TO LEAVE. LATEST WAR MOVES. Echo of Shakee Incident, Last Year.

A third official head, is soon to fall, for official announcement will soon be made of the “resignation” of Lam Chu-ham, chairman of the Agriculture Department. This stepping out of office, which will follow the resignations of the heads of the organisation and propaganda departments, announced yesterday in the “China Mail,” will be the third definite result of the famous “eight resolutions” of General Chang Kai-shek which bar Communists from high places in the Government and from commissions higher than lieutenancies in the Nationalist Army.

Lam Chu-ham, it is understood, protests "with some vehemence that he is not really a Communist, but nevertheless he will soon have a successor.

Reports in the Press that Foo Ping-sheung, Commissioner for Foreign Affairs for Kwangtung province, may soon resign, are incorrect. He will not give up his portfolio at this time. Mr. Foo's resignation, had it been submitted, would have had no relationship to the Government's Communist house-cleaning.

headline: Big Military Camp.
text:
To-day, the Tenth and Eleventh divisions of the Fourth Army left here for Shiukwan, the northern end of the Yueh-Han Railway, to reinforce the defeated troops which have been retreating southward to the Kwangtung border. It is announced that Shuen Chow, in Kwangsi, will be made the main military and ration supply base for the Nationalist forces in Kwangsi province.

Noon of June 4 has been set as the time for a monster mass meeting of the Unions and Kuomintang organisations of Canton at which sympathy will be expressed for the striking miners of Great Britain. The meeting will be held at the Kwangtung University parade ground; and every organisation represented will be taxed $5. In addition, a popular subscription for the British miners will be launched on that day.

headline: China / PLANS OF WAR.
text:
TALK ABOUT TAKING CANTON.

The Kuomintang Nationalist Government of Canton is not planning all hopes in its fight against Wu Pei-fu solely upon the prowess of the armies of Kwangtung and Kwangsi provinces. Instead, the military and government leaders here are nourishing a not entirely impracticable hope that the summer will witness a tremendous thrust southward by the reorganised Kuominchun armies (of the "Christian General".)

The plan is to rally the southern Nationalist forces for a push north, and for the Kuominchun, after winning Shansi province, to cut down through Shensi and the rich eastern provinces, through Kweichau province, and so make a Junction with Chang Kai-shek's Canton forces in Hunan or Kwangsi. An ambitious plan, but one not impossible of accomplishment, particularly if the Kuominchun can continue to win against Wu Pei-fu sufficiently to cause a withdrawal of south-bound armies, and so give Canton a breathing space.

There is one fly in the ointment. The Kuominchun is admittedly being munitioned from Russia. What will they be willing to do for Canton if the movement to oust Communists from Nationalist government positions continues to be pressed?

The Enemy's Secrets. Meanwhile the Nationalist Government claim to have discovered the details of Wu Pei-fu's plan for an advance against the South, which "includes many stray strategies and treasons. The announcement of this plan, as given out here to-day, follows:

Generals "Chan Kwing-ming, Ngai Bong-ping, Lin" Fu, Tang Chi-yao and Ma Tsi are said to have been chosen to head the movement in Kiangsi against Kwangtung and the Kuomintang. Of these the second, Ngai Bong-ping is rather popular in Canton. He was at one time chief of police, and about one year agb scornfully refused the post of Mayor, now held by Dr. C. C. Wu. When he was offered the job he is said to have replied that he would not have it as a gift, because the Government was dominated by Reds.

Wu Pei-fu's plan is detailed as planning to attack Kiangsi and Hunan, then to appoint Tang Yui-tsu as commander-in-chief in Kiangsi and drive Fang Poon-yan out of that province. This portion of the plan has already been worked out.

Subsequent steps are to include helping Ip Hoi-yun to overthrow Tong Shang-chi in Hunan and make Ho Yiu-tso Hunan's commander-in-chief. This plan is now, apparently, working with great success.

The next step is said to be to attack Kwangsi; to help Lin Fu, Shen Hung-ying, Ma Tsi and Lau Taun-wan to recall their old troops and to invade Kwangsi by way of Kweilin and Liuchow; to get Tang Chi-yao to send his troops to Kwangsi by way of Pakshek, and to order Yeng Kwun-yu, Lau Chiluk and other local leaders to collect their old soldiers scattered in southern Klangsi, and to ask Chan Kwing-ming and Ngai-Bong-ping to gather bandits and volunteers from the three big rivers, of Kwangtung and to declare war against the Nationalist Government. This would make it impossible for Canton to send help to Kwangsi. Ammunition, rifles and field guns will be sent from Hankow, Chen Kin-min will find money for the five provincial armies, and Lau Taun-wan will go to Yunnan to persuade Tang Chi-yao to cooperate with Wu Pei-fu. headline: Jहाஜி / THE MISSING MAN.
text:
SPOTTED BY FORESTER..

A sensation was caused at the Central Magistracy this morning during the hearing of a charge of unlawful possession of camphor wood against two women from Shaukiwan when a Chinese spectator from the body of the Court was taken into custody by a forest guard. He was identified as the man who escaped at the time of the raid on Saturday morning.

A pathetic circumstance mentioned in Court was that since the arrest of the two women a three-year old son of one of them had accidentally fallen from a verandah and was in a serious condition in hospital. In view of this the prosecution did not press the case and the woman was leniently dealt with by a fine of $15. The other woman who had been fined $50 for a similar offence recently was fined $100, or eight weeks' hard labour.

When the man arrested inside the Court was subsequently charged with being concerned along with the women in the removal of wood, he claimed to be a victim of mistaken identity. Evidence was given of his escape during the raid, and on his own admission that he was a friend of the unfortunate woman in the case he was found guilty and fined $75, or six weeks' hard labour.

headline: INGRATITUDE.
text:
CHINESE YOUTH ROBS HIS MASTER.

AN INCORRIGIBLE ROGUE.

A gold wristlet watch and a tongue scraper which had been converted into a wrist-band-found on the person of a Chinese youth arrested at a tea house were identified as part of property stolen from the residence of Dr. Kew, No. 47, Wong Nei Chong Road.

The youth pleaded guilty to a charge of larceny before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Defendant was formerly employed under Dr. Kew to look after the dogs and this enabled him to enter the house and steal articles from time to time.

Dr. Kew said that he had done quite a lot for the boy in an endeavour to make him good, but he persisted in robbing him even after running away from the house. He asked that defendant be given a flogging and then banished.

His Worship remarked that flowing was not provided for offence of this nature and sentenced defendant to six months hard labour.

headline: COMMUNISTS GO.
text:
The Nationalist Army has been absolutely purged of Communists, and because of the drastic action taken against Reds in the land forces, the Communists of the Navy are rapidly resigning or producing evidence that they no longer belong to the Communist Party.

Many months ago, when General Chang Kai-shek was a "mystery man" and when his attitude on Communism was not known, the Kuomintang voted to put a "party observer" in every army office, in every company of the army, and on every ship of the navy. These men were really known spies. In the navy in particular these "observers" often incited the men to disobey orders from their superiors.

To-day it is announced that all Communist "observers" have been weeded out of the Nationalist armies from the First to the Sixth Armies, inclusive, and that those in the Navy are resigning pell-mell. Even Chan Kung-pak, head of the Peasant-Labour Bureau, long known as a Red, has turned violently and vocally anti-Communist.

In short, to day the Communists here are reduced to working secretly and by subterfuge, just as the anti-Communists worked before General Chang Kai-shek took his stand against Bolshevism and the Russian on May 15. Whether from fright, conviction or expediency cannot be told, but daily scores of people are resigning, at least nominally from the Communist organisation.

With troops still moving North, the Political Propaganda Department has just organised a Preparatory Committee of War Time Political Propaganda, with Chen Konk-pok as the chairman. This committee is composed of representatives of the Political Department of each army, and also of Kuomintang delegates. The committee will work at spreading Kuomintang principles among the populations of villages and towns captured by the Kuomintang armies.

Li Chang-tat, chief of police, has issued a proclamation saying that he has been informed that both detectives and soldiers have been helping to smuggle passengers and goods to and from the Hongkong boats. He demands that this practice cease, and threatens heavy penalty to any persons caught violating the order.

Eight hundred policemen have been detailed to help Chang Kai-shek's soldiers to patrol the streets. There will be mixed squads of 20 men to each block. At first it was thought that this order was to help prevent unhappy clashes to-morrow, May 30, the first anniversary of the Shanghai shootings, but officials declare the patrol will be of indefinite duration.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
text:
Washington, April 5.—That Britain was wise enough to block the holding of the so-called Economic Conference proposed through the League of Nations leaked out here to-day through Russian propaganda telegrams which credited the “necucisation” against the British to the head of the Central Union of Co-operative Societies. Nothing but praise was heard from those expressing an opinion regarding the British stand.

The proposal to convene the International economic conference, it was stated, was brought up by Mons. Loueller, the French delegate, to a meeting of the League Just, December.

The purpose of the Conference, its promoters said, was to devise a way for international regulation of production, and distribution of the most important categories of raw materials, such as iron ore, coal, cotton, copper, petroleum and rubber. It also proposed to busy itself about and also to seek a solution of customs liabilities, preparations, loans, and the world's depreciated currencies. As a result of violent opposition by the British delegate, whose country, he said, was not interested in the conference, it has practically "died a booming." About all that is left of the grandiose scheme is a "preparatory committee." This committee is not functioning as yet according to the Russian reports. “This so-called Economic Conference is an outrage,” said a member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, “and is merely a befalled attempt to get on record before the world and have the news disseminated that a plan is on foot to communicate the world's raw materials. The danger is that such a scheme if given wide publicity would furnish fodder for some of the bovine brains that are doing all they can to bumper the producers in favour of the slickers who would like to live off the community.”—“China Press.”

headline: NEW CLUB
text: Efforts are being made to or gain the bankers' club in London for the exclusive use of active or retired members of the banking profession, and premises have been obtained in the West End where financiers may entertain their customers and friends. An institution of this kind was proposed several years ago but plans were laid aside on account of the war. London bankers in the past have in their club affiliations been no Brahmin caste. They may be found on the membership rolls of the Union, Oxford and Cambridge. Athenæum, the Carlton, the Reform, the Marlborough, the United Service, the Pall Mall or a dozen other organisations. Special features proposed, apart from the usual facilities and comfort, of a club, will be the organisation of one of the finest banking and commercial libraries in the world; an information bureau capable of dealing with all points in banking and commercial matters, particularly law and accountancy; and an attractive home for country and foreign members visiting London.

headline: PAPERS LONDON POLICE SEIZED.
text:
"NATIVES OF ORIENT."

There has been considerable discussion of late (says a London paper in mail week) on the advisability of the Home Office disclosing more of the discoveries made by the police in the raid on the Communist Party headquarters last October, which resulted in the conviction and imprisonment of twelve of the Communist leaders.

The haul was one of the largest of the kind ever made by Scotland Yard.

Detective-Sergeant Renshaw, of the Special Branch, stated during the court proceedings that a quarter of a million items of documents, books, files, and the like were seized.

headline: 12 Van Loads:
text:
They made 12 van loads, and their removal occupied seven hours.

At the trial only a few documents were rendered as evidence, and the impression was given that the Attorney-General had decided to produce the minimum number thought necessary.

Subsequent events, such as the implication of university undergraduates and natives of the Orient in Communist propaganda, have suggested that discoveries of a serious nature, other than those revealed in court, were made.

Only certain facts relating to the extent to which the British Communist Party has been subsidised from abroad since 1920 were disclosed to the jury.

Members of Parliament's beliefs that the publication of further details of the discoveries would be of service.

headline: RELIGIOUS WORK.
text:
EVANGELISATION IN NEW TERRITORIES.

ANNUAL MEETING

The conditions in the New Territories, in the various Churches this year, have been very good, states the annual report of the Hongkong and New Territories Evangelisation Society.

The report goes on to state that the members baptised have increased and the contributions have not decreased. The preachers and members of Committee in the various places have been sincere and faithful, and have shown resource in dealing with affairs, and the evangelistic work in the villages has often far exceeded expectations.

The accounts showed a total income for the year of about $8,400, raised in fairly equal proportions by European and Chinese contributions.

The annual meeting at which the report was presented was held in the lecture hall of Union Church, the Rev. J. Kirk Maconachie presiding.

Addresses by the- Society's Chinese workers followed, the Rev. H. R. Wells translating.

The superintendent evangelist, Rev. Li Shu-kwal, who, together with Mr. Wells takes general oversight of the work, made some interesting references to the fact that in spite of all the troubles in Kwangtung and Hongkong, no difficulties had appeared in the relations between foreign and Chinese elements in the whole course of the year's operations. The reason for that, in his opinion, is that in Christian work and principle, goodwill and consequent unity are achieved, and there lies the hope of the future.

Amongst those present were the Revs. Dr. Pearce and J. H. Johnson, Dr. (Mrs.) Hickling, Dr. (Miss) A. Sydenham, Dr. Ashton, Dr. Early, Dr. Hollings, Capt. W. Davison, Messrs. A. S. D. Cousland, E. B. Cubey, A. H. Mackenzie, J. L. MacPherson, C. C. Hickling and many Chinese ladies and gentlemen. Mrs. Ho Shu-lau, Hon. Secretary, and Mr. E. R. Dovey, Hon. Treasurer, were also present, the latter pointing out that with more funds the work could be much extended.

headline: FOILED BY PRINCESS.
text:
NOVE INFINATED BY THIRATS.

An evil which is even now embittering the lives of scores of Society women without the outside world knowing anything of it has been dragged into the limelight through the courageous action of a woman who holds a high place in Parisian society. She is a princess, very young and of striking beauty.

Last summer, while she was enjoying a holiday at one of the most fashionable sensible resorts in Normandy, she found among her numerous admirers a young Czech named Zdenek Kahn, reputed to be a rich member of Viennese society.

He was not only a man of highly polished manners, but a perfect dancer and a fine athlete. He often danced with the princess and attended some of the tea parties given at her villa.

When the holidays ended and the princess returned to Paris, the young man went back to Vienna and completely faded from her memory until on New Year's Eve she received a letter in which he mentioned their senside acquaintance and said that he was in desperate need of money.

He threatened that unless the princess sent him ten thousand francs by return of post he would make her the centre of a scandal by telling her husband some very unpleasant stories.

With the strength born on a clear conscience, the princess simply ignored the young man's threat and sent his letter to a lawyer in Vienna, so that the police might keep an eye on him. But only a day after she had posted it she received another surprise when Kuhn telephoned to tell her that he had come to Paris to receive the money personally and that he must have it before noon. He made an appointment to meet her at the Porte Champrerret "tube" station, where she must hand over to him ten thousand francs in bank notes; or risk the consequences.

The princess, showing greater wisdom than is usually associated with her years, placed the whole case before her husband, and then told the police about it; and, acting on their advice, she kept the appointment, taking with her ten thousand franc banknotes, of which she had given the numbers to the authorities.

headline: HERO-WORSHIP
text:
THE WRONG SPIRIT.

There is in many ways, said Sir William Joynson-Hicks, the Home Secretary, a feeling of lawlessness in the Old Country.

"Take the case of a murder, for instance," he continued. "What spirit is it that forgets the murdered person and makes the murderer oftentimes something of a hero? It is wrong. "I am speaking of many cases I have had before me so often during the last eighteen months of men and women signing petitions by the thousand for reprieving some utterly cruel murder. People forget, not merely the murdered person, but it may be the wife and children who are left to battle with the world owing to that murder.

"Not only in murder cases but in other cases I find over and over again that the sympathy is somehow for the criminal other than for the law."

When petitions were poured in asking that men should be let out of prison who had been convicted by a jury of their own countrymen after fair trial and sentenced to by no means severe penalties they could not understand the feeling in Englishmen at the present time—he thought it must be perhaps the result of the war—against the administration of the law.

headline: BRITISH ART.
text:
PRIME MINISTER'S SYMPATHY

Sir Joseph Duveen, of the Firm of art dealers, in a lotter to the Prime Minister, Mr. Stenley Baldwin, appealing for encouragement of British art and artists, has written recently:

It is not the popular and highly paid posttext parameter about whom I am here concerned and for whom I would enlist your sympathy; it is the very much larger number of the unfamed but skillful craftsmen. In all the arts who lack the support which they deserve to receive. I am not asking for money or for the creation of any public fund. Even more important to artists than money is the encouragement arising from a sympathetic attention to their efforts. On that alone, however, they cannot live. Their work must find purchasers if they are to be put in position to produce more.

Mr. Baldwin's Relatives.

Mr. Arthur Ponsonby, a member of the British aristocracy who joined the Labour Party and was a member of the first Labour Cabinet as Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, has now become an absolute pacifist. (His father was General the Right Hon. Sir Henry Ponsonby, and his mother was a granddaughter of Earl Grey.) Mr. Ponsonby recently published a book urging the people to refuse to take up arms in the next war, and he is now circulating copies of a letter to the Prime Minister, which he asks people to sign, containing the following pledge:

headline: SURGICAL TRIUMPH.
text:
GIRE PARALYSED NOW ABLE TO WALK.

After being unable to walk for twelve years, Miss Bertha Johnston, of Newcastle, is now able to walk round her ward in the Loyal National Orthopaedic Hospital. Great Portland Street, W., with the aid of a stick. She has been suffering from infantile paralysis since the age of seven. Admitted to the hospital in March of last year, she has since undergone five operations and received other expert treatment, and recently the surgeons' success was first tested. She was taken from her bed and put on her feet, with a small knee support and crutches. A few days later she was walking round the ward.

The girl is overcome with gratitude and pleasure and is longing to go home. Meanwhile the hospital is experiencing great difficulty in securing the necessary funds to provide more beds for similar cases all over the country.

headline: SOVIET'S COFFIN.
text:
MOSCOW AND FENG.

The Marbin correspondent of the Shanghai Mercury writes on March 24:—

Marshall Wu. Fei-fu having declared in a communication that he he proposes convening a representative National Assembly for the purpose of bringing into existence a legal central government, and Marshal Chang Tso-lin having affirmed that he has no desire to take a prominent part in the formation of the new government except desiring to remove every vestige of Bolshvism from China, it is generally believed in Harbin that the field on the coffin of Soviet activities in the Chinese Republic will shortly be nailed and the coffin itself given an unostentatious burial.

There is considerable perturbation visible in Soviet circles in Barbin and all the so-called "commercial agents" of Moscow have been holding conferences day in and day out these past couple of weeks. In view of the fact, that the mills in Russia are not even able to fill the domestic demand for goods, it is not difficult to conclude that not all the "commercial agents" of the Soviet government are what they are represented to be.

That they should be, highly nerve-strung over the impending wholesale collapse of the Nationists is only to be expected for with a untitled China against them, the Soviet government and its agents out here will have to look for fresh laurels. Moreover, the seizure of the Volunteer Fleet steamer "Oleg" off Taikub by the Fengtian navy after the discovery was made that the vessel was loaded to the gunwales with arms and ammunition, will not help the Reds at all in their professions off friendship for the Chinese nation.

Moscow is said to have involved the iso-called Christian General and his suite to escape into Russia and it is thought likely that Feng Yu-hsiang will accept this invitation. According to a Mukden report, he has just announced that he would proceed to Europe, via Russia and that he has definitely decided to withdraw from politics. It is, generally believed here, however, that Moscow is about the furthest point the worthy Marshal would go and it is considered even likely that he would attempt, whilst there, to reorganise his movement against Chang Tso-lin and Wu Pei-fu.

There is a mournful tone apparent in the vituperations of the Soviet Press against the Imperialistic Powers and their recent ultimatum to Peking, but amongst the non-Reds jubilation reigns supreme over the prospect of the early passing of the Bolsheviks in China.

It is given out that a joint attack would be made in due course against Canton and it is considered certain that in the South also the deathknell of Bolshevism will be sounded; thereby depriving Comrade Borodin of his advisory post with the Cantonese "government."

Dear Sir,

Having been informed that you are interested and open for a deal in a live business proposition I take the liberty of presenting to you what seems to me a most wonderful business...in which, no doubt, you will take a live interest and perhaps advise me by return the amount of stock you wish to subscribe towards the formation of the company.

The object of the company is to operate a large cat ranch near Manchester where land can be purchased cheaply for the purpose.

To start with we want a million cats. Each will average about 12 kittens per year; the skins run from 6d each for the white ones to 2/6d for the pure black ones. This will give us 12,000,000 skins per year to sell at an average price of 1/6d each making our revenue $2,500 per day. A man can skin about 60 cats per day at 5s per day wage and it will take 120 men to operate the ranch, therefore the net profit will be $2,470 per day.

We feed the cats on rats and start a rat ranch. The rats multiply four times as fast as the cats, so that if we start with a million rats we shall have four rats per cat each day, then we will feed the rats on the carcasses of the cats from which the skins have already been taken, giving each rat one quarter of a cat.

It will thus be seen that the business will be self acting and automatic throughout. The cats will eat the rats and the rats will eat the cats and we shall have the ukins.

A waiting your prompt reply, and trusting you will appreciate the opportunity to get rich quickly.

Yours faithfully,

headline: Manchurian Independence.
text:
The ex-Governor is a man of about 54, of medium stature, with a long drooping moustache and kindly, intelligent eyes. He answers questions quickly and directly, without circumlocution.

"I do not believe in the independence of Manchuria," he told a foreigner. Manchuria must be closely connected with the rest of China. It must carry out the decrees of the Peking Government, though, of course, where that government is tinged with Soviet ideas, Manchuria cannot obey such decrees as show such influence.

"The Three Eastern Provinces should hold aloof from the fighting in the rest of China. The wishes of the people and their welfare should be the guiding principles in their government. The people want to carry out the peaceful development of Manchuria so that they may attain prosperity. They are,averse to war, and for that reason Manchuria should refrain from sending troops south of the Wall."

“The danger which Manchuria must guard against is that represented by Soviet Russia and its influences. Russia is now handing the Chinese Eastern Railway as if it belonged entirely to her, as if the Chinese were not part owners. The question as to how this may be counteracted was outside my province. It belongs to the jurisdiction of the Kirin Provincial Government. But the question of Soviet propaganda concerns all Manchuria. It is being spread about in two channels, through the soldiers and through the poor classes. I do not believe that there is any danger of military invasion on the part of Russia now or for the next two or three years; but I fear that after that such a danger will exist.”

headline: COAL CRISIS. HOME PAPER ON COM- MISSIONS REPORT
text:
The study of the Coal Commission's report, so far as it can be justly appreciated without the evidence and appendices in the unpublished second and third volumes to which it refers, will leave most readers with mixed feelings. As an account of the present position of the industry and the circumstances by which it has been brought about, the report leaves little to be desired. The urgency with which an early conclusion was needed is not disguised, and at times has tended to curtail the detail into which the enquiry was pursued, perhaps with no detriment to the result; but the report covers the whole ground with a deliberation and clearness that shows no sign of haste, and for years to come it is

Important analysis of the subject "and", perhaps, the most useful, available collection of authentic data bearing on it. When, however, passing from its historical description and varied evidence with which the Commission had to deal, the report passes to the constructive suggestions for which the whole country has been waiting, it loses the grip of the situation that it appeared to have. Its recommendations seem unlikely to be approved by either of the parties to the enquiry; but, indeed, even if they were adopted by both, they would not be adequate to the emergency. The large majority of them, even if they were all desirable and practicable, which is by no means admitted on all competent hands, could not come into operation for a long time; and the industry is so placed that much of it must have collapsed long before then if measures immediately applicable cannot be found.

Whatever else may be done—and much must be done, before the industry will be again on its feet, and its customer industries are satisfied enough as to its stability to resume their normal ordering—the increase of wages procured because of the few months' vanished boom, and the reduction of hours by which the miners are distinguished from all other workers in the country, must be renounced. The miners have, in fact, been at issue not with the owners, but with the users, and the issue has been, shortly, whether the users will pay them as much more money than other unsheltered workmen as they ask for working as much shorter hours. In the most practical way the users have declined; and it is to the users that any concession has to be made. The owners can derive no advantage from it without sharing the advantage automatically with the workers under the existing agreement; and the workers stand in a common need with the owners of every advantage that they can derive from what remedial measures can be promptly taken. Not the least of the advantages they would reap would be the return of the disposition to venture more in the business of the mines, from which the uncertainty of the temper of their men seems to be a principal deterrent. —Engineering.

headline: NEAT COMPLIMENT. / FOREIGN ADMINISTRATION OF BANKS / CHINESE TRUST.
text:
Under the arresting title, "Love in Action," the head of Hangchow Hospital has laid bare his heart, and it were well (says the "China Press") that the first part at least of the annual report he has prepared could be translated and sent broadcast among the millions of Chinese who have benefited by the efforts of Dr. Duncan Main and the other thousands of medical missionaries who have laboured here for so many decades. How little we thought, he says, at the beginning of the year that our students would leave us in a body and that we should have to pass through such a time of anti-British and anti-foreign hatred. Yet Dr. Main is not a bit pessimistic and deems it "the most important thing to day to be able to try to see and understand the other man's viewpoint.

Happy is the man who believes in his fellow, for it is better, asserts Dr. Main, to be deceived in some things than to be suspicious in all things, and he adds, if you want, to borrow trouble, there are always people willing to lend it without security. While pointing out that the anti-foreign agitation, though now grown faint, may be revived and the clamour to get rid of all foreigners may recrudescence, yet a great work has been accomplished and the work will last no matter what happens to the worker.

The bitter part of the whole sorry business is that during this crucial process of transition which Chinese thought is undergoing, in comes the strange doctrine of Bolshevism, which is just the opposite to that in China's ancient civilisation, and the principles which they have always believed in, and if it spreads, things will go from bad to worse. Dr. Main expresses, the profound hope that the Chinese will fight the demon Bolshevism with a unity that is strength and devote themselves to internal reform and development, and leave other things of less importance alone. He says: It is too soon really for China to demand cancellation of old treaties with countries that are her best friends and willing to help her out of all her troubles. These will come in due time when China has put her house in order and is a real China and can trust herself, and can be wholly and fully trusted by the world. Quas is very much struck by the fact

that the Chinese repose implicit trust in the foreigner when it comes to finding a safe and secure repository for their treasure. When any real political trouble breaks out in these parts, there is a great increase of deposits in the foreign banks in Shanghai. And when trouble is expected here, many valuable possessions are brought to us for safe keeping—surely the most effective compliment that could be paid to the benign character of foreign administration, illustrating a fresh that recent misunderstanding between foreigners and Chinese have been at best superficial—and artificial.

Bermondsey Borough Council desire an office boy in their works department at a wage of 30s. per week.

When Walter James Thorrinton, 28, a gas-fitter, was charged at Wimbledon with deserting his wife and two children, it was stated that he ran away with his mother-in-law, who was 45.

In common with the surrounding areas we have been treated to a liberal supply of rain, which has delayed various building operations at Now 13, 018, 10 and 23, and has cut up some of the public which however have been attended to by the roadmen.

The gardens and newly planted trees have benefitted, and the island is looking at its best. The palms must also have interfered with the attendance at the big theatre (second one has since been in progress) for which special lunches were run from Hongkong. Dr. and Mrs. Minett left yesterday, having stayed an extra week-end to witness the school sports.

The athletic meeting went off very successfully; the weather conditions were ideal, as it was not too hot for the students taking part in the long list of events. The local "stadium" presented an animated scene; there was a good number of visitors present. There were several new features this year. The committee had thoughtfully provided a grandstand in the shape of a matshed shelter for the accommodation of the visitors; in case of wet weather, refreshments were also provided. Then the local mission schools attended in force and contributed several musical items. Some of the Hongkong schools had sent teams for the invitation relay race, which event was keenly contested. A likely winner had the misfortune to drop the flag so putting his team out of the running. Several of the events, notably the hopping race, had to be run again owing to a dead-head.

The hill race and the ung-of-war were specially interesting. The members of the committee are to be congratulated for the successful issue of their efforts.

We are soon to lose another of the owner-residents in the person of Mr. G. E. Wetton, who leaves shortly for England.

Congratulations on their work during the difficult period of the strike and boycott were extended by Mr. E. the Governor to the various sections of the Hongkong Police Force yesterday on the occasion of the annual inspection.

The parade was under the command of the Hon. Mr. B. D. C. Wolfe, (Captain Superintendent of Police) and there were also present Mr. D. Burlingham (D. S. F.), Mr. F. H. King (Director of Criminal Intelligence Department). Inspector Blackman (Divisional Inspector of the Central Station).

Among the guests present work Mr. R. C. Tredwell (American Consultant-General), Mr. R. E., Lindseil Mr. H. Bloxham, Mr. E. Ralph and Mr. J. Ralston.

On the arrival of His Excellency the Governor, who was accompanied by Capt. Swinton A.D.C., the parade presented arms and the Royal Salute was sounded by the buglers. The Governor then inspected the Force after which the awards (a complete list of which has already appeared in the "China Mail"). were presented.

headline: The Governor's Speech
text:
Addressing the gathering His excellence said:

Officers' N.C.Os. and men of the Hongkong Polka Force.

Hongkong Police Force. It am glad to have this opportunity of seeing you on parade and of congratulating you on your fine record during the critical period of the strike and boycott. In a despatch to me dated December 30th last the Secretary of State for the Colonies writes:—“I have to express my satisfaction at learning of the loyalty displayed by the Chinese members of the force and my appreciation of the work of the Police in this trying crisis.” This tribute is well deserved. Out of 533 Cantonese police, only seven deserted. Of 353 Wei-hai-well men only three deserted. Out of 105 Chinese clerks, telephone operators and sergeant interpreters, only seven deserted. Of 233 Chinese Water Police ratings, only nine seamen and five stokers deserted. Not a single coxswain or engineer left his post. This is all the more creditable because a large number of the Water Police are members of the Seamen's Union.

From the middle of June to the middle of August the European Police were on eight hours duty instead of six. No leave could be granted and all ranks had to be confined to their own districts. This was also the ease with the Indian and Chinese Contingents. No complaints of any kind were made and all ranks worked most cheerfully.

Remarkable work was done by the Police Casual Labour Department. From June 22 to July, 26 about 25,000 coolies were collected and sent out to work. In addition to supplying the men, the Police officers in charge had in great many cases to arrange for their food and for their payment. The Police officers employed in the Casual Labour Department had frequently to work from 5,45 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sometimes later.

A special word of praise is due to the Police along the frontier of the New Territory, where owing to the outrageous behaviour of armed strike pickets, our constables and our police launches were frequently under fire and we were involved in a kind of guerilla warfare. The steadiness, self-control, courage and discretion of all ranks under these conditions were admirable. The gratitude of the Colony has been well earned by the Hongkong Police Force during the past ten months and it is a great pleasure to me to have this opportunity, on behalf of the whole community, of thanking you publicly.

headline: BANKRUPTCY.ECHO.
text:
MANAGING PARTNER IN TROUBLE.

A Chinese managing partner was charged at the Central Magistracy yesterday with making false statements to the Official Receiver relating to the affairs of the Wing Shing firm, of Koshing Street, and on other counts of falsifying the account books.

Mr. E. S. C. Brooks prosecuted and Mr. L. R. Andrewes appeared for the defence. Mr. M. W. Lo gave evidence of having prepared a sale agreement relating to the firm on the instructions of the accused. In reply to a question he said that he advised the accused to have the sale gazetted. Other evidence was taken and the case was adorned until

Avising out of an incident at Causeway, Buy in which a Chinese was finally injured by a motor cycle," Mr. S. J. Squire was charged before Major C. Wilson at the Central Magistency yesterday afternoon with manalaughter, and also with driving a motor cycle in reckless manner.

Mr. J. A. Gordon Leask defended and Mr. H. S. Fitzroy watched proceedings on behalf of deceased relatives.

The first witness, a Chinese contable, said that he was on point duty at the junction at 9.15 p.m. on April 17 when he saw two motor cycles driven by Europeans with no pillion passengers travelling very fast towards the central district. The cycles touched each other in the middle of the road before passing the post and one of them turned into Caroline Road. The other ran over the man seated on the pavement and hit the tramway shelter. The driver of the machine fell on to the ground and was rendered unconscious. Witness also said there were two other Europeans on the scene shortly after the accident.

Dr. W. L. Paterson said the Chinese was admitted to the Government Civil Hospital and operated on immediately. Witness found the case hopeless and the man died two hours later. He thought the wound which proved fatal could have been caused by the front number plate of the motor cycle.

Witness said that Mr. Squire was also admitted. He had allight abrasions and was suffering from shock.

At this stage further hearing was adjourned until Friday afternoon.
