headline: SEAMENS MISSION
text:
Though the whole year in the prospect is overshadowed by the disturbing events which occurred during the latter half, and we are inclined to think of 1925 almost entirely in the terms of "Strike and Boycott," we must not lose sight of the fact that the opening months appeared to present hopes of increase of trade and consequent general prosperity in the Colony. The disappointment of these hopes has thus seemed all the more dis

Early in March the Chaplain returned from home leave, and very soon afterwards the Rev. N. A. Peel who had been in charge for the time received orders to go to Bombay, paid a flying visit to Peking and finally sailed for India towards the end of April, leaving behind him in Hongkong the memory of a happy and charming personality.

It was not first intended that the work should be carried on by two chaplains, but the serious financial position of the Society locally made it unadvisable to arrange for another assistant chaplain to come out and also made it necessary to close down the Kowloon Institute, the running of which had proved a greater drain on the General Fund than "was originally" estimated. Thereafter the work for a month or two fell into the ordinary summer routine, when it was judely interrupted by the outbreak of trouble in June.

For a few days there seemed a distinct chance that the Institute Staff would remain unimpaired, but the receipt of one of the notorious "dagger" letters of intimidation brought out the servants on bloc, with the exception of three, the No. 1 and the No. 2 Boys, and the Manager's House Boy, who throughout all the trouble and afterwards did their full share of work in keeping things going.

The exposure of boys took place of a Sunday just ten minutes before evening service was due to begin As it was, there were no intending worshippers, " and the staff had a once to deal with the necessary changes in house routine. For the time it was decided that no boarders could be taken in except those already in residence, and all casual meals were ruled out. The boarders, where possible, took over the cleaning of their own cabins. Mrs. Sellwood, the Manager's wife, did the necessary marketing. The Manager's House Boy proved himself to be a really first rate cook, the other two boys looked after the ground floor of the building and the general service, while the rest of the Housework was taken on by the Chaplain, the Manager and his wife. The Chaplain and the Manager also had various duties to perform in connection with the defence and running of essential services in the Colony... All the boarders had meanwhile taken on jobs in various capacities as bakers, tramwyumen, in charge of tugs and lighters, etc., etc. At first it was necessary to have a European continually on duty in the entrance hall. During the first few days the work was various panicky alarms from some of our neighbours. " For instance care man-man in with a report of attempted a son and so on. All this naturally put a temporary start to the g" cater part of our usual work, more especially as the "Dayspring" was also laid up for lack of " a crew. It was particularly annoying in that from the Institute we could see day by day the great number of vessels lying in Kowloon. Buy waiting and mostly waiting in vain for their usual "runs" to be opened up again. It was fortunate that the launch coxgwin though at first intimidated "out" with the rest of the crew kept an eye on the launch and reported at the Institute after a couple of days, undertaking very necessary painting work in side the building until, after four weeks, the motor launch crews returned to work, and our activities in that respect were resumed. It was however considerably

It was however considerably longer before we were able to get together a sufficient number of servants to enable us to open up the Institute to its full extent, though the utmost praise is due to the staff who did wonders in carrying on, at a time when they might justifiably have been content with doing the bare minimum to make life in the Institute possible.

So soon as the "Dayspring" was at work again we re-started the bathing picnics, though this was the only form of outdoor entertainment possible till late in the year, the tennis parties being out of the question, considering the fact that most if not all of our usual hostages were like ourselves running their households with no servants or a very greatly reduced staff. Entertaining under such

conditions was of course not to be expected. In one respect, the trouble strangely enough brought us more indoor social work than is usually the case in the hot weather, for no sooner had H.M.S. "Hermes" with her aeroplanes arrived in port than arrangements for ship's company's dances were made and from about the middle of August to the end of the year there were as a general rule at least two dances a week in the Institute Hall as well as occasional Whist Drives. The Dance Club from the Flagship, H.M.S. "Haykins" also booked the Hall for regular weekly dances. We must pay grateful tribute to the willing spirit displayed by the organisers of these dances in falling in with our house rules and regulations. There were two or three carnival dances at one of which we were fortunate in having a large contingent from the crew of one of the big Tourist Ships, and just before Christmas, with the assistance of the Flagship, we entertained the ship's company of the French Flagship "Jules Michelet," at a dance, being honoured by the presence of Rear Admiral M. Basire, the French Consul, and several of the leading French residents in the Colony, as well as of course many of our British friends.

Our Christmas festivities took the form of a dinner followed by games in old fashioned style, and this party was quite an international affair, as we had men from British American and French ships. The ship's company of the "Jules Michele!" presented an old French Naval Engraving to the Institute as a token of appreciation, before their vessel left Hongkong.

We were delighted to welcome Lady Clementi at the Institute's room after her arrival in the Colony. Her interest in the welfare of the seafaring classes in Hongkong is well known, and as far as we are concerned her sympathy has taken the practical form of organising a Ladies' Entertainment Committee. In addition to the already existing Tennis Committee, for running periodical entertainments of various sorts in the Institute. The offer of the use of a tennis court at Government House was also very greatly appreciated, though circumstances so far have not enabled us to take advantage of this privilege.

It is not likely that the tennis parties as run formerly will be carried on in quite the same way until shipping and trade has resumed its more or less normal state, but we are sincerely grateful to Mrs. D. G. M. Bernard and other friends for their interest and help in arranging that the outdoor, social activities should not suffer more than necessary owing to the prevalent trouble. In the early part of the year of course tennis parties were held, and for the kindness in carrying those out we thank all those concerned.

Mention has already been made of our bathing parties, which were brought to a stop for two months, but were resumed as soon as practicable. Needless to say they proved as popular as ever. The "Daysspring," with the exception of the period specified, carried on her good work throughout the year in undiminished activity. Our thanks are due to all who in one way or another made it possible for us to keep her as clean and smart as such a vessel should be.

The loss sustained by the Society owing to the Strike and Boycott is shewn most clearly when we come to deal with statistics. The numbers of seafarers attending our Church Services were seriously affected, a misfortune if it can be called so, which we shared with the branch in Shanghai. In both "stations" for Sunday after Sunday, where previously the seafolk attendance had averaged about 25 or more according to the shipping in port, the numbers dropped to single figures. In spite of this, however, in Hongkong we are only some, 120 "down" on the 1924 figures, while we are thankful to be able to report that there is a slight increase in the number of attendances at Celebrations of the Holy Communion.

Owing to the presence in part of so many of H.M. Vessels for longer times than usual our indoor social figures show an increase, though those quoted only record attendances of seafarers at "shows" organised by us, and does not include ship's company dances which for the most part are run by the Ships' Dancing Clubs.

The beds occupied during the year also show a decrease, for it must be remembered that during part of the trouble men were not allowed to sleep ashore, but had to return on board each night, and also that for some little time, only those men who were already boarding in the Institute were able to sleep third owing to the greatly diminished staff being only able to cope with that much of the work. When we come to deal with finance, we find there the most evident results of all the trouble. And in this we have cause for very careful and anxious thought.

headline: THE CHINA MAIL
text:
The largest demonstration of women since the days of the Suffragettes was carried out under the auspices of the Women's Guild of Empire to-day, when 20,000 marched from the City to the Albert Hall to participate in an anti-strike meeting.

The gathering was composed of all classes of the community. A large proportion of the demonstrators reached the Metropolis in special trains and charabances from Scotland, Wales and the provinces. There was some display of unsympathetic feeling.

We started the year with an adverse Balance of over $11,500; and our aim was to clear at least some of this off during 1926 Circumstances unfortunately proved against us, and for the rest of the twelve months all we could hope to do was to keep the work going.

The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation were good enough to allow us to increase the mortgage on the Seamen's Institute from $60,000 to $90,000, covering not only the Reclamation Fund No. 2 Account, but also the overdraft on the Current Account, up to a limit of $15,000. This enabled us to carry on, but the end of December came with the limit nearly reached, and certain investments bringing in no interest. A further result of the boycott was the increase in unemployment most of those men so unfortunately situated being officers and engineers of the River Steamers, whose savings were soon exhausted. These men we could not possibly refuse to take in at the Institute, for the fault was not theirs, and at any time it seemed likely that their posts in the steamers would be open again, and though when able to do so, they will undoubtedly repay us any money owed us, this sad state of affairs has made it increasingly hard for us to make both ends meet. We always have certain bad debts mostly incurred by men who made vague promises to pay some time men whom we are here for the very purpose of helping and could help far more easily if they would only help themselves. If these debts could be repaid we should be in a much better position, but as it is we have had to limit the extent of our help to the most necessary and reasonable cases. Needless to say, it is most difficult to say "No," when perhaps another chance may make all the difference. The year finished financially with a debit balance of $15,278.31, bad debts amounting to $2,063.00.

The financial stress as already stated was one of the causes of the closing of the Kowloon Institute. At one time it seemed likely that we should be able to let the building and in fact all had been done but the signing of the papers, but it was discovered during an inspection of the structure that one of the walls had very recently developed signs of weakness, due it is believed to the thrust of the roof, and the cost of even the most necessary repairs alone was prohibitive considering the exhausted state of our exchequer. At the close of the year no definite decision had been made as to the future of the building. We have received from many sources generous and willing assistance in trying to raise money. In April the Band of the 1st Battalion of the East Surrey Regiment, by kind permission of Lieut.-Colonel Montague Bates, C.B., D.S.O., gave a very successful orchestra concert on our behalf in the Theatre Royal, the Hongkong Jockey Club made a large donation, and St. Stephen's Girls' College sent a substantial sum as a part of the proceeds of a concert given by them in the School Hall. The Institute of Engineers and Ship builders of Hongkong again voted a substantial grant to us.

To one and all then we extend our grateful thanks for help given in so many different ways. We feel that though at present our position is straitened, yet so much sympathy has been shown us that we should be proving ourselves culpably lacking in faith and in belief in our great cause and above all in our Leader did we give way to despondency. We believe that the call has gone out that this work shall be done, and we believe that He Who has bidden us do it will give us the strength and the means and therefore that the period of stress through which we are now passing is merely a means to increase our faith and to make us more entirely dependent on Him Who said "According to your faith be it unto you." G. T. Waldegrave

by. outsiders and by intriguing politicians. On the other hand there was a group that spent much time on working up a knowledge of national problems. Usually they tried to use moderate measures, and consulted their faculties and other foreigners whom they deemed to be sympathetic. They had done a great deal for their country in the past. One might go back 2,000 years and find them going out to help their country. Usually they got it "in the neck," though not perhaps as in Peking a month ago. But in the long run, what they did created public opinion. They were a force to be reckoned with, and would do things in the future. If foreigners took a more sympathetic attitude toward them it would keep the more conservative group to gain the mastery and to take control out of the hands of the radicals.

Rotarian Harvey, in tendering the Club's thanks to Mr. Klingman for his address, said he had always contended that students should find no place in active politics. His business gave him considerable knowledge of educational institutions in this country, and he generally found that in well organised Mission schools and private institutions there was very little trouble. Most of the trouble emanated from the national Colleges, where there was usually corruption from the head downward. One reason for discontent was the lack of opportunity for those who were completing their studies. However, there were no students in the world he admired more highly than, for instance, those of Nankai and of the Hui Wen Middle School in Tientsin. They had great difficulties in getting an efficient education, because owing to the absence of native text books they had to acquire their education through an acquired language. In such institutions the students were found at work from early morning till late at night. They were a most industrious lot and he respected every one of them. headline: CHINESE STUDE
text: Three main reasons why the Chinese students played so big a part in this country were suggested by Mr. Harry F. Kingman, in the course of a talk to members of the Tientsin Rotary Club at the weekly gathering at the Astor House recently. The first was the traditional respect and reverence of the Chinese for educated people. They had always looked to the scholarly for leadership, and here the educated classes enjoyed a prestige which students in other countries did not have. Secondly, the students of China were organised. Since May 80 they had developed an organisation capable of creating a national movement in three or four days. Thirdly, in China at present there was only a comparatively small group of people who understood national affairs and took an interest in them, and who were at the same time disinterested. Of that small group the students formed a considerable proportion. Many people felt that the students, no matter how many mistakes they made, were not trying to get something for themselves, and that although they sometimes used asining methods their ideal was right, and naturally that gave them a hearing with the common people.

headline: Students Off the Right Road.

Three United States army planes, equipped with wireless, left Camp Nichols on April 26 for Aparri, where they will await the arrival of Captains Loriga and Galianza, the Spanish Madrid-to-Manila fliers, (says the "Manila Bulletin.")

The planes are of the latest type in use by the aviation corps in the Philippines. They are piloted by First Lt. Paul L. Williams, Corregidor, First Lt. Stanley M. Umstead, Corregidor, and First Lt. Harry M. Mills, Camp Stotsenburg.

The three American filers will escort the Spanish airmen from Aparri to Camp Nichols. The American and Spanish filers will come down over the Cagayan Valley, Isabela province, Bayombong, Nueva Vizcaya province; Balete Pass, Nueva Vizcaya province; San Jose, Nueva Vizcaya province, and Camp Stotsenburg, Pampanga. It is understood that twelve places from Camp Stotsenburg will accompany the filers from there to Camp Nichols.

There are many thinking people in South Africa who are alarmed at the colour segregation policy of the present Government. These people have found an outspoken champion of their thoughts in the Bishop of Pretoria, Dr. Talbot, who has not only attacked the native and Asiatic policy of the Government, but has now shown many of the dangers and the fallacies that He hidden in the Colour Bar Bill. It would seem that this bill limiting the labour activities of the native, will shortly be on the Statute-book of Me. Union. A solemn "warning of the probable consequences has been written by the Bishop of Pretoria in the March issue of "Kingdom," the official organ of his diocese.

Beginning with the argument that Christianity stands or falls by its assertion of the equal value of all souls before God, Dr. Talbot goes on:—

At present the great mass of native life is at a lower level of human attainment than the European. Not that we can say that the native is inherently inferior to the European. Evidence from America of what has been attained by the negro suggests that he is not inherently inferior, but that he is in the main at a lower level of development compared with the European. It would be sheer sentimentality to deny this.

Predilection for Cheap Labour. And yet this conclusion does not mitigate my deep-sealed dismay at the trend of present South African legislation at the expense of the native. I cannot think that the need to protect the white worker from being swamped by native labour justifies the introduction of the principle of the colour bar into the law of the land. I do not disregard unsympathetically the anxiety of white labour lest it be swamped, for, after all, it is working with a partner—namely, capital—that has evinced again and again as terrible predilection for cheap labour. I noticed that the President of the Chamber of Mines in a recent public speech had little more to contribute to the discussion of the problems of South African industry than the contention that the one thing to do was to import and to keep on importing as much cheap native labour to the mines as possible. But I do believe that the protection of the white worker should be secured by custom, by negotiation and regulation within industry, and not by legislation.

The passing of the bill of the Assembly is an evil omen for the future. Even though it is leniently and gently administered it cannot but engender a sense in the intelligent native's mind that the white man means to keep the black man down. It is not only a question of its actual provisions nor its administration, but its symbolic character. It will symbolise the inherent inferiority of the native and the resolve to use him only as a means to white convenience. It will hang in front of native hope and aspiration that which suppresses, confines, and excludes. I think it is a blind and essentially tyrannical measure, and if it is finally ratified it will have inevitably disastrous results to the true peace and wealth of South Africa. It makes it worse that the bill includes Indians with natives. In its scope, for the argument about actual inferiority is not nearly so strong in regard to the Indian as in regard to the Bantu. There are in India, and there may well be in South Africa, Indians who though of dark skin are on a level with the finest flower of European culture. That an able gifted son of India should be debarred on the ground of colour from rising to his fullest development and capacity is a great wrong; and it brings out into added relief the injustice done to the Bantu people.

Encourage Native Progress. Surely this legislation is in the wrong direction—namely, that of discouraging native growth. The right direction is that of encouraging native progress. If the black men can rise to the level of capacity with the white men, then it should be the endeavour of the white men not to keep them out but to bring them in at the white level of conditions and reward. This would entail the surmounting of great difficulties. It would be no short cut to this end, it would be no solution of the native problem. There is no short cut, there is no solution. There is no short cut through this whole business.

SHANGHAI WANTS NEW BUILDING The American Consulate-General announces that Consul General Cunningham has received from Congressman Dyer a telegram stating that the Senate had passed the Foreign Service Buildings Act of 1928. It is believed that the Senate has passed the bill in practically the same form in which it was passed by the House on March 15, and if so the bill will become a law immediately upon signature by the President. The funds will be available after July 1.

The bill carries an appropriation: of G.$10,000,000 to be allocated for foreign service buildings in the various parts of the world under the direction of the Foreign Service Buildings Commission, which is composed of the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Commerce, the Chairman and the Ranking Minority Member of the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate, and the Chairman and Ranking Minority Member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives. The personnel of the Committee at the present time therefore will be Frank B. Kellogg, Andrew W. Mellon, Herbert Hoover, Senator William E. Borah of Idaho, Senator Claude A. Swanson of Virginia, Congressman Stephen G. Porter of Pennsylvania and Congressman J. Charles Linthicum of Maryland. Consult General Cunningham believes that the next step which should be taken is to convince the Foreign Service Buildings Commission, of the importance of Shanghai and also of the amount which should be allocated for the construction of building here. He believes that there is a good chance of participating in the early allocation of the funds but it is essential that every American consider it his duty to make known to his friends in the United States the importance and the needs of this port.

One of the strongest arguments in favour of Shanghai is the large number of United States Government officials functioning here, the Department of State being represented by the Consulate-General and the United States Court for China; the Department of Commerce by the offices of the Trade Commissioner, Registrar of the China Trade Act and United States Shipping Board Representative; the Treasury Attache and the Public Health Service; and the United States Navy being represented ashore by the Navy. Commander Sir Graham Bower, R.N., K.C.M.G. (Ex-President of Grotius Society and Member of the Council of International Law Association), writing in "The Navy" says:

War between nations is a conflict of wills. It may be a commercial war, a war for the acquisition of territory, or a war in defence of an ally, but in every case it is a menna by which a nation seeks to coerce or resist the will of another nation. It is not merely a conflict of armies or navies, but a conflict of nations, and it is possible that the will of a nation may be coerced whilst its armies and navies are still undefeated. But in war between civilised nations it has been generally recognised that the methods of coercion shall be so limited that useless cruelty and useless suffering shall not be imposed. Montesquieu's dictum remains as true to day as when it was published more than a century and a half ago. In his "Esprit des Lois" he tells us that "The Law of Nations is naturally founded on this principle, that different nations ought, in time of peace, to do one another all the good they can, and, in time of war, as little injury as possible without prejudicing their real interests. The object of war is victory that of victory conquest, and that of conquest preservation. From this and the preceding principle all these rules are derived which constitute the Law of Nations."

War is cruel. It is as cruel to kill a soldier as it is to kill a child. But civilised nations recognise that because the killing of soldiers and sailors is necessary to victory it is legitimate, whilst the killing of non-combatants, women and children, is illegitimate because the death of non-combatants, women and children does not weaken the enemy's power of resistance. It inflicts useless and unprofitable suffering, and strengthens the national will to resist. From this root principle civilised nations have sought to establish a clear distinction between combatants and non-combatants in time of war.

The weapons of war have been improved and new weapons have been invented which have been more deadly or more effective means of coercion. The breech loading rifles and machine-gun's were more deadly and more effective than the spears of the Dervishes, but their use was legitimate so long as they were used against combatants and not against non-combatants. The submarine is a new weapon of war, an instrument for the coercion of the will of the enemy, and it follows that it is a legitimate weapon of war so long as it is used as a means of coercing an enemy nation and does not inflict unprofitable loss or suffering on non-combatants. There can be no objection to the legitimate use of the submarine. There is the strongest possible objection to its misuse. That the submarine was misused on many occasions in the great European war cannot be disputed; but it is also true that on many other occasions it was used, legitimately as weapon of war, in strict observance of the laws of war. Its main use was that of a commerce destroyer, but it was also used, and effectively used, both in the North Sea and at the Dardanelles, as weapon against warships, whilst the British submarine rendered valuable service in the Heligolan. Bight as the advanced outposts of the British Fleet and as commerce destroyers and fighting ships in the Baltic. It is not too much to say that Riga was saved by the torpedoing of the "Moltke" by a British submarine.

And since the war the submarine has been developed. In the early years of the war the submarine was a vessel of small size with a limited radius of action. Our latest submarine, the X1, is a vessel of 2,700 tons surface displacement and can circumnavigate the world.

The torpedo has been popularly regarded as the chief weapon of the submarine. That it is its most deadly weapon is true, but it is also true that it is not the weapon that has been most in use. For instance, during her cruise in the Mediterranean, in June, 1916, the German U36 sunk forty-one vessels, but out of this number only two were sunk by torpedo. The gun was the most economical and the favourite weapon of the submarine, and the torpedo was, as a rule, only used against a vessel known to be, or suspected of being armed.

During the war the German submarine proved efficient in two roles: as a weapon of coast defence, and as a commerce destroyer. No one disputes that the use of the submarine as a weapon of coast defence is legitimate and the only question open to discussion is: How far and under what

The Volunteer Defence Corps parade ground was the scene yesterday afternoon of a rally of the local Boy Scout troops and of their inspection by H.E. the Governor. Sir Cecil Clementi.

The arrival of His Excellency, who was accompanied by Lady Clementi, was the signal for the salute and the inspection followed after which an interesting series of displays was given embracing the various branches of Scouterraft. The Volunteer band of H.M.S. "Durban" played appropriate music throughout the afternoon.

On the conclusion of the display, His Excellency presented awards to various members of the troops, these being the Prince of Wales' Banner for "general proficiency and smartness, which was won by the 7th Troop (Sai-yingpun School)": the Silver Medal and certificate signed by Sir R. Baden Fowell to Scout Master Braga of the 1st Hongkong Troop for services rendered in rescuing a girl at the Po. Hing. Fong. collapse on July 18, last year; letters of commendation to Troop Leader Kwok Mok-hoi, of the 13th Troop for rendering first aid to injured persons on two occasions, and to Scout Chan King-ming for aid rendered to the Health Authorities in discovering a case of concealed small-pox.

Two Scout Masters were presented with warrants of appointment, and took the Scout Promise in full view of the assemblage.

After His Excellency had been welcomed by the Rev. G. T. Waldegrave, Commissioner and Deputy Camp Chief, the Scouts were addressed briefly by His Excellency who stressed the need for an increase in Scout Masters, particularly in the Chinese troops. If the graduates and undergraduates of the Hongkong University would interest themselves in the movement, they would be able to instil that fine spirit which had met the Bolshevik menace last year. If last year in the schools there had been a strong Scout detachment, there would have been no such youthful folly as the schoolboy strike.

The Scouts were a brotherhood of boys, and they would eventually become a brotherhood of men. Their training was such that it would be of great value, not only to their motherland, but to the world in general. Concluding, His Excellency pledged his support to the movement and assured all those present of his assistance in whatever capacity it might be needed.

The Commissioner was assisted by Lt. Colonel T. A. Robertson, O.B.E. His Excellency the Governor attended in his capacity as Chief Scout.

The troops taking part were:— Rover Scouts. — Sea Rover Patrol, Roving Fifth Patrols, 6th H. K. Rover Patrol; Scout Troops. — H. K. Sea Scouts, St. Joseph's College, St. Andrew's, Kowloon, 1st Wanchal Wesleyan, Murray, "Roving Fifth," Ellis Kadoorie School, Saiyingpun School, 1st South China Athletic Association, Taikoo Scottish, St. Paul's College, Ying Wa College, 2nd S. C. A. A., 1st Taikoo Chinese, 2nd Taikoo Chinese, 3rd Taikoo Chinese, 1st Yaumati Central, and Japanese H. K. B. S. A., as well as the following: Wolf Cub units.—"Bulldog," attached to 5th Troop, St. Andrew's, Kowloon, and Peak.

The programme was as follows:—

Ambulance display, Wolf Cub display, Jujitsu and Japanese fencing, Ambulance instruction, Scout games and physical exercises, Bamboo tower construction, Trek cart drill, Pyramids, Chinese boxing exercises, Highland dancing, Scout games and mimetic exercises, Camping, Tent pitching and striking, Signalling, Fleet manœuvres (illustrating control of fleet by signals, and concluding with the signal to “Chase the enemy,” by 1st Sea Scouts, under Chief Yeoman of Signals Smith, H.M.S. “Tamar,” each Scout representing a warship, Fire-fighting, Ambulance work, Signalling, and Cycle stretcher work. The fire fighting display included a jump into the life-saving sheet from the cornice of the Headquarters of Sub-Officer Chan, of the Hongkong Fire Brigade, who was in charge of that particular branch of the display. The charge of manslaughter against Mr. S. J. Squire, of the Hongkong Electric Company, arising out of the death of a Chinese from injuries received when he was run into by a motor cycle while seated near the tramway shelter at Causeway Bay was continued before Major Wilson at the Central Magistracy yesterday. Mr. J. A. Gordon Leask, defending, submitted witnesses to lengthy cross-examination. Mr. H. S. Fitzroy appeared on behalf of deceased's relatives. The first witness called was a coolie employed by the Tramway Company, who corroborated the evidence, given by other witnesses at previous hearings. Answering a question, witness said it seemed to him as if there were two persons on the machine.

Sub-Inspector Field and Sergeant Rozeskwy who were proceeding to Bay View in Rischas after a bomb raid were the next witnesses. They passed the machine about a hundred yards from the spot where the accident occurred and immediately they reached Bay View Police Station they heard of the accident. Sub-Inspector Field said he remarked to the Sergeant the way the machines were being driven. He estimated the speed between 35 and 40 miles an hour. One of the machines was observed to be carrying a pillow passenger. Sergeant Rozeskwy described the machines as terrific. He thought the one was trying to overtake the other, as they were so close together.

Evidence of damage to the machine was given by Sergeant Roberts who held the opinion that the machine must have been ridden at an excessive speed to cause the damage.

Sub-Inspector Alexander said that when Mr. Squire was cautioned and charged he preferred not to say anything. Mr. Lenski said he understood the Chinese made a statement before his death, but Chief Inspector Kent replied that the man died almost immediately after admission to hospital.

The case for the prosecution being closed, hearing was adjourned until this afternoon.

headline: THE SOVIET GHASTLY FAILURE OF SYNDICATED INDUSTRIES.
text:
Munchoull April 26,—Nowcomers from Soviet Russia report an extraordinary state of affairs as being in existence in that country, and inasmuch as some of them have been at one time or another other directly or indirectly connected with the Soviet Government but have now escaped to the Far East for refuge—being no longer able to stand the numerous impositions and acts of red-tape on the part of the powers that be, with the consequent impossible living conditions—there is no reason to doubt their statements. These newcomers represent men of all walks of life, some being engineers, textile workers and physicians, others, theatre artists, musicians and hospital attendants. What these people have reported is entirely different from the colourful accounts disseminated in the outside world under Soviet auspices. "You will" be interested to hear," said an engineer who formerly worked in a Soviet-front-foundry, "that living conditions have become so bad in Soviet Russia that professional men are one by one seeking means to escape to the outside world. We thought at first that in course of time conditions would so improve under the agis of the Government that comfortable employment would eventually be found by all, but after waiting nine long years for amelioration we have decided we have had enough.

People Poorer Than Ever. "The Soviet Government forcibly reminds us of the truth of the saying, 'Stealing from Peter to pay Paul.' Although there has been considerable talk of modifications in the Soviet financial and economic policies, the fact remains that private initiative is taxed to the utmost limit. Thus, we have worked for the Government have been obliged to buy our necessities from government organisations, and the prices quoted by these are at all times higher than those quoted by smugglers. We have found, in this way, that the wages received from the government are promptly snatched back by the Government.' After nine years of this sort of thing, it is no wonder we are poorer, off-to-day than we were in the beginning."

In order to be able to get out of the country, this informant said he had to hoodwink the Government with the information that he wished to gather fresh engineering knowledge and experience in Japanese institutions and had to give a pledge that he would return to Soviet Russia and that, whilst abroad, he would not concert with reactionaries.

Mills Denuded of Machinery. A textile-worker said that most of the mills in Soviet Russia are working only part-time both on account of luck of adequate machinery and inefficiency on the part of the Government comptrollers. These mills are unable to cover even one-fourth of the local demand for textiles, but this has not prevented the Soviet Government from establishing a "Textile Syndicate" with countless branches and agencies abroad. The fact of the matter, this textile-worker said, is that the Soviet Government has effected an arrangement with certain German mills to supply the "Syndicate" with German-made textiles, bearing the labels of the "Syndicate's" mills. The "Soviet Government is losing millions every year in these "Syndicate" operations which are, of course, intended for propaganda more than anything else.

IS IT THE HAT?

A physician who is now on his way to Shanghai said that it was impossible for him to conduct his own practice. The Soviet Government herded all physicians like so many sheep and told them what und what not to do as though evup in medical knowledge the Government knew more than men who had worked their way up in the profession. Under all sorts of red-ace, medical knowledge in Soviet Russia has declined by at least 30 per cent. until at the present time the common whisper in Russia is that the surest way to see the next world would be to enter one of the Soviet "sanitariums." Opera For Workmen Unpopular. An opera singer, now in Japan, and a violinist said that the Soviet Government considered music as an article instead of an art. In Moscow and Leningrad, they had to render concerts daily for the benefit of common labourers whose lack of appreciation of the performers' art was illustrated by the fact that during the progress of a concert there would be fighting going on in the hall at the same time. The artistes received no money but board and lodging. The former consisted usually of un savoury dishes turned out by government soup kitchens, whereas the latter meant a small, cold room mongrely furnished. The opera-singer had also to give a similar pledge to that given by

The opera-singer had also to give a similar pledge to that given by the engineer already mentioned before he was allowed to leave Russia with his wife and children They have all now found a home in Harbin.

In order to frustrate many people as possible from going abroad, the Soviet Government has recently revised its fees for passport Non-union members will now have to pay something like 300 dollars and union members 200 dollars for a passport. Even at these exorbitant rates, it takes months for anyone to secure a passport. A sorts of impositions are made up the population, and artificial methods to bring about a "satisfactory trade balance" are resorted to at every turn. Thus, during March, the Commissary for Trade reported that the "satisfaction balance" stood at 420,000 roubles. The fact of the matter was the during that month a good deal of goods imported into the country were held up on the frontiers of Europe and Asia to make way for exports.

Criticism of Foreign Policy. There is great dissatisfaction in the country over its political and economical situation. The Government is being subjected to sarcastic criticisms in regard to China policy and at China, during a meeting for the discussion of Marshal Chang Tso-lin's deman for Ambassador Karakhan's recall speaker after speaker denounce the shortsightedness of the Soviet agents abroad. The gathering has to be dispersed by the police, a heated had the speakers become eventually.

In connection with Comrade Karakhan, the engineer said, this was not the first time his recall had been demanded by a foreign Government. Comrade Karakhan, while acting as Soviet envoy, to Latvia, and subsequently as Soviet envoy to Poland, was requested to both the Latvian and Polish Governments to make himself scarce in view of his activities as a propagandist against these Governments. "It would be interesting," this engineer remarked, "to know whether the Soviet Government still considers Karakhan an abidylomat."

Commissars' Childish Stupidity. In Moscow, the Commissars are much annoyed with Japan. They had expected the Japanese Government to interfere in the Chinese demand for Comrade Karakhan withdrawal, but Tokyo having done nothing in this direction, they have arrived at the conclusion, through typically Soviet logic that Japan is not a friend of Russia. Indeed no one has said that Japan was a friend of Soviet Russia, but commonsense would have told these Commissars that no Government could interfere with another Government on behalf of a third Government without running the risk of creating resentment. Investigators from abroad are shown around all the bright sides and the newcomers from Soviet Russia predict that the party of British Conservative members who have just left for that country on an investigation trip will be shown not what they should see but what the Soviet Government would like them to see. Although the Soviet government has promised the party in entirely free hand, it would see to it that the "rudes" would only conduct Sir Frank Nelson, Mr Robert Boothby, Captain R. C. Bourne and Lieutenant-Colonel Russell-Moore through an especially created fairyland. headline: RUSSIA'S DEFEAT IN CHINA.
text:
OVERREACH THEMSELVES AND

The defeat of the Kuominchun army in North China by the combined forces of Chang Tso-lin and Wu Fei-fu marks the end of Soviet Russia's influence in North China and gives strength to the anti-Communist movement throughout China. "Feng Yu-hslang was avowedly the ally of Soviet Russia. He frequently accepted assistance in arms and money from the Bolshevik Government, the success or failure of his enterprise depending to a great extent on this assistance from Russia. His British and Japanese orientation was to a large extent the result of Russian instigation. In such circumstances, his defeat became as much an international necessity as it was an internal political necessity. For the conduct of the Kuomichun Government in Peking was fast leading to a complete dislocation of the relationship between China and the Western Powers and further irritation of the Powers by the Kuominchun Government would undoubtedly have led to some form of foreign intervention, which foreigners in China deprecate as much as do the Chinese themselves.

Furthermore, the advance of Soviet Russia into China by means of a Chinese ally, was leading to a situation which would require Japan to safeguard her position in Manchuria and Mongolia. It is difficult even to imagine what international complications might have resulted from this unfortunate imperilling of the peace of the Pacific by the Chinese allies of Soviet Russia, and the foreign Powers have much cause for gratitude in the defeat of the Kuomintang by a Chinese army.

headline: A War of Revenge:
text: It must not, however, be presumed that Feng Yu-hsiang and his Soviet allies are altogether out of the field. They have a vast area in Mongolia, then continued preparation, in a sparsely populated region where there are few observers who can intelligently record their conduct. It is to be assumed that they will utilise the geographical suitability of this area to prepare for the day when they can swoop down on Peking in an effort to wrest from China its government, while all the time giving to the world the impression that the Chinese themselves are conducting the quarrel. Again, it is the Japanese who will have to be in constant vigilance against Soviet machinations. For whereas other foreign Powers may suffer in trade and in prestige from the Soviet propaganda and politics in China, Japan is concerned with the protection of vital interests, with the consideration of her supplies of food and raw materials, and with the knowledge that all Russian activities whether conducted by the old imperialist Russia or by Soviet Russia, are designed for the fighting a war of revenge for the defeat of Russia by the Japanese at the beginning of this century.

headline: In Canton:
text:
In South China, Russian influence is also on the wane. During the past year, the Soviet Government has been able to afford the Cantonese Government considerable assistance in connection with the reorganisation of the Canton army. For a while the Russians were able to have it all their own way in Canton. Because of the strike and boycott against Great Britain and the popular objection to all unequal treaties and the antagonism to imperialist powers, Russia stood out as an exceptionally friendly power. Russian ways and Russian ideas became popular in Canton and the presence of a big, unemployed, angry body of strikers from Hongkong gave the Russians the opportunity to conduct a strong Bolshevik propaganda and to increase the power of the Communist Party in South China.

The Russians, however, over-talked themselves. They gave the appearance of bossing the show. They tried to manage affairs in Canton as though it were their government and not the government of the people of the province of Kuangtung. Although the Cantonese dislike giving the appearance of ingratitude to the people who had been of such assistance to them, they nevertheless were forced to remove many of the Russians from their high positions. At the present moment a powerful anti-communist tendency is developing in Canton, and it is to be expected that the days of the Communist Party in Canton, are numbered.

Soviet Russia suffered in China from a lack of comprehension of the Oriental character. Nothing offends the Oriental more than the suggestion that he is dependent upon western assistance for his development. The Oriental does not mind employing western ways and western ideas. Both Japanese and Chinese have at times and are

still employing western ideas and assistance but some Westerners hold that the Eastern peoples can do nothing at all without foreign supervision. The Russians apparently believe that the Chinese could not conduct an anti-British movement without their assistance. They boasted of their great accomplishment in Canton, they spoke of the Kuomintang party almost as being their own property. They have even attempted a coup d'état against the existing Government in Canton. Therein lies their weakness, and their mistake. They over-renched themselves and lost out. Their failure in Canton is even more important than their failure in North China, and it is doubtful if they will ever recover the opportunities they have lost. Far Eastern Review.

Since the boycott, silk is shipped in native craft, from Hongkong to Whampon, where, after paying the illicit taxes imposed by the Strike Committee, it is often loaded into old and unsuitable trumps, steamers of small tonnage, carried to ports such as Shanghai or Keelung, and again transhipped to the ocean steamer bound for Europe or America. One instance of the destructive nature of the present boycott may here be quoted. headline: BANGKOK CHOLERA
text:
TARTING INCREASE IN DUCATION BY CINEMA. There has been a startling increase in the number of cholera cases in Bangkok, as shown by the report of the Acting Medical Officer of Health for the week ended May 8. There were notified 255 cases and 145 deaths. This is a big jump over the figures of the previous week, when there were 143 cases and 88 deaths. The following are the figures for the last six weeks:—

In the registration area of Bangkok 5,538 persons were inoculated against cholera by the Division of the Medical Officer of Health during the week ended May 1, and 1,508 persons during the week ending May 8. Within the last week three cases of cholera have broken out among the boarders of the Assumption College. Two of these proved fatal and one boy is on the way to recovery at the temporary ward in the Palace of H.R.H. Prince Jainad. As soon as the first case was discovered on Friday last, the Director of the College informed the medical authorities and after a thorough inspection of the premises it was pronounced that "the latrimes' cook-house and other buildings were in a very sanitary condition. Every precaution was taken, and practically all the students, numbering over a thousand have been inoculated against the disease. Regarding day scholars, there have been two cases; both of which proved fatal. Never in the history of the institution has there been an epidemic of cholera amongst the students. It is gratifying to note that there have been no cases reported during the last two days, and one may assume that with the great care taken there is no fear of the disease spreading amongst the students of the College.

headline: JAPAN AND EGYPT / NEGOTIATIONS FOR TREATY.
text:
The "Mainichf" reports that negotiations have just been opened between Mr. Yokoyama, the Japanese Consul-General at Alexandria, and the Egyptian Government for the conclusion of a commercial treaty. In view of the marked growth of trade with Egypt, says the Osaka journal, the Japanese Foreign Office has decided to open negotiations with that country for the conclusion of a treaty of commerce and navigation, and has caused the Japanese Consul-General at Alexandria to sound the Egyptian Government on the subject. The ready consent of the Government to these overtures having been obtained, pourparlers have quite recently been opened between him and the Egyptian Foreign Office. It is said that the Japanese Government means to conclude a permanent treaty, not a temporary one. There has hitherto existed no treaty between the two countries.

text:

The following items of interest are extracted from thó Harbour Mutter's report for 1925:—

The total shipping entering and clearing at ports in the Colony during the year 1925 amounted to 370,177 vessels of 41,469,884 tons, which compared with the figures of 1924 show a decrease of 384,315 vessels and a decrease of 15,261,493 tons.

Of the above 41,336 vessels of 32,179,063 tons were engaged in foreign trade as compared with 57,765 vessels of 38,770,499 tons, in 1924.

This decrease in ships and tonnage is due to the recent strike and the present boycott in South China.

Foreign ocean-going vessels have decreased by 1,911 ships and by 2,243,124 tons or 22.3 per cent. in numbers and 13.1 per cent. in tonnage. This decrease in ships and tonnage is due to the recent strike and the present boycott in South China.

British river steamers have decreased by 3,062 ships with a decrease in tonnage, of 1,069,546 tons or 43.0 per cent. in numbers and 16.3 per cent. in tonnage. This decrease in ships and tonnage is due to the recent strike and the present boycott in South China.

Junks in foreign trade show a decrease of 6,578 vessels, and a decrease of 847039 tons or 23.9 percent. in numbers and 25.6 percent. in tonnage. This decrease is due to the recent strike and the present boycott in South China.

headline: CHANG'S COUP.
text:
COMMUNISTS TO MAKE FRESH BID FOR POWER

AN UNSATISFACTORY TRUCE

All is not peace and harmony in the "Kuomintang. The Communist faction of the Canton Nationalist Government is not accepting with any grace the recent political coup of General Chang Kai-shek and his supporters, whereby Communist influence in the Government is sharply curbed and clearly delineated.

This means that the struggle for supremacy will go on, and that present conditions mark only an unsatisfactory truce. The next trial of strength will take place in August, when the regular meeting of the Central Executive Committee will be held here, the protracted sessions which began May 15 having been extraordinary sessions.

At the next meeting the moderates will make a determined effort to oust the Communists entirely. Already they are charging bad faith on the part of the radicals, and the fomenting of new intrigues. The "truce" with the Communists was made for the sake of peace at home while the northern military expedition is under way, but the present attitude of the Communists is said to be frustrating that motive.

One charge heard in official circles is that the Communists manifest a spirit of obstruction toward the settling of troublesome outside affairs, such as the conciliatory settlement of the Hongkong boycott, the settlement of the Oil monopoly, and other foreign affairs. Such obstructionist tactics are held by the moderates to be tantamount to treason, for they tend to cripple the Government in the conduct of the campaign against Wu Pei-fu.

The Communists, for instance, are finding ready allies in the more radical of the labouring, and union men. One subject which came up for discussion in a star-chamber season was the matter of abolishing the strikers' and picketers' courts when the Hongkong boycott is called off. The moderates insisted that these extra-legal courts would have to be abolished, but the radicals and labour men insist that they shall continue to function to handle all cases connected with any kind of strike that may be going on. The Communists gave their support to this contention:

The Government does not dare to carry over its policies along this line by a show of force, for to do so would be openly to force all the labour and union adherents into open allegiance with the Communist elements.

Preparing For May 30. Meanwhile preparations are under way for a gigantic meeting of memorial and protest on May 30, the first anniversary of the Shanghai incident. There will be a great deal of parading and speech making, with central meetings at the East Parade Ground and at the amphitheatre of Kwangtung University.

The police and military, however, will do all they can (as they did on May 1 and on May 7) to keep the demonstrators away from the Shakee and the general vicinity of Shumeen.

Currency Depreciation. The General Chamber of Commerce has circularised all the guilds and important merchants of Canton concerning recent events which for a time tended to depreciate the value of the Central Bank Notes. The Chamber of Commerce announces support of the Government edict which threatens arrest and punishment not only for people who refuse to accept the notes at par, but also for those who spread disquieting rumours about the value of the paper money.

headline: CARGO SEIZED.
text:
How Canton watermen dived into the river, rather than face the strike pickets, is related by passengers who have come down to Hongkong.

On Saturday night, or in the small hours of Sunday morning, a number of shots were fired. It appears that two native boats, loaded with about 20 tubes of (fresh water) fish, valued at over $1,000, were making for the s.s. "Lungshan." An allegation has been made that "permission had been arranged," whatever that may mean—and it is given only for what it is worth.

When 500 feet or so off shore, the boats were fired at; presumably by boycott pickets. One of the first shots hit a helmsman who either fell or jumped into the river. Another fokl was also struck, and he went overboard. When the fire got within range, several others followed.

The foreign warships trained their searchlights on the spot. One report is that a boat was lowered, and two of the refugees were thus saved. The fish boats and the cargoons are stated to have been seized by the pickets.

headline: SITUATION INTENSER
text: London, May 7. A communique states that there are no serious disorders in any part of the country. The work of feeding the people and maintaining the light and power for essential communications is being successfully accomplished. Over 2,000 trains ran yesterday — nearly double that of Wednesday. There is a substantial improvement on the main lines. The suburban services are arranging for protection. The London motor buses are running most satisfactorily and constantly increasing in numbers. But the situation is becoming inteniser. The climax has not yet been reached. Orders have been issued by the leaders of the Railways and Transport Unions to do their utmost to paralyse and breakdown, the supply of food and the necessaries of life. Intimation. The communique says that intimidation by disorderly crowds and picketing has occurred in many places, and may soon occur in many more. The Government has directed the authorities to repress and overcome these criminal obstructions. The recruitment of special contactables all over the country is vigorously and rapidly pressing. headline: RUSSIAN LABOUR. / INDO-CHINA / STEAM NAVIGATION CO LTD.
text: British workers, who imagine that Russian labour conditions are ideal, will find a good deal to interest them in the report which Mr. Tomsky gave to the 14th Congress at Moscow of the Communist Party. Mr. Tomsky, who is chairman of the All-Russian Council of Trade Unions, says, for instance, that, in principle, strikes in State undertakings are prohibited. A strike in a proletarian State is a proof of some defect in the State machinery, or of the weakness of the trade unions, or of lack of education on the parts of the workers. The trade unions must do everything in their power to settle disputes in State undertakings by means of conciliation or arbitration, and at all costs to avoid strikes. There have recently been certain irregularities in the settlement of disputes. Instead of being settled by conciliation and arbitration, some of these disputes have been referred to the Communist party organisations. Such action impairs the authority of the regular institutions, makes non-party workers lose confidence in their union and in the impartiality of the decisions taken, and ends by embittering disputes and disorganising the whole labour movement. In private undertakings, or the other hand, any form of dispute is allowed; but a strike may be declared only in the event of the failure of conciliation and arbitration. In no case should the trade unions exercise any administrative pressure on the private employer, for this tends to weaken the worker's notion of the class struggle and the power of the trade union. The trade union should rather strengthen the authority of the Commissariat of Labour as an impartial arbitrator.

Hongkong, Tuesday, April 6, 1926. ASSETS TO THE COLONY.

The Hongkong Government's grants to unemployed officers of the British Mercantile Marine are touched upon in the latest issue of Shipping and Engineering (Shanghai). Locally, of course, it is known that the grants offered were the outcome of a Board of

investigation into cases of hardship occasioned through the strike and the boycott. Amongst those most concerned there has been no great rush to participate in the grant. Many have been idle for months; their little capital has been well eaten into—in some cases of married officers doubtless melted away by now—but they shrink from what some are inclined to look upon as a dole; that hateful word begotten of the unemployed problem at Home. It has never been intended that the grants here should smack either of doles or charity; and it is a great pity that such an unfortunate misconception ever arose. As our Shanghai contemporary rightly puts it:

It should not be forgotten that these officers are actually an asset to the Colony (we are referring entirely to those who have been thrown out of employment through the boycott and whose services, if the boycott were fully lifted, would be in immediate demand for the benefit of the Colony's trade), and that the Hongkong Government, in deciding to make them grants from public funds, is doing nothing more than is just. These men are respectable members of an honourable profession, many of them having families to support, and it was an obvious necessity, if their services were to be kept available in the event of a full resumption of shipping services, that the Government should take steps to keep them "going."

The grants range from two dollars a day in the case of single men to a maximum of five dollars in the case of married men, due regard being paid to the circumstances of each particular case. Were these grants—not too generous by any means—to be taken advantage of by all (and not merely a few) whom they are designed to aid in the Colony's own interests and also paid promptly, the community would feel that the Government was doing something of which to be justly proud. But—and why there should always be a but we know not—our Shanghai contemporary refers to a local report of delays in paying out grants already passed by the Board of Investigation. It continues:— From private information which we have received from Hongkong the regrettable and unnecessary delay in making payment may be placed wholly at the doors of the Hongkong Treasury. Department. Whilst it has come generally to be admitted that only in the most exceptional circumstances will any Department of any Government do anything quickly and in a business-like manner, it is submitted that the present circumstances are sufficiently exceptional, and the need of monetary relief by those affect

ed sufficiently acute, to warrant even a Treasury Department departing from precedent and practice and producing without delay money the payment of which has been approved by the competent authorities, and the need of which is so urgent to the grantees. Surely the Treasury Department of the Hong Kong Government is not so overburdened with labour that it takes weeks to issue money for grants to some of the Colony's best non-official public servants. If it is, then some other method should be devised, and quickly, whereby the payments approved by the Grants Committee will reach those for whom they are intended in a reasonable time.

Our northern contemporary has been quoted so fully not with any desire to "fling mud" at the Hongkong Government, but to show the great amount of interest taken in the subject of these grants outside this Colony. When a journal of the standing of Shipping and Engineering gives prominence to an alleged grievance of this nature—even though it rests on the usually flimsy base of private information—it is time for something to be done. Either the allegation of undue delays in paying out these grants is beside the mark (in which event they can be officially denied) or there is some foundation for it (in which event the local authorities should be trusted to remedy the defect immediately). The good name of the Colony is at stake. And the community requires official enlightenment of the true position of affairs!

The initial difficulty in following Chinese militarism is the number of leaders who figure in the strife they create and recreate. A more important one is the difficulty foreigners find in seeing reason in all that is done in the cause of China's reunification. Reunification, it might be said what sins are committed in thy name! Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang will go down in Chinese history as "the Christian General". His "braves" have been known to sing hymns — they have probably entered into "battle" with the tune of "Onward Christian Soldiers" ringing in their ears—while a Methodist clergyman is said to have been engaged to minister to the spiritual wants of the General's troops. Feng's publicity department is beyond criticism. Like consistent, well-arranged advertisements, he sticks in the memory. His exploits—Christian and otherwise—are always likely to receive first consideration. His latest intention is to pawn—by pawn we mean put in safe keeping—his Marshal's baton, and lie him, not to a nunnery, as the poet would have it, but to a Moscow factory, there to study politico-economic conditions. This must be an ideal factory for workmen—unless workmen would rather work than study. And Feng is going to use the result of his study on his return to his native land. The change, he says, "does not disturb me." All this savours of a nice little holiday. How the knowledge acquired in Russia of economic conditions there, is going to benefit conditions in China, is not quite apparent. Some of China's troubles—economic and otherwise—are of her own seeking. And these troubles include militarists—Christian or otherwise. Perhaps the good marshal seeks to become China's Mussolini. We must hope for the best.

The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyod proceeds on leave to-morrow by the s.s. "Sarpedon."

In educational circles the usual interest was manifested in the annual presentation of prizes at the Wah Yan School, where the Vice Chancellor of the University gave an inspiring address to the pupils. In Club land the week has been noteworthy on account of the decision of the Kowloon Bowling Green Club to form itself into a limited liability company with the object of simplifying the issue of debentures for the erection of the new pavilion, operations on which are expected to be commenced next month. When completed the new pavilion should greatly add to the amenities of this part of Kowloon. At the annual meeting of the Kowloon Golf Club it was decided not to raise the annual subscription, as was at one time mooted. Interport sporting relations have been improved by a visit to Hongkong of a Portuguese football team from Shanghai, an interesting series of matches being played in spite of inclement weather on one or two days. The Fanling Hunt Club held another enjoyable steeplechase meeting on Monday, although the attendance of the general public was not so good as was anticipated. The celebrated Australian cueist, George Gray, is in the Colony but his first match at the Engineers' Institute proved a fiasco, the champion being completely off form.

Home affairs have been rather subdued during the week, no doubt due to the aftermath of the Easter holidays. The Coal Commission's report has again been the most prominent theme of discussion, which "alternated between fears of another crisis and hopes of an amicable compromise between the miners and the coal owners. The Prince of Wales has reached the convalescent stage and has gone to Sandwich; whilst the latest reports of the condition of His Majesty, the King's sister, Princess Victoria, who was rather seriously ill, have been of a reassuring nature. Hongkong: It is to be trusted that adequate arrangements will be made for their reception here. Mr. Alan Cobham is making arrangements to add to his aerial feats by a flight this time to Australia—a country which is making very great headway in the art of aviation. There is also talk of a flight by Japanese airmen from Tokyo to the Dutch East Indies via Hongkong or Manila.

Coming to matters in the Overseas Possessions, there have been religious feuds in Calcutta and a strike of mill workers as the outcome of allegations of assault on a coolie by a European — allegations that have been denied. Apparently it does not require much of these days to stir up the industrial malcontents in India, thanks to the careful coaching of the extremists, assisted covertly, no doubt, by the Communists. Aviation has figured very much in the week's news, the greatest enthusiasm being evinced in Madrid over the departure for Manila of three Spanish "aces." As these are expected to touch at

In foreign politics the sensation of the week has been the attempt on the life of Signor Mussolini, the Dictator of Italy, by an eccentric British lady connected with the Peerage, who claims to have accomplished a "lofty mission." The outrage has horrified the whole world and instead of calling attention to whatever undesirable features there may be in Fascism, has only made of Mussolini a greater national hero than ever. Nowadays "lofty missions" are not accomplished by the revolver or the sword. France has been stirred by a national appeal for voluntary subscriptions to pay off all the debts of the nation, and General Joffre has been appointed President of the National Committee. M. Malvy, a stormy petrel in war time, who was recently appointed Minister of the Interior, has resigned. Even nations may forgive and yet not forget! The dove of peace has appeared on the horizon in Morocco, and Abd el Krim has sent an emissary to talk for him in regard to terms of settlement. Greece reports a trifling and short-lived mutiny of troops, whilst the ancient city of Bagdad is threatened by unprecedented

To all outward appearances the position in Canton remains a stalemate, but it is on the cards that any day may produce important developments in regard to the boycott. This being so, the matter need not be further discussed here. The civil war in the North proceeds "normally" fighting one day and rurours of peace pourfurlers the next. Some day or some year the Chinese may awaken to the realisation that militarism is the greatest curse of that unhappy country.

Monday next should be a redletter day in your history. For the first time for years you are being asked to record what some of you, perhaps, never imagined you possessed a vote. Two public-spirited gentlemen seek your suffrages, and to serve you on the Sanitary Board. These gentlemen—if we know them bright—are not place-hunters, or limelight seekers. They are members of an honourable profession, the first qualification for membership of which is knowledge. They seek to place that knowledge at the service of the community in a sphere that is highly important—sanitation. Much has been said recently in criticism of the sanitary measures in vogue in this Colony. We may be a city of fragrant streams, but, alas! we are also a city of fragrant smells. The Sanitary Board may be likened to a poor man striving against adversity. Its powers are limited, for ever in the shadow is that which has been described as a Benevolent Government, overriding, cutting down, and literally throwing cold water on schemes which aim at longevity, or a more healthy state of existence. The Sanitary Board is well served by its co-opted and elected members. A vacancy occurs which must be filled. Two candidates compliment you by asking you to consider their claims to serve you. They compliment you by the implied suggestion that you are interested in the Colony's health and that you do really think about the Colony's needs. The least you can do is to return that compliment by deciding between now and Monday for whom you will vote; and to take care that your vote is cast.

The “China Mail” takes no sides and does not recommend. It does urge you to exercise that which seems to have been given you because you are likely to be called to serve upon a jury—in its way a tribute that you are an intelligent entity, capable of thinking and acting. Judges are as sympathetic and soft-hearted as other people is a reminder of a debate in the House of Commons 50 years back. Mr. Attorney-General Coleridge was supporting a Woman's Suffrage Bill, and, in-stancing the aptitudes of women for careers then closed to them, he remarked that many women had the graceful qualities of sympathy and so were well fitted to adorn the bench of judges. All this impressed the House. All old Serjeant Dowse got up to oppose. "His argument," said the Serjeant, "seems to be this—that because some judges are old women, therefore old women ought to be judges."

headline: SMUGGLERS'. HOST OF TRICKS.
text:
News of a brisk smuggling trade in rubber, due to the export revestictions imposed on the planters, is contained in dispatches from Penang, Straits Settlements. Such news smacks of a romantic past through which fitted Malay pirates, with—for Western counterpart—picaroons and rapparees and guardacootas. The old-time smuggler looms in the modern eye as a bronzed man with a kerchief on his head, standing in the red glow of a fire flaring on a high hill above a rocky inlet. The fact is, according to those who have surveyed the situation, that the art and science of smuggling was never at a finer point nor more extensive than today. The age of radio, swift sea-scout guards and vigilant aeroplanes may in time be called the golden age of smuggling.

Puncheons and bales did for the contrabandist of other days. But he would be astounded, and perhaps sometimes shocked, at the thousand refinements developed by modern underground traffic in silk, cotton, wheat, diamonds, narcotics, coolies, aliens, liquor, arms, rubber and lesser items. Its leaders reported that there had been a heavy increase in the illicit traffic, against which the last Canadian Parliament enacted, more stringent laws. Paris mannequins are not needed on the Canadian border. The work is done on a rough, and ready basis, like the trade in rum or that in Canadian wheat, which crosses into Minnesota, or North Dakota by night in rumbling farm wagons. The Canadian border has furnished plenty of finesse, nevertheless, One instance which caused worry not long ago was that of a police dog with a collar. It would be taken into Canada in a car openly, but never twice in succession along the same road. A night or two, then the dog would trot back into the United States with its collar full of opium. The beast was trained to let no one touch it, but its master and one confederate, and it knew its way home. The only effective move against it would be to shoot every-collared police dog on sight.

If the smuggler ever looked like a picture book pirate, now he—or she—may saunter past the Customs men as spick and span as a mannequin. She is, in fact, a mannequin, running back and forth between France and England as diligently as an endless belt, and on each trip wearing half a dozen suits of those sheer silk garments which were taxed so high under the new British silk duties. This sort of smuggler has driven the Customs guard at Dover and Folkestone frantle trying to catch her, for a mere glance will not show whether she has on a single pair of stockings or eight; and as for the other things—

Rear-Admiral F.C. Billard of the Coast Guard recently said that, as far as the United States was concerned, smuggling at sea had practically disappeared and running had been reduced. In one aspect or another, however, smuggling has given the United States such increased concern in recent years that it has been found necessary to make ten new treaties with various nations.

Rum row off New York has its counterpart in the East Indies, where rubber running has sprung into a thriving industry, with wealthy interests as higher-ups. Coolies do the actual work, landing the cargoes in the Dutch East Indies for export and drawing big money for doing it, with compensation if they are caught. There are other parts of the world where smuggling to-dry is a maritime affair, but some of the chief problems of the United States, aside from the coast. Ilquor trade are created by hland smuggling.

The public hears a good deal of border rum-runners, but not much about the cotton and silk smugglers along the Canadian line. When the Canadian cotton industry summed up its last year, however,

This dog has a fellow smuggler on the Mexican border—a burrow with the homing instinct. It carried liquor worth $240 a trip. Hoofprints in sand where there should have been none gave the clue. In England smugglers have gone farther in the use of animals, employing homing pigeons to bring in cocaine. That was a trick discovered in Limehouse after Chang, the biggest power in London's Chinatown, had been deported, says an exchange. Less striking methods are favoured by the gem contrabandists who use the Canadian route. The native in the South African diamond mines who sneaks out a raw diamond uses the simplest methods, such as swallowing it if need be. The traveller via Canada often manifests the subtlety of simplicity. One, of note in his profession according to the authorities, was caught in a sleeping car in Vermont recently. His compartment showed nothing but traveller's equipment such as collar box and talcum can, but in these and their like 37 packages of uncut diamonds were found. The trip, if successful, would have saved £5,000 in duties.

The ways of the smuggler are shrewder than ever, and his goods more varied. An alien crawls toward the American side along the girders under a Niagara Falls bridge. A Turkish refugee sets up housekeeping in a small Berlin flat with 85 rugs. A sailing ship is reported missing in the Baltic and is sighted later with a new coat of paint. A clerk in a Paris shop tells something to an American official, and waits for his 25 per cent reward when the customer has been caught forgetting to declare her purchase on her arrival here. A string of coolies flies past a cactus in Lower California and somewhere in the Near East the top cargo under a linen sail is only a mask for guns. They are all chapters in the same twentieth century story.
