The General Chamber of Commerce has expressed its opinion in favour of the re-opening of the Statistics Office, whilst the Chinese Chamber is apparently half-hearted. Meanwhile, until the Government considers both views the arrears of statistics are getting further behind, and valuable ground is being rapidly lost. Before the strike commenced the value of the Statistics Office was not taken into account from the mere point of view of expenditure. It was just swept away in the first flush of enthusiasm over the retrenchment campaign. If its reopening now is not justified, its existence up to the middle of last year could not possibly be defended. But it is conceded on all sides that it did do valuable work, and not even a Government official would admit that the expenditure on it was money wasted. In these days of keen international competition a country without statistics is surely inviting that state of lethargy that lends to decay in all that affects its trade.

headline: RICKSHAS
text:
It is remarkable the number of people who persist deliberately in not seeing the wood for the trees. Here is an individual—if not fashioned as a god—entitled to claim that God made man in his own image. Yet this person will see what is known as'red,' if the word 'indicating' Hongkong's ancient road vehicle is not spelt as he thinks it should be. Jinrikisha it probably is. "Ricsha, ricksha, rickshaw, it may be, but there is only one way—and that is his. Talk to this type of person about the social conditions attached to the calling of a puller of humanity, and he is found uninterested......Having written in full sympathy with a class who perform a most useful function, it is not likely, at this late hour of the day, that we shall take back what we have said. Our strictures, if any, are towards those who control the ricksha traffic. There are, for instance, rules governing in what manner a ricksha may be used. It is ordinarily licensed to convey human beings. There is a rule we believe that prohibits the conveyance of "sides" of meat and articles of food in large quantities. And yet how often does one see a vehicle so used! We think another rule should be added, and that is to prohibit a ricksha being used to convey a person suffering from an infectious illness. How often this happens, we know not. But the spectacle is fairly common of poor sufferers, looking lost to this world, being taken to some place, presumably for treatment. We have full sympathy with the lot of those unable to secure and pay for an ambulance; but it should not be difficult for a simple method to be devised that would cater for those who need to be taken to hospital. The matter does not appear to have been thought of. Here then is a further opportunity for the sympathetic to demonstrate their sympathy, or for the Police department to devise a plan which will prevent possible contamination and consequent suffering by those who may use an "unclean" ricksha.

headline: PREMIER MOVES
text:
Conl Owners May Be Summoned.

The "coal situation" underwent a further development to-day. The Executive of the Miners' Federation was received at Downing Street by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour as Secretary for Mines, and a discussion took place on the difficulties which have anise in connection with the coal owners' proposals for district negotiations.

The Prime Minister thereupon undertook to get into touch with the coal owners Association as soon as possible and asked the miners Executive to be available early next week for further discussions.

It is understood that the Prime Minister will call the coal owners into conference in the course of the day.

Hope for Resumption. In the afternoon the Miners' Executive met the Industrial Committee of the Trades, Union Congress and reported the result of their interview with the Prime Minister.

A communication was subsequently issued, in which the hope was expressed that as a result of the miners' meeting with the Prime Minister an early resumption of the negotiations with the coal owners would be possible. As, however, it was not anticipated that anything definite on this point would be known until early next week the Miners' Executive and the Industrial Committee of the Trades Union Congress would not meet again until next Wednesday morning, unless some development occurred in the meantime.

Subsequently Mr. Herbert Smith and Mr. A. J. Cock, President and Secretary, respectively, of the Miners' Federation, left for Brussels to attend to-morrow's meeting of the Executive of the Miners' Internationale.

Wu, but beyond saying that these were cordial and friendly and that they will be resumed before the formal conference between the Canton and Hongkong delegates the public is left to imagine a lot. It is something, however, to learn that Mr. Kemp, on behalf of the Hongkong Government, informed Dr. Wu that under no circumstances would the Hongkong Government pay anything in the way of pay for the strikers or compensation in any shape or form, and that it would not countenance any such payments by others. The British Consul-General in Canton, Sir James Jamieson, arrived in Hongkong during the week and left on Friday for a trip to the Old Country on leave. It may be expected that most of his holiday will be spent at the Foreign Office, in which case Sir Austen Chamberlain's replies to questions in the House of Commons may prove a trifle more illuminating and informative in future than in the recent past. Hongkong has been favoured with a visit from one of the two Danish aviators who are flying to Japan, but this aerial "ace" called at Canton and gave Hongkong the go by—only to find that after all he may be obliged to bring his machine to this Colony and "take off" here on his departure to Shanghai and Japan. Whilst the "Wets" and the "Drys" have been enjoying almost hectic week of controversy before the Senate Committee of Enquiry into Prohibition the "Wets" here had a miniature field day on Friday. The annual meeting of the shareholders of Gande, Price & Co., Limited, disclosed a good business in the wine trade during the year, and if the profits were not quite so good as in the previous year they were sufficient to allow of a dividend being declared. The annual meeting of the Lawn Bowls Association was held during the week, when it was wisely decided to revert to the system in vogue before last season of deciding the open singles championship. Fifteen entries were received for the League competition, a Club new to the Association being welcomed, namely, the Club de Recreio.

At Home the Coal Commission's report has again provided the chief topic for Reuter and the British Wireless Service. On Thursday it appeared as if the negotiations between the coal owners and the miners would break down completely, but the Prime Minister's intervention has provided a ray of hope. Still, there is time yet for a genuine crisis to arise, just as there is time for both sides to decide to come to a mutual agreement on the controversial points at issue. It is noteworthy that His Majesty the King has summoned the Prime Minister to Windsor to discuss the position. An engineering crisis is threatened, the conference of Engineering Employers and Trade Unions on the national demand for a pound weekly wage increase having failed to reach an agreement. The Trade Unions are now considering the question of

authorising a strike ballot in London and districts. The Labour members have run riot in the House of Commons on the Economy Bill, thirteen of their number being ejected in the course of an all-night sitting. They apparently must do something in the spectacular line to impress the "free and independent" electors, who returned them to Westminster!

Amongst foreign topics the serious menace of Bagdad created no little anxiety for some days, the flood level being fifteen leeft above the city. Fortunately the breach in the River Tigris has been repaired by a thousand men depositing thousands of sand bags in the river from barges. And the populace of Bagdad have been relieved of the fear of inundation. The Spanish aviators who are flying to Manila from Madrid are having their movements duly reported. Their leader, Captain Estevez, however, has been left behind between Cairo and Amman and has not yet been located, although his machine has been found intact. His two comrades were yesterday reported to have reached Agra.

The Allied forces in the North of China have closed in on the Kuominchun armies, who have been compelled to evacuate Peking, Tuan Chi-juli, who recently took refuge in the Legation Quarter, has returned to the Presidential Palace and resumed the functions of his office. Tsao Kun, the ex-President, who was recently released from confinement by the Kuominchun, has now gone to the Legation Quarter. The Allied commanders have avowed their intention to suppress Bolshevism, and the Mukden War Lord has clearly hinted that if M. Karakhan values his skin he had better quit Peking.

headline: THE CHURCHES
text:
Rarely, if ever, do customs change in things Clerical. An exception may be cited in the Community Church at Shanghai which is a place for the community, and where the modern is introduced. to a remarkable degree. In Hongkong the dignity of the Church of England service contrasts with the simpleness of the services at the Union and Wesleyan Churches. It cannot be said that these three places attract the crowd to its services. So much the worse for the crowd perhaps. But there may be something in the thought that if people won't go to church, the church must go to the people. How? That must be for padres and workers themselves to decide. In these days of debaters, and the move to get men on their feet to speak what is in their minds, could not the Church do something to aid the thought of man in matters of religion? Congregations, we are told, sit mute and torpid, sluggishly allowing divine truths and human errors to flow indiscriminately down the channels of their ears. Preachers are from four to six feet above criticism. That is the trouble. Much might be gained in alertness and attention if congregations were expected to raise questions upon the sermon, at all events after it was over. For there is frequently some point in a sermon open to doubt, and a questioner would always remember his question if not the answer. This is not a new idea; but it is an idea with tremendous possibilities. It contains a challenge. It might, if adopted, attract the "gas-bags." Properly managed it should attract the thoughtful person; the doubting Thomases; and the many who are perplexed, and remain so because they see no clear way out from the morass of their perplexity.

It is reported in Command. Orders that Flight Lieut. L. Wanless O'Gowan, R.A.F. disembarked from the s.s. "Macedonia" on April 1, and assumed the duties of Air Staff Officer on that date.

headline: OLD ORDER CHANGETH.
text:
"It's an ill wind that blows nobody any good," the old saying goes. One result of a recent bankruptcy case is that a new Chinese shop has been established, replete with most forms of modern display whilst neighbouring competitors are content with things as they are. "This is characteristic of a great many branches of Chinese trade. A walk through the native business quarter will show the layman that there is abundant room for craftsmanship in setting off a business."

Along Queen's Road, facing the Central Market, have been a number of shops which are generally known as storekeepers. The writer remembers every one of them for the last twenty years. With an established clientele; they made their yearly profits, and were therefore satisfied. Each one looked very much like the others.

A few months ago, one of them was closed. It now seems either that the stock has either been cleared, or that what has remained has changed hands.

The new owner has arranged his establishment on very different lines. 'Touches of décoration here, better lighting there, a generally "showy" display of the lines carried, and many other knick-knacks combine to impress the eye.

There was one phase of “olo custom” that “was not ignored. This was the string of firecrackers which went off one morning this week when the new firm formally opened its doors to the public.

Looking For Bargains. One of the crowd of idlers that stood around for no apparent reason—they were not admiring the contents of the shop—was heard to make a remark. His manner had to be seen to be appreciated. "This shop must be very miserly," he confided to a younger man. "Several people have been in and made purchases, but not one of them got a bargain."

When a Chinese business opens, the first customer is given a genuine bargain, probably getting an article three or four times (either in quantity or quality) the value paid by him. This is probably a courtesy of old times. The first “client” of a pawnshop can usually hand up an old, worn pair of cotton trousers and get a loan of $2 or so, which would be more than what the garment originally cost. Accordingly, a new pawnshop is besieged with men of the coolie class when it commences business, and the struggle for the “bargain” resolves itself into a case of the survival of the fittest.

The idler's. grouse recorded alone may have been based on the fact that this generosity was dispensed with in the present hard times.

A practical joker who looked in for a moment or two, looked at the scene: disapprovingly. As though speaking to himself, and with a shake of the head, he said: "Oh, here's a splendid opportunity for pickpockets." When the writer approached him for further information he retorted: "If you don't believe me, stand back in the crowd the next time there is a big wedding or funeral procession and watch the pickpockets at work." He guaranteed that anybody could see the light-fingered fraternity. From a side view, so the speaker mentioned, the job was crude in the extreme. One man would pretend to jostle people about for a better view, meanwhile feeling what was inside pockets. On a prize being fixed, the thief would get in front of the victim; put the right hand under the left armpit, and extract the article "under cover" of the left shoulder and arm. If there was a chase, a confederate tricked the victim up, and then kept him engaged on an argument for "pushing into him."

headline: STOLEN RIFLES
text:
The chief armourer of the Chinese cruiser "Kwong Ching" was found not guilty yesterday at the Kowloon Magistracy on a charge of larceny of five rifles, held in trust for General Chan-Kwong-min, but on the charge of aiding and abetting he was found guilty and sentenced to one month's hard labour.

His Worship, Mr. J. H. B. Nihil, said that he was satisfied that defendant was not the prime-mover in the undertaking and the leniency of the sentence was due to the fact that he had taken into consideration the previous good record of the accused and the peculiar circumstances suffered on the cruiser with

stancés suffered on the cruiser with regard to wages.

The $100 found on the accused was ordered to be returned to the captain as the money was the proceeds of the larceny.

In the course of the concluding evidence, the captain and second officer, recalled, denied complicity in the sale of these or any other arms that had been on the cruiser.

organ of the Council for the Foreign Settlement of Shanghai, is distinctly bright and readable. It publishes changes in the personnel of the Diplomatic Corps, Volunteer Corps Orders, and reports by the Watch Committee on hotels, taverns, and restaurants (which give the list of applications and the manner of dealing with them). Space is given to road extensions and widenings, sales of Municipal properties, excerpts from minutes of the Works Committee, the Public Utilities Committee, the Foreign Education Committee (Hongkong Board of Education, please note!) Municipal staff changes, extracts from the order books of each week relative to every phase of Municipal activity, and even a Municipal Band programme (on which, by the way, Mrs. Bowes-Smith, of Hongkong, figures prominently). Nor does the up-to-date spirit end here, for there are very useful reports for March by the Commissioner of Police and the Acting Chief Officer of the Fire Brigade. The Police report in itself is valuable. It not only gives statistics of crime, but it reviews in an intelligent manner the main events concerning the Police. Forced during the month. It comments on the local agitation against the Central Government, anti-foreign agitation, lawlessness in Chinese territory, the awakening of the Chinese to the dangers of Bolshevik, Russian affairs, and political matters. There is even a small section devoted to dogs—the number in the kennies, the number seized by the Police, the number shot, and so forth. Next follows the report on the Fire Brigade for March.

It will be seen that there is no waiting in Shanghai for annual reports of Departments to be issued any time from six to eighteen months after the close of a year. Monthly reports are prepared and published as soon as possible in the Municipal Gazette. Every ratepayer within the Shanghai Municipality is apprised through the Gazette of everything that he ought to know.

Recently something was said of the need for a brighter Hongkong. Why not begin with a brighter Government Gazette? If it can be done in Shanghai by the Municipality, why not in Hongkong by the Government? The suggestion is thrown out in the hope that one of the enterprising Unofficial members of the Legislative Council will take it up with the authorities with a view at least to improving on-the-dry-as-dust organised by the Government at present.

MONEYLENDERS. Hongkong has long since attended to the question of money-lenders. Money lending is an every day fact of business and social life. Without it many would find it hard to function business could not be carried on. Moneylenders, however, is generally speaking, a term to denote a class who lend money at a high rate of interest. In Hongkong, moneylenders are registered. They seem to belong to one class of the community and their operations seem to be done with another class. We are not certain if

the regulations permitting them to carry on business stipulates the maximum interest they may charge. Such does not seem to be the case, bearing in mind that it has happened that the Court has expressed itself clearly on the question of what is a reasonable interest. At Home, the crying scandal of unregistered money-lenders has long been in evidence. They operate chiefly amongst the poorer classes, and transactions, in number at any rate, are upon a colossal scale. Much of the misery in slum quarters can be traced to their work. Greed has killed all signs of benevolence or charity. Much would have much more—"full measure, pressed down, and running over." The House of Commons has given ear to a private Bill—which the Government will support—to control moneylenders. They are to be licensed and licences will only be given upon the submission of certificates fulfilling certain qualifications. There are other conditions which will lead to greater control. The one thing that surprises those interested in social questions is that forty-eight percent is laid down as the rate of interest for loans, "but this is not intended to be the maximum." There seems here to be an encouragement to all and sundry to indulge in a Wallingfordian effort to get rich quickly. Surely forty-eight per cent, as a seeming minimum is outrageous!

headline: AMATEUR 'TEC.
text:
ALLEGED PLOT TO KILL HUSBAND.

TEA-HOUSE WHISPERS.

How an alleged plot in which a wife is concerned, to kill her husband, was revealed by an amateur detective who followed up a clue, is now being investigated by the police.

Yesterday, the Yaumati Police Court was crowded with spectators who wanted to see what the woman looked like but they were denied.

It is alleged that a young barber was in a tea-house with several bad characters. From snatches of their conversation, a Chinese suspected that something was amiss. He trailed them to different places in Yaumati and then informed the Police.

The husband in the case is the master of a ricsha depot. His wife is middle-aged and they have been married for about twenty years. The master of the house recently took a concubine. He is said to be in the habit of visiting a friend's house regularly every night to partake of opium. The amateur detective is believed to have seen the barber, and one of the gang of rowdies—a man with one eye—standing outside the friend's house to identify the husband. The barber and the one-eyed man are alleged to have conversed in the tea-house where the plot was hatched. Ten dollars "bargain money" is stated to have been paid over by the barber five dollars went for "expenses" and the balance of $85 out of a total of $100 promised for the job, was deposited with a shop. Half of the deposit receipt is said to have been found on the barber, who in turn is suspected of having been given the money by the woman. The barber and the woman are now in custody, pending inquiries. When the detective went to the rendezvous, he arrested—after a struggle—the one-eyed man, on whom was found a dagger. On a charge of being in possession with an unlawful motive, this man was yesterday sentenced to a year's hard labour.

headline: SUSPICIOUS / CAUGHT A THIEF
text:
While at Shaukiwan Road yesterday, Sanitary Inspector Taylor overheard a washerman's complaint to another that he lost a quantity of clothing put out to dry. Shortly after, the Inspector was proceeding on his motor cycle along the reclamation when he spied a man carrying a bundle in circumstances which appeared to be suspicious. A search brought to light the missing clothing, which was identified by the owner.

These facts were mentioned by Sub-Inspector Field when the man was charged with larceny before Mr. R. E. Lindseil at the Central Magistracy this morning and a plea of "guilty" was tendered.

The sentence was fourteen days hard labour.

headline: BOMB CASE. / LAST OF ARRESTED MEN DISCHARGED. NO EVIDENCE
text:
The charge of possession of bomb material at No. 24, Yee Wo Street, Causeway Bay, against the last of the arrested men (two having already been discharged) was dropped at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Sub-Inspector Field said that about fourteen coolies lived at the house and it was hard to get evidence against one particular man. He was satisfied with the further investigations he had made and did not wish to proceed with the case.

The "Magistrate (Mr. Lindsell) accordingly discharged the man.

headline: HIT IN THE EYE. CHARGE AGAINST AMERICAN SEAMAN.
text: Harold Little, a member of the "President Jefferson" crew, was sentenced to one week's imprisonment and was further ordered to pay $5 as compensation in an assault case heard at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning. Evidence showed that while on the way to the ship words passed between him and a cargo coolie and the man was hit in the eye. Following this incident all the coolies wanted to go on strike, but they were persuaded not to do so.

headline: LOCAL CHRISTIAN EDUCATION.
text: To say that missionaries are the cause of all the trouble in China—or that they are primarily responsible for the outbreak of anti-foreignism in China,—is a serious statement. If an extremist—one in favour of reform by revolution—made the statement, we might well dismiss the matter as not worth a moment's consideration. Similarly if a Russian Bolshevik or a Communist Chinese made it, not much regard need be paid to it. But the statement comes from a Briton—one entitled to be heard; one wielding a formidable pen and prepared to justify his statements. Leaving the larger issue to one side, as beyond intimate knowledge, except where direct contact has been made with missions and missionaries in China—does the statement hold water locally? There will be no question that it does not. Whilst there is a measure of medical missionary work being carried on in the Colony, and a large measure of evangelistic work in the villages of the New Territories, missionary effort is principally centred in education: Few know little or anything about Christian education of a primary character carried on in different parts of the Colony. It is of course not unhonoured, but it is certainly unsung. Day by day, teaching in the vernacular is carried on by devoted Chinese teachers under the supervision of foreign Christian missionaries. The larger schools are more in the public gaze by reason of the class of education taught and the influence they have on the lives of hundreds of Chinese of both sexes. The strike may have found school-boys in these institutions tinged with the spirit of nationalism and inclined to assert what we may easily describe as a feeling of patriotism. To ascribe any ill-effects from such manifestations to missionaries would be as unjust as it would be absurd. All the institutions we have in mind are staffed, as a general rule, by enthusiasts in a cause who devote their lives to educate and influence. The boards or committees invariably include Chinese who appreciate what is being done, and appreciate it in a remarkable and practical manner by giving and raising large sums for buildings and endowments. No school of this character is a closed preserva. It is open to the light of inspection and where Government grants are given.

headline: TRAFFIC CHARGE.
text:
KOWLOON INCIDENT.

An accident in which four ricsha coolies were struck by a motor bus and injured at Gas colone Road had a sequel at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday when the bus driver was charged with dangerous driving and having inefficient brakes.

One of the coolies giving evidence said that the bus must have been travelling like a race horse. Asked whether he would return to the hospital after giving evidence, another coolie said he intended seeing a Chinese doctor, as he had no faith in foreign medicine.

The case was adjourned.

headline: SHALLOW LIES.
text:
PARTNER TO DELIBERATE FRAUD.

CHINESE CONVICTED

At the Central Magistracy yesterday, Mr. E. Davidson called further evidence for the prosecution in a charge against a managing partner of conspiring to defraud the Him Yick firm of $8,200. It was stated at previous hearings that when depositors applied for the return of their money the accused put them off with a remark that the affairs of the firm had not been adjusted.

Mr. J. T. Prior, for the defence, said that another man was instructed to make the payments, but it was not known whether he had done so, as he had not been seen since the case began. There was nothing to show that the promissory notes were forgeries and he thought his client had been easily imposed upon.

The Magistrate (Mr. Lindsell) pointed out that accused had obviously lied in the witness box, to which Mr. Prior said that the lies were extremely shallow and he did not think the man was lying by art.

Accused was found guilty of a deliberate fraud and sentenced to three months' hard labour.

headline: CREW SAVED FROM BLAZING SHIP
text:
SHIRCO

One of the most thrilling stories in local shipping history was enacted in the Malacen Straits, about 23 miles from Singapore, last night, says the "Straits Times" of April 23, when the Straits Steamship Company's "Penang" caught fire and was a total loss, the crew being saved by several ships which stood by.

The "Penang" which is a vessel of 870 tons gross, and was built as far back as 1881, runs between Singapore, Fort Swettenham and Port Dickson. Yesterday she left Singapore at four o'clock with a general cargo and thirteen deck passengers. She had a crew of about fifty Malays and Chinese, and there were 2,500 tins of kerosine in her after hold.

At about seven p.m., when the ship was nine miles north of the Sultan Shoal light, the alarm of fire was raised, and flames shot up from the fore hold. The fire-hoses were immediately got to work, the boats slung out, and all other precautions taken, but it was quite impossible to check the flames. It is believed that the fire started among some straw, and its intensity was due to the fact that some Chinese sambu caught alight. It was evident in ten minutes that there was no chance of extinguishing the fire, and the Chinese, who had taken boat stations, let the boats away. The tackle became tangled, and the European officers had to cut the lines to free the boats. Had it not been for the fact that men were clining to lines and tackle in the water around the "Penang" Captain Ure would have attempted to beach the ship and he did in fact try to do so, but had to stop the engines to save the men in the water. The anchor was then dropped.

After a short time it became impossible to stay on the ship. The hant and fumes were overpowering, and the fumes were blown aft by the wind, so that it was impossible to get forward at all. The Chinese coolies had already left the ship, and since they had taken the boats the Malay crew and European officers were left to save themselves as best they could. Rafts and everything that would float were made use of, but some of the Malays had to swim until they were picked up. Captain Ure and his officers told a "Straits Times" representative this morning that all the Malays behaved splendidly and especially John, the Malay boatswain who did a great deal of gallant work. The young second engineer and the Chinese steward were overcome by the gaps and fainted, and the Malays picked them up and saw that they got into the boats and throughout the Malays behaved in a manner worthy of that seafaring traditions.

At Home the most absorbing topic has naturally been the coal crisis and the certainty now of the pits closing down owing to the failure of the owners and the miners to agree on the report of the Royal Commission. The Prime Minister has been exercising himself to the utmost in the interests of industrial peace, but the miners have rejected the owners' amended offer and the strike began at midnight yesterday. The London engineers have decided to strike for an extra £1 a week wages, so that the "merry month of May" is likely to be a misnomer in this year of grace. The features of Mr. Winston Churchill's Budget speech, which he delivered in the House of Commons on Monday, were that there would have been a profit this year but for the Coal Subsidy, that a new betting tax will be introduced, that a considerable sum of money from motor taxes will be diverted from the Road Fund to the general funds of the exchequer, and that the Trade Facilities Act, excepting where it safeguards "key" industries, will be repealed. The greatest controversy has arisen in regard to the betting tax, which has been assailed both by bookmakers and church folk, whilst an authority like Lord Lonsdale is of opinion that the revenue to be secured will not be worth the trouble of collecting it. The Labourites in the House of Commons received an accession to their strength in the person of Miss Susan Lawrence, who won East Ham North-by-election and fills the place of a Conservative.

CLUB'S PROGRESS ENGINEERS INSTITUTE ANNUAL MEETING OFFICERS ELECTED

Mr. J. Ormiston, the incoming President of the Club, presided at the annual meeting of the Institution of Engineers and Shipbuilders, held at the Club premises in King's Building yesterday.

After the annual report, already published in the "China Mail," had been read, the Chairman expressed regret at the small attendance.

The question of the distribution of funds to certain charities was raised, and Mr. Ormiston said he was quite sure that the members were of the opinion that the usual donations should be continued.

The meeting voted the usual contributions to charities. These were:

British Legion, £50; St. Dustan's £50; London Hospital £20; Glasgow Royal Infirmary £20; Dr. Barnardo's £20; Orphan Homes of Scotland £10; Shaftesbury Home and "Arethusa" Training Ship £10; Royal National Lifeboat Inst. £10; Seamen's Hospital £10; and Hongkong Seamen's Institute $500.

Of many a dull and uninteresting week locally of late the current one will be hard to beat. Its record can be written down in small type and small compass. If we take our pleasures seriously assuredly do we not indulge over much in mirth when a wet spell is too much protracted. The only really outstanding event of the week has been a conference of business men with His Excellency the Governor regarc.ng an effort to bring the Volunteer Corps up to the maximum of efficiency. This by no means insinuates that the Corps has been of inferior quality in the immediate past. In fact the services it rendered to the community since the critical days of the outbreak of the strike up to the date of demobilisation earned for it permanent gratitude. What it has done before it will be found able and ready to do again. The local branch of the Navy League has held its annual meeting, when a membership of 120 was reported and the finances disclosed to be better even than those of a year ago. Still, a membership of 120 is very poor. There ought to be at least 400 members. The Portuguese Consul-General, Senhor Cerveira de Albuquerque, has been congratulated on the elevation by his Government to the rank of a first-class Consul-General. The relations between the Consul-General and the Government and people of Hongkong have ever been of the happiest, and we re-echo the wish that he will be long spared to fulfill his Consular duties in this Colony. In the world of sport it was hoped to have an exhibition of tennis during the brief visit to Hongkong of the Philippines. Davis Cup team, but unfortunately, the weather ruled it out of the question. The Kowloon Football Club are to be congratulated on bringing off a "double" by winning both the Shield and the

ony. Towards the end of the year they were rather depleted, but a duorum was maintained. The officers elected were—President, Mr. J. Ormiston: vice-presidents, Messrs. L. J. Blackburn, secretary, Mr. P. T. Farrell, treasurer, Mr. Wallace; lBrarian, Mr. W. J. Stokes auditors, Messrs. Lowe, Bingham, and Matthews. The committee was constituted as follows: Messrs. J. Ormiston, E. W. Blackburn, R. Hunter, B. L. Frost, W. Lang, T. J. Blackburn, R. M. Johnston, J. M. Welch, S. C. M. Cutting, A. Heyey, P. T. Farrell and J. Brook. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman. CONSTABLES DEATI ENQUIRY INTO KING'S PAR MYSTERY. FORMAL EVIDENCE

Further evidence was given yesterday as to the death of a Weihaiwei constable who was found in King's Park with wounds in this throat, Mr. J. H. B. Nihill holding an enquiry at the Kowloon Magistracy. The Coroner sat with a jury, comprising Messrs. J. T. Humphreys (foreman), I. F. da Rocha and Chung Ying-chiu. Dr. T. Smalley said that the wounds in the dead constable's neck were exceedingly serious; while there were also wounds on the little finger of the right hand. There were no wounds to suggest that deceased had struggled before his death. The wound in the neck reached right down the vertebrae column, severing all the vessels and structures on its way. The whole wound was composed of seven separate incisions, which ran into each other. The cause of death was an incised wound of the throat and haemorrhage.

In answer to the Coroner, witness said the wound could not have been self-inflicted. The man had been dead for about 36 hours when witness saw him.

Detective Sergeant Kennedy gave evidence of finding the body after receiving information as to its location. He said that he found it lying in a hollow of the ground near a rock.

Further evidence was given by a Chinese married woman who stated the deceased and another man had visited her from time to time, and that on one occasion she had heard them conversing together.

At this juncture the Coroner adjourned the inquiry, which it is expected will last for some time, as there are a considerable number of witnesses to give evidence.

headline: President's Address
text:
The president, Mr. B. L. Frost, said,—I think you will agree with me that, taking the adverse circumstances into consideration, caused by the strike and boycott, we can consider this our thirty-fifth annual report a highly satisfactory one. Our profits for the years' working only amount to $4,084.69 against nearly $8,000 in 1924.

Curiously enough the first and last quarters of the year were the worst and the third quarter, when we were going through the worst of the strike, was the best one. Our membership stands at about the same number as in 1924, but I regret to say that we have lost. By death no fewer than 14 members. Our sympathies go out to the friends who have been left to mourn their loss.

Our worthy friend and Hon. Librarian, Mr. Stokes, took a well earned holiday during the year and I am afraid that members must have noticed a difference in the working of the library during his absence. I am pleased to say that he has returned to the post with renewed energies and when the alterations are completed and he has the library and reading room arranged to his and, I am sure, every other member's satisfaction, there will be few places of its kind which will be better than ours.

It has been a pleasure to see that the interest in billiards has increased and that the competitions are so keenly contested. I am sorry that the prizes are not ready for distribution this evening.

As retiring president and as a member who is leaving the Colony after nearly 22 years and as a member of this institution for some 14 years, it is a great pleasure to me to know that the Institution has at last expanded and that as soon as the alterations are completed will be the second social club in the Colony, in size, but first in popularity.

This, I think, is due to the fact that we have no cliques and that the committee extends the hand of fellowship to whatever stranger may happen to become a member of the Institution.

I wish the Institution all success and trust that with the extension given a trial, and with the co-operation of all the members to make the new venture a huge success, that at the next annual general meeting you may be able to revert to the old rate of subscription.

Proposing, the election of Mr. J. Ormiston as president, Mr. Frost said he had taken a keen interest in the welfare and work of the Institution, and he was quite sure that they could have no one more capable of carrying out the onerous duties of president. Mr. Ormiston thanked the members for the honour, and said he had taken a keen interest in the Institution since 1909. He referred to the offices he had held since that time, and said he would do his utmost to further the interests of the Institution and the members. Mr. Frost, proposing the election of Messrs. L. J. Blackburn and E. W. Blackmore, as vice-presidents, said that the members who were there during the strike knew that these two gentlemen helped them to carry on. He did not know where they would have been; were it not for their assistance? New Officers Mr. Ormiston referred to the last committed and said it was a very excellent team and worked carefully and in complete harm. THE GREAT PYRAMID SUBJECT OF UNIVERSITY LECTURE BIBLE REFERENCE

The Great Pyramid, one of the group known as the nine pyramids of Glach and situated ten miles to the west of the modern city of Glach on the edge of the Saharn, was the subject of a lunar illustrated lecture at the University last night by Mr. D. O. de Silva. Over a hundred coloured slides were shown. The lecturer said that although it was certain that the pyramid was by far the oldest building in the world, it was not so old as 5,000 or 6,000 years, as was sometimes claimed. Professor C. Piazzi Smith, Astronomer Royal for Scotland, had demonstrated that the building contained within itself the evidence which established the date of its erection as 2,140 B.C. The Great Pyramid was therefore a little over 4,000 years old.

The�ur, that far from being designed by Cheops, the reigning Pharaoh of the time Cheops and his subjects were compelled to engage in the work, the purpose of which they did not understand, by a mysterious people named Hykscs, or Shepherd Kings who invaded Egypt from the East, subjected the people and in addition to closing their idolatrous temples compelled them to build the pyramid for a certain purpose, leaving it when they evacuated as an object of reverential wonder, an inscrutable mystery for forty long centuries. The ancient Sphinx, which lies close to the Great Pyramid, is sometimes depicted, said the lecturer, to appear to be almost as huge as the Great Pyramid, but this was due to a false impression of perspective. Brief reference was made to the absence of authentic knowledge about the Sphinx and the attempt which had been made at much expense to find out if chambers were contained inside by piercing its immense bulk with a boring rod.

Although the people of Egypt, imagining the Great Pyramid to be built as a tomb, constructed others which were used for this purpose, the lecturer claimed that the designer of it was inspired by higher motives than the construction of a last resting place of a dead monarch. The lecturer claimed that the motive behind its construction was that it should symbolise the Christian life and the way of salvation, a theory first voiced by a young Scotsman of Leith, Robert Monzies. Each passage and chamber had its own symbolical meaning, claimed the lecturer; it could be likened to a Bible in stone. Biblical reference to the Pyramid was also claimed by the lecturer, references in the book of Job being given.

The passage ways of the Great Pyramid symbolised the various coyenants of the Divine Plan, stated the lecturer, illustrating his analogy by means of slides and description. The whole of the time features of the Bible were corroborated by the Pyramid-inch measurements and the correspondence were so exact that he, with others who had made a study of it, were convinced that they were “intended by the Divine Architect to confirm their faith in the times and seasons of the Scriptures.” The Pyramid measurements corroborated the Bible chronology and the fact that “this monument foretold by means of its symbolism and time measurements that the autumn of the year 1914 would witness the beginning of the great time of trouble now in progress, should prove of absorbing interest to all.” The Great Pyramid, stated the lecturer, was God's sign and witness to the Christian now and to the world in the coming Age. The Great Pyramid was truly a "miracle in stone." headline: HOPE ABANDONED.
text:
Not only is there a stoppage of the coal pits at Home, but the latest advices received here at con to-day officially announce that the negotiations to aفترت have been broken off. Thus the whole country is now in the throes of a universal industrial strife that is nothing short of a calamity. It may be recalled that on August 6 last year the Prime Minister, in moving a Supplemental Vote of £10,000,000 “in subvention” of wages,” explained the position which led to the Cabinet’s decision. He said that there were only two alternatives—to have a stoppage or to find a way out—and he contended that he had chosen the only honourable way of averting a stoppage. He had secured at a price a respite which he believed would be of immense value. If they were again confronted with such a challenge, he added, no minority in a free country had ever yet coerced the whole community. In conclusion, the Prime Minister declared: “If the time should come when the community has to protect itself the community will do so and the response of the community will astonish the forces of anarchy throughout the world.”

On the same historic occasion Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, the Labour leader, expressed the hope that peace would be brought to a trade that would never be at peace until there was a living wage as a minimum and until it was organised nationally. Mr. Lloyd George described the truce as nationalism in its worst form.

To-day the threat of August last has become a grim reality. The dogs of industrial war have been let loose. Not only a mining lock-out but a 'general strike' of all Trade Unionists has come to pass. Hope has entirely gone. And the country as a whole must submit and must suffer the consequences. It is unthinkable that the crisis will be permitted to be of long duration. There must be found some means to restore the industrial equilibrium so rudely shattered.

As Mr. L. N. Leafe, the Chairman at the annual meeting of the China Association, declared, there must be thousands and thousands of Chinese longing that a rallying point might arise to which all those who desire peace and order in the country might concentrate to achieve their common aim—the country's peace.

It is naturally a moot point at the moment whether that rallying point will be found as an outcome of the civil war now proceeding in the North and on which may hinge to a great extent the future of the South. The Allied leaders, Marshal Chang, and Marshall Wu Pei-fu, have certainly commenced auspiciously with their emphatic declaration first of all to rid the country of Bolshevism. How far they are prepared to continue with this laudable policy once a truce has been declared may be a different matter entirely. The best friends of China can only hope that before the militarists suck the country dry the real issue at stake—the ultimate salvation of China—will be brought home to those thousands of Chinese who are patiently awaiting a rallying point on which to concentrate in the country's interests.

headline: PROSPECTS IN CHINA.
text: Of greater interest, than usual is the report of the China Association's annual meeting in London. Events in the North and South of China have moved so rapidly since the previous annual meeting, that an altogether new set of circumstances is presented to-day as compared with twelve months ago. The opinions of those on the spot we know full well. What is thought in London cannot fail to appeal to us out here, especially among the members of such bodies as the China Association and the China's committee—the latter a very new organisation brought into being at the instance of Lord Southborough with the paternal blessing of the Foreign Office. It was feared at one time by some publicists that these two Associations might clash or at least overlap each other in their respective activities. The reverse has proved to be the case for the report of the annual meeting discloses the gratifying fact not only that they are working in the closest concord but that Lord Southborough has actually been elected President of the much older organisation. This must make for smoothness in the machinery set up in London to deal with China's problems, besides ensuring that those at Home, official and unofficial alike, are placed from time to time in possession of the most authentic and up to date information as to the course of events out here. There have been, and still are, so many misconceptions in Great Britain as to the position of affairs—in spite of the excellent propaganda work by the respective branches of the China Association in Hongkong and Shanghai—that at times we have almost despaired of the Home public and the Home politicians and statesmen being placed in possession of actual facts as against baseless rumours and senseless misstatements. In the speeches made at the annual meeting of the China Association, the note of confidence and hope rang out strongly. There

headline: ANOTHER BREAKDOWN
text:
"Hope deferred maketh the heart sick." There must have been thousands at Home yesterday imbued with optimism that the worst would not really come to pass and that there would, after all, be no general strike. The debate in the House of Commons, in its opening stages, did not promise too much The Prime Minister cast all the blame on the Trades' Union Congress for its threat of a general strike, which even that sturdy Liberal, Mr. Lloyd George, condemned as unwise. The Labourites, on the other hand, took up the cudgels for the miners and their Trade Union confreres, holding that there could be no reduction of miners' wages until they actually saw the programme for the reconstruction of the coal industry. Toward the end of the debate a ray of hope was forthcoming. The Chancellor of the Exchequer intimated that the Government was prepared to resume its laborious task of the past few days and resume the negotiations if the challenge of a general strike were first withdrawn. This ought to have meant also the withdrawal by the employers of their notices to the miners, so that both sides could re-enter the sphere of negotiation untramelled by threats or ultimatum.

In any case, the cold fact has to be recorded that negotiations were resumed between the Cabinet on the one side and the Trades Union Congress on the other only to fall at 11.30 p.m. Half an hour later a general strike was proclaimed. From official sources it is learned that the country is quiet—normal is the term used—and that volunteers are pouring in to assist in the maintenance of the necessaries of life. Regrets at this stage are superfluous. Both parties to the dispute, as well as the Government, have made an irrevocable decision fully aware of the calamity to the nation's commercial and financial welfare. All the leeway in industry during the past few years goes for nothing! The duration of the crisis will now vitally depend on the temper of the people, who have a right to be protected from the insidious effects of national industrial strife.

headline: FIGMENT
text:
Chung Wah was the Chinese for China, added counsel. It was a fact that in 1922 defendant was in business in that street under the name of Chung Wah but the full name was the Chung Wah photo, engraving company and it remained a photo engraving business throughout the whole of 1922. In 1923 (the middle of April), the prisoner acquired a printing business from the Sun Man printing company and carried on business in a different street, Yau Chi Street, carrying it on in the long name of Sau Yat Tong. The business was actually transferred on May 30.

...It is the case for the prosecution, continued counsel, that all the material forgeries in this case were completed by May 3 and 4 that was the inside portion of certain leaves of books. And yet there would be evidence called to show that actual printing machinery did not reach the premises of the Chung Wah in Tai Shan Street until ten days after May 3.

Further, Tam Lay had stated that the printing was done on the first floor. Evidence would be called to show that when printing was actually commenced it was done on the ground floor which was naturally the floor one would expect printing presses to be on.

Tam Lay further stated that a printer of a certain name was employed by the Chung Wah either during his time or a few days before he left and that it was this man who had handed to him certain slips which he had deposed to. It would be the case for the second prisoner, corroborated by others, that there had never been an employee of that name at the Chung Wah. The change of name from that of a photograving company to that of a combined photo engraving and printing business also did not come about until June.

These were some of the things which went to show that it was impossible for prisoner to have committed this crime, continued counsel. If necessary, he hoped that it would not be found necessary; he could, however, call evidence as to the nature of the various kind of type purchased by the establishment and the dates. The significant point, however, was that neither the two of the alleged employees were in the employ of the Chung Wah. Counsel suggested that the whole affair was a fiqument of the imagination of Tam Lay.

The other evidence which was alleged to implicate the second prisoner was that of the "ex-solicitor's clerk, Chang Sam, who said that he knew the second prisoner and had known him for a great number of years and that he had seen him first of all at the house of the first prisoner in Alveston Street. That was not so. Prisoner had never met him there and the evidence of Chang Sam in this respect was uncorroborated. Prisoner's denial was, however, corroborated by the evidence of the first prisoner who had stated that he had never met the second prisoner at his house.

The Alleged Confession. Chang Sam had also mentioned the house of a certain Dr. It was true that the second prisoner had sometimes gone there but he certainly made no confession to Chang Sam such as Chang Sam stated he had. And was it likely, continued counsel, when the doctor himself had stated in evidence that whilst prisoner was there, either himself or some member of his family had always been present, that these "wonderful stories" of confession could have in fact been made?

The third place where Chang Sam stated that he met the second defendant, continued counsel, was on the first floor of the Bank of East Asia. He said that they went together to meet a mutual friend, a Mr. Ho, for the purpose of endeavouring to borrow money for a civil action. Second prisoner had had nothing whatever to do with a civil action, stated counsel, and, moreover, he did not even know this Mr. Ho. The matter would not rest merely on his statement to this effect but on the witness of Mr. Ho himself. Mr. Ho had been under sub poena by the Crown and it had not been open to the defence to approach him until the Crown had closed their case but now that this was in fact done the defence had got into touch with Mr. Ho and he would give evidence that he had never seen the second prisoner and that he had never come in company with anyone else to borrow money.

This concluded his case for the second prisoner, remarked counsel, with the exception of a document which had been mentioned in the course of the trial by a witness who stated that he had found it at the house of the second prisoner at the time of the arrest, that he had said nothing about it at the time but that later

in the day he had handed it to Inspector Fallon, in charge of the police case. He did not intend to make any charges with reference to this "perfectly colourless" document said counsel. All it was alleged to show was that somebody was to meet somebody else at Fook Lau Lane for the purpose of meeting a friend. Second prisoner knew nothing whatever about the document, had not to his knowledge seen it before and did not know how it came to be where it was stated to be in his house.

Another “Expert” Another witness called for the defence yesterday afternoon stated that in his opinion, the handwriting on the labels of exhibits “Emma” and “Nina” was the same.

Witness was Li Tsze-nam, also qualified for the degree "kulyan" (Chinese equivalent of M.A.) He stated that he was tutor to the children of H.E. Leung Shi-yi.

(Chinese equivalent of M.A.) He stated that he was tutor to the children of H.E. Leung Shi-yi. Mr. Jenkin said that the fact that witness was a tutor did not make him a handwriting expert. His Lordship said that anyone who wrote Chinese was an expert in a way. The fact that witness was qualified in the writing of Chinese was sufficient to warrant his knowing something about it. In cross-examination, Mr. Jenkin asked witness what reason he had for stating that there was no difference in the handwriting. Witness replied that the formation of the characters was the same. He agreed that there were some little difference, but thought those differences might occur in writing by one person. He held that a person's disposition was an important factor in handwriting. Asked as to when he was requested to give evidence in the case, witness said that he had been approached four days ago.

ment, through the Earl of Birkenhead, in the House of Lords, has firmly ruled that there can be no possible question of resuming the negotiations so long as the threat of the general strike holds the field. In this decision the Government will assuredly be most strongly supported by the mass of public opinion. That threat of a general strike was a deplorable error of judgment on the part of the Labourites at the most critical moment of the negotiations which at one stage promised so well. As Mr. Lloyd George said in effect in the House of Commons yesterday that the general strike has obscured the merits of the miners' case. He might have gone further and declared that the miners' case has been swamped altogether so far as public interest both within and without the United Kingdom, is concerned. The Trade Unionists have ranged themselves against the whole nation, and they cannot complain if by so doing they have jeopardised the miners' case and alienated the sympathies of thousands. No great heed may be paid to the reports of disturbances in various parts of the country. It was only to be expected that in the first stage of a general strike many of the unruly elements would be let loose and imagine that by lawless acts against tramcars and omnihouses they have made of themselves veritable heroes. They will soon find that respect for the law is essential in their own interests, for the forces of the Crown are more than sufficient to cope with all the hotheads and intimidators, as was proved last year even in the small Colony of Hongkong. Summed up, it may safely be declared that although nothing tangible is reported in the direction of a truce, the position is not yet irretrievable.

headline: NO ADVANCE.
text:
From the voluminous reports of the events of the second day of the general strike at Home, it will be seen that no advance has been made toward a resumption of the negotiations which so unhappily broke down at the last moment. The only verdict possible on the whole miserable business is that volunteered by an American newspaper, which describes it as a tragedy. That it undoubtedly is. The only ray of hope comes from the House of Commons, where all Parties in the debate on the emergency regulations appeared most anxious to assist in the search for a formula on the basis of which the negotiations could be resumed. Even a typical Labourite emphasized the need for resumption, lest the action of some hot-heads might precipitate a catastrophe. Moreover, some light on the situation was thrown by the Labour member for Derby, Mr. J. H. Thomas, who was one of the Negotiating Committee of the Trades Union Congress, who revealed that the Labourites had a formula prepared for presenta

tion to the Prime Minister when the negotiations were so precipitately broken off. That disclosure has created quite a stir in political circles, and there is bound to be an urgent demand for popular curiosity as to the nature of the formula to be satisfied.

headline: GROPING ITS WAY. / PROVINCIAL DISORDERS
text:
According to unofficial reports from the provinces the most disorderly place so far is glasgow, where mounted police were called out in the Parkhead district to epel attacks on trancars and notor buses.

One tramway, inspector was hauled off a car and assaulted so badly that he had to be taken to hospital.

The windows of another car were smashed, but the passengers escaped injury.

Omnibuses in the Renfrewshire district had to be withdrawn after a number were forced to speed up and escaped from their pursuing assailants.

Reports of cars being overturned have been received from Renfrew and Nottingham, whilst in Dundee the Manager of the tramways tried to run a car but the strikers blocked the line and the car was abandoned.

In Nottingham the strikers seized the carburetters and poured out the petrol of omnibuses worked by volunteers.

A Baton Charge. A crowd of 6,000 at Stoke-on-Trent, to-day stoned an omnibus, which the police were protecting, breaking the windows. The police charged with their batons, injuring a number. There were five arrests.

It is estimated that 100 trancars and omnibuses are operating in Edinburgh, being worked mostly by students.

Riotly per cent. of the tramway employees in Portsmouth resumed, when they were threatened with dismissal.

Extra Police were drafted into Newcastle and soon quelled attacks on the motor buses.

Destroyers have arrived at Newcastle and Middlesbrough. The battleship Hood and the cruisers Warspite and Comus have arrived on the Clyde.

The Comus is proceeding upriver from Greenock.

Reports from the mining area of South Wales depict that life is normal. The miners are working in their gardens or playing football, cricket, and quoits.

Owing to the Stepney Borough Trade Council calling out the day employees of the Municipal electric works the London Hospital was deprived of light and power yesterday. The X-ray work and electrical treatment were consequently suspended.

The power facilities were restored in the evening, the ban apparently applying to the day shift only.

"Daily Mail" Repeats Leading Article.

The "Daily Mail" appeared in the afternoon in the shape of a penny photographed typewritten news sheet printed on both sides. It includes Monday's leading article: "For King and Country," the refusal of the workers to print which led to the non-publication of Monday's "Daily Mail."

A column editorial to-day is headed: "Looking to Baldwin to act." It says that the lawful Government must act strongly and its opponents will collapse very quickly. It refers to Italy as an example of a Virile Western Government.

A new feature in London is the appearance of a flood of little job-printed handbill newspapers, which are selling like hot cakes at threepence each. The news is mostly stale, being a repetition of the broadcast bulletin and the Chester racing results. The postal authorities announce that the telephones and telegraphs are so congested that the calls on the wires must be reduced to a minimum. "Midnight" at Noon! An extraordinary pall of darkness like midnight spread over London at noon, intensifying the traffic congestion. Fortunately it soon lifted. Irish Communications. Malls between the Irish Free State and Great Britain are suspended. Sallings between Holyhead and Dublin are cancelled. The Cross Channel Dover-Calais service is functioning with one stemmer each day. No trains are moving in Carlisle. Passengers arriving there from London are taken to Edinburgh in Coventry is flooded with orders for bicycles from London, which it is unable to fulfil.

It appears in regard to the disorders in Newcastle that the crowd stoned the motor buses at Wallsond-on-Tyne yesterday evening. Two workmen were medically treated. The omnibus drove on knocking down two or three strikers.

An unusual feature is that the London electric trains are being driven by men attired in plus fours and golf caps.

A humorous incident occurred in Eccleston Square. An Ex-Service Men's Association Band entered the north side playing: Land of Hope and Glory. It proceeded to the west side, where are the headquarters of the Trade Unions Congress and struck up "The Red Flag" being greeted with showers of coppers from the windows.

headline: GLASGOW CARS.
text:
There is an improvement in Glasgow to-day in the tramway situation. It is announced that 114 tramcars are running. There is also a slight improvement in the railway services.

An emergency news sheet appeared in Glasgow as the result of the morning and evening newspapers joining editorial forces.

Half the railway services are running in Liverpool.

headline: A NEW INTEREST
text:
Listless groups of strikers and street corner loafers in London get a new interest in life with the appearance of news boys, who have found a lucrative substitute for newspapers by selling single-sheet racing and cricket results, for which a "profiteering charge of threepence" is made. The "Evening Standard" was on sale in the West-end to-night, the proprietors devoting the receipts to charity.

A few sporadic cases of rioting have so far occurred but have been speedily handled by the administration of batons which the Police evidently consider more efficacious than a prosecution for the type of individual involved.

headline: SEDITIONS!
text:
A prosecution—the first under the Emergency Powers Act—was held in Manchester, William Stoker, described as a company director, being sentenced to two months' imprisonment in the second division for an "act calculated to cause disaffection amongst the Forces and civilians."

It was stated that Stoker's high-powered car was standing outside the Socialist Hall at Openshaw ready to convey to Glasgow 1,600 copies of the Workers' daily, which, the prosecution alleged, Stoker knew contained seditious matter. Notice of an appeal was given.

The latest disturbances occurred in Albert Square, Manchester, where the Police dispersed a large demonstration of unemployed, also in West London and South-East London, where attempts were made to prevent buses running. The Police restored order. They have the situation well in hand everywhere, though heavy calls are made on their alertness to prevent the crowds who were dispersed forming again elsewhere.

The Trades Union Congress, in one of their few communiques, say that in the course of instruction given to the Unions they emphasised as essential the industrial nature of the dispute

The congress claim that resolutions have been received from the French, Dutch, American, Canadian and Irish movements promising to do their utmost to bring the matter to a successful issue.

Publication Sanctioned. After some hours the Police sanctioned the printing of the "British Worker", which consists of eight sheets of the size of Punch. It contains a special message to the workers from the Trades Union Congress emphasising that this is an industrial dispute and urging exemplary conduct. It specially asks pickets to avoid obstruction.

Protection Assured. An official notice has been issued to the printing trade, bespeaking the intention of the Government to insist on the inclusion in any settlement of a clause preventing Trade Unions victimising any man remaining at work or resuming work during the dispute, and adding that men doing their duty to the country in the present crisis will not be left unprotected from subsequent reprisals.

headline: "VERY REASSURING."
text:
Position Summed Up Last Night.

The official view to night is very reassuring and that the railway service is much better than the second day of any previous strike affecting the railways, whilst a general improvement is being made, for instance, at Liverpool where 1,000 young men are organised into squads to assist in any way they may be required.

The opinion is expressed that ample Forces are available to main- tain law and order.

Supplies of fuel and food are regarded as sufficient to sustain life though not prosperity, for several weeks.

A pleasing feature is the fortitude and good temper shown by the bulk of the population.

It is quite evident that General Lee Bullard and his fellow members of the National Security League in America fear that the present industrial upheaval in Great Britain may be the golden opportunity for which the Communists have so long been-waiting. But it is the extremists and the agitators behind the scenes who are most to be dreaded by reason of their corrupting influence.

The Government has done well so far in its measures to cope with the strike situation, but it will assuredly bring victory for law and order much nearer by launching a systematic campaign against Communists...and...Communist Societies whose boast it is to trample under foot the very flag that gives them greater freedom than any other flag in the world.

headline: FIGHT AGAINST COMMUNISM
text:
Whatever views may be held at Home or in other parts of the Empire in regard to the general strike it is refreshing to see that in America there is no delusion. Reuter tells us to day that at the close of a National Security League meeting in New York, General Lee Bullard cabled to Mr. Baldwin:

"All who believe in democratic and constitutional Governmentment and oppose the destructive policy of Revolutionary Communism in its attempt on the present social order are with you in your fight."

That outspoken denunciation of Communism and its effects, taken in conjunction with the threats of some of the Labour members of Parliament in the House of Commons yesterday, ought to make the so-called friends of labour at Home pause and think. For years the Communists have been endeavouring to obtain a footing in the inner circles of Trade Unionism both at Home and in Australia by a species of propaganda and a form of machination that is nothing if not subtle and wily. They have set out to displace Trade Union officials themselves with the one view of controlling the whole Trade Union machinery. That they have failed in most of their objectives is a matter for gratification. But, one or even a dozen failures is nothing to the Communist! He is under orders from Moscow and Moscow must be obeyed, for the very simple reason that Moscow supplies the money for his insidious propaganda.

It would probably not be correct to say that the Trade Union movement at Home is honeycombed with Communists or Communist influences. But a general strike is undoubtedly playing into the hands of the Communist intimidators and agitators. The working classes with a grievance, real or imaginary, against Capital fall a too easy prey to the silver

There are about 130 Chinese laundry shops in the Colony, says the "Kung Sheung Yat Po," employing over three hundred men between them. Two washermen guilds are in existence, both men and masters belonging to either of them. The average pay of each man is over $10 a month, and the employees' request for higher remuneration has been granted by the employers. Smoking in an opium divan, possession of opium and misconduct as a police officer formed charges against a Chinese constable, Cheong Shing (P.C. 9) at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday. He was convicted on all charges, fines of $1, $25 and $10 respectively being imposed. AUDITORIUM OPENED. The annual membership and financial campaign of the Chinese Y.M.C.A. closed on Wednesday evening. The campaign netted 1,600 members and $19,960, which is considerably in excess of what the workers aimed at. Eight teams of members were organized to carry out the campaign, the winning team netting $6,318.

headline: Hongkong, Monday, May 10, 1926. / ONLY ONE TOPIC.
text:
Local affairs are in grave danger of being completely overshadowed, neglected, and swamped by the all absorbing topic of the general strike at Home. With the unenviable conditions prevailing in the Old Country there will be undoubtedly very sincere sympathy—more, indeed, than what could be possible; however, we are, than before the period of stress and trial through which this Colony itself passed last year.

Whatever the Labour Party may say about the lack, of partiality on the part of the British Government organ, it must be said that so far a splendid epitome of each day's news is being supplied by the ubiquitous Reuter, supplemented when the atmospheric conditions are favourable by the British wireless service. Both are quite impartial and as unbiased as it is possible for such agencies as Reuter's to be. There has been no needless striving after effect. The facts and developments from hour to hour are cabled in a severely plain and unvarnished form. But even were they suspect to the Home Government's influences—which, of course, is unthinkable—the readers_overoverseas can obtain a very fair idea of the actual position that has unfortunately arisen. And no matter by which agency or in what form the eables arrive the general strike is naturally the topic of the hour out here. It may be regretted, of course, that the general strike at Home, consequent on the failure of the negotiations between the miners and the coal owners, has occurred just when people in this Colony were beginning to imagine that the coast was clear for the heads at the Foreign Office and the Colonial Office to concentrate on the Canton impasse. It was fervently hoped that the visit of Sir James Jamieson, the Consul-General at Canton, would afford an opportunity for the negotiations between Hongkong and Canton to take a much more practical shape than apparently has been possible of late. As it is now, with the hands of the Ministers in Downing Street fully tied with their own domestic strike, it is to be feared that the Canton

being in the background more than ever.

There is at the same something like a lull in purely local affairs. Neither the Government nor the public in general seem to have the vim to impart some "ginger" into the life of the Colony. Everything is all a matter of routine, with "not an effort to lift the place out of the rut of the commonplace". Now and again something is done or said to create public interest, but that soon flickers out and nobody seems to be much concerned. Judging from appearances it looks as if this state of coma must be tolerated so long as the crisis at Home continues. For that let it be repeated, is the only subject on which people can be induced to talk seriously.

headline: ACCIDENTS
text: There was a collision between a taxi and a tram car while both vehicles were proceeding in the same direction at Praya East near the Naval Canteen yesterday. The hand rail of the tram car was bent and the motor car received damage to one of the mudguards. While carrying cargo from the steam launch "Yuen Sang" to the Eastern Street wharf, a coolie lost his balance and fell into the harbour. An Indian policeman rescued the man who was none the worse for his immersion.

If he preferred to spring his evidence as something in the nature of a surprise for the prosecution at the trial he got a certain advantage and the law says he is entitled so to do. But he could not claim that his evidence was in every way equal to that of the prosecution. It had to be borne in mind that opportunity had been given at the magistracy to test the evidence adduced by the prosecution and that if the true defence was withheld at the magistracy no opportunity had been given to test it. It was only fair to the prisoners to say that when charged they denied at the earliest opportunity the charges brought against them and to the prosecution that they had had time to produce matter on which to rely for rebutting the charges which were in course of formation against them.

Onus On Crown. The onus of bringing home the guilt of the prisoners, it should be borne in mind, was on the Crown. It was necessary for the case against the two men to be proved beyond all reasonable doubt. "You cannot expect absolute certainty in matters of this kind," said His Lordship. "What the law requires is not absolute conviction in your minds, with regard to guilt but a reasonably belief that the facts proved on behalf of the prosecution point to the guilt of the accused. You must be satisfied beyond all reasonable doubt that the charge has been brought home."

His Lordship then went on to deal with the evidence, the first conflict in which, he stated, was with regard to the actual deposit of the book, the first prisoner-stating that he himself had taken the book to the Wing-On Company and the cashier stating definitely that it was not the first prisoner who brought it.
