headline: DRINK
text:
BRITISH CONCESSIONS TO AMERICA.

WATCH ON SUSPECTS.

The United States negotiations with Great Britain with the object of —minimising the smuggling of liquor have. It is stated, already yielded four important voluntary concessions on the part of Great Britain.

Firstly.—Permitting American cutters to visit the outlying British Islands in the Atlantic. provided that previous notice is given to the Colonial authorities, thus enabling a suspected vessel to be kept under continuous observation.

Secondly.—Great Britain will forbid the admission of ships on the British Registry unless their bona fide British nationally is proved.

Thirdly.—The Bahuman authorities will exercise greater vigilance in preventing vessels clearing with dishonest intent.

Finally.—The British Government will prosecute owners and masters of vessels for fraudulently securing a clearance provided the United States, furnishes evidence on which such prosecution can be based.

An Austro-Polish Arbitration Treaty has been signed, and will be valid for three years.

headline: COMMUNISTS'
text:
SENSATIONAL CASE OPENS IN PARIS.

NOTABLE WITNESSES

Paris: April 19.

The trial, which is expected to last a fortnight, has opened at the Seine Assizes of two Communists, Clere and Bernadon, on a charge of willful murder in connection with a shooting affair on April 29, 1925.

The circumstances pointed carefully to an organised attack on Fascisti, of whom four were killed and eleven wounded.

Clerc and Bernadon were arrested holding revolvers. The former says that he fired in self-defence. The latter asserts that he picked up but did not fire a revolver.

A number of celebrities have been called as witnesses, including MM. Caillaux, Leon Blum, Malvy, Paul Boncour and Blasco Banez, whose connection with the case is not clear. The majority have written to the Judge regretting that they are otherwise engaged.

headline: MOROCCO PEACE.
text:
(Havas Agency.)

The Riffians will depart for their headquarters by aeroplane in order to make a report. The pourparlers will be resumed on their return.

Rifflan Objections.

headline: LOCARNO TREATY
text:
RATIFICATIONS NOT YET DEPOSITED.

NO DEFAULTERS ULTIMATELY

Rugby; April 19.

Sir Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, replying to a question in the House of Commons, said that none of the contracting parties had so far deposited their ratification of the Treaty of Locarno with the League of Nations at Geneva.

A Labour member asked if there was any doubt that some Government might not ratify the Treaty.

Sir A. Chamberlain replied: 'Certainly not; there is no doubt about it.'

headline: Mr. Baldwin Speaks Out.
text:
British Wireless Service.

Rugby.

Although no definite progress was made at the Prime Minister's Conference this morning with the leaders of the conf owners and the miners Mr. Baldwin succeeded in introducing a better spirit into the proceedings, and at his suggestion sub-committees of each side were appointed to continue the negotiations.

Mr. Baldwin told the soul owners and the miners that he was there representing neither side, but was representing the country, which was a very much bigger thing than either. Another fact to be remembered was that whether a stoppage occurred or not the parties would have to negotiate at some time, but negotiations after a stoppage were not necessarily faster than before and every one was in a worse pecuniary position.

Night Knot.

After regretting that we deadlock had been reached. Mr. Baldwin called on Mr. Evan Williams to state the reasons for the deadlock from the coal owners' point of view and asked Mr. Herbert Smith to state the reasons from the miners' stand-point.

Having heard their respective statements the Prime Minister said:

"I think it is quite plain that at the moment you have tied yourselves up into a pretty tight knot. What I have got to try to do is to get that knot untied or cut. Now, from my point of view it is perfectly impossible in an assembly of this size to make any steps toward solving that knot, and I am going to ask each side if they will be good enough to retire and select a small number who will come and talk with me. If should be very glad if those small bodies of representatives would keep themselves at my disposal, and I shall be very glad to begin this afternoon talking to them to see what way there is of getting over the first at least which has presented itself to day and possibly discuss to such a point that it may be necessary for us all to meet again."

The Prime Minister concluded by reminding the delegates that the subsidy to the coal industry would expire at the end of the month. Time was, therefore, of value.

Sub-committees of the coal owners and miners, each consisting of nine members, met the Prime Minister separately during the afternoon.

headline: FINDING A COMPROMISE
text:

The difficulties of finding a compromise between the owners' demand for district wages agreements and the miner's insistence on a national agreement are illustrated by the fact that the miners in some districts receive free coal, and in other districts free houses are provided for married miners. It is understood that the Prime Minister made certain suggestions to the owners in regard to a national agreement.

It is stated that the owners have returned to their districts with the object of discussing the possibility of resuming negotiations on the basis of a national agreement and a national minimum.

The miners are of opinion that if the owners are prepared to concede the principle of a national minimum, however small, the negotiations could continue on a more hopeful footing.

headline: RUSSIAN TREATY.
text:
WHAT GERMANY HAS SIGNED IN BERLIN

WAR CONTINGENCIES.

The text of the Russo-German Treaty has been issued and comprises four articles.

It begins by stating that both will do everything toward maintaining peace, and that they are convinced that the interests of the Russian and German peoples necessitate an intimate co-operation.

Firstly,—The basis of relations between the two Governments remains the Treaty of Rapallo, and they will remain in friendly touching in order to reach an understanding on political and economic questions.

Secondly.—Should one of the signatories, in spite of its peaceful attitude, be attacked by a third Power or several Powers, then the other signatory shall remain neutral throughout the entire conflict.

Thirdly.—If a coalition of three Powers is formed with the object of imposing an economic or financial boycott against one of the signatories, the other shall not join the coalition.

Fourthly.—The Treaty will last or five years. Before the expiry of the Treaty both parties will keep each other informed in regard to the further orientation of their political relations.

In a covering, letter to M. Krestinsky, the Soviet Ambassador, Dr. Stresemann, German Minister for Foreign Affairs, emphasises that Germany's entry into the League of Nations cannot be an obstacle to the development of friendly Russo-German relations. The German Government is determined to assist in making the idea of peaceful settlement in international disputes a reality, but in the unlikely event of efforts contradicting this basic idea of peace being directed against Russia then Germany will oppose them as strongly as possible.

League Obligations.

The principles of German policy toward the Soviet cannot be influenced by Germany's loyal adherence to the obligations ensuing on her entry into the League concerning Articles XVI. and XVII. of the Covenant of the League on questions of sanctions, which are applicable to Russia only in the event of Russia warning against another country.

The question as to whether Russia is the attacker can be de- delded only with Germany's full agreement, so that accusations by other countries shall not be binding for Germany if Germany is not convinced of their justification.

headline: WHITE STAR LINE.
text:
REPORTS OF SALE TO BRITISH PREMATURE

NEGOTIATIONS IN PROGRESS

New York, April 26. Messrs. Morgan, Grenfell and Company, and Mr. P. A. Franklin, President of the International Mercantile Marine Company, views as "premature" the reports in the Press.

They have authorised an announcement that negotiations are proceeding for the purchase of shares in the White Star Line by a British group represented by Messrs. Morgan, Grenfell and Company. A provisional agreement has been reached, but the numerous details will take time to arrange.

A dennite announcement will be made when a settlement is reached, but in the meanwhile it may be stated that, if the negotiations mature, Messrs. Furness, Withy and Company will be the principal shipping interest in the purchasing syndicate.

headline: PEACE PARLEYS
text:
"LATER "NEWS HOPEFUL

The Franco-Spanish Governments have fixed May 1 as the time limit for the conclusion of negotiations with the Riffs. If no agreement is reached, then the Franco-Spanish troops will resume the offensive.

Udja, April 26. The French and Spaniards have agreed to, wavel the preliminary conditions of the peace conference. The Riffs' delegates are expected to return to the conference and proceed on the basis of the original terms.

It was reported on April 19 that the difficulties which have arisen in the Moroccan peace conference, in connection with which one of the Rim delegates has flown in a French aeroplane to consult with Abd-el-Krim and the Chiefs of the Tribes; is explained in a statement by the Riff delegates that they are unable to accept, without modification, the Franco-Spanish demands for the immediate release of prisoners and the unhindered advance of Franco-Spanish troops on certain positions at present occupied by Riffs before the official negotiations have opened.—A Paris cable of April 21 reported: A report from Ujnd states that the Morocco Peace Conference broke up this evening; no decision being reached in regard to the preliminaries for the peace negotiations. The date of the next conference has not been fixed, the delegates wishing to consult their Governments prior to another meeting.

headline: ACROSS SIBERIA.
text:
LONDON TO CHINA IN THIRTEEN DAYS

IMPORTANT AGREEMENT

The “Morning Post” says that news has been received in London that an agreement has been reached in principle between the Soviet Government and the International Sleeping Car Company for the restoration of the Trans-Siberian express, whereby it will be possible to reach China overland from London in 13 days and Japan in 14 days.

The agreement has not yet been signed, but there is excellent reason to believe that it soon will be.

Plans for the d)lication of the Trans-Siberian part of the line are being considered. The fares will approximate to steamship fares.

headline: SHEER HUMBUG
text:
CAUSTIC COMMENT ON BUDGET SPEECH

PROFLIGATU AND BANKRUPT.

In the House of Commons to-day Opposition Day in connection with the Budget was fully taken advantage of by Mr. P. Snowden in accusing Mr. Winston Churchill of increasing national expenditure by £30,000,000 in 18 months and making an outrageous settlement with Italy simply in order to get £4,000,000 to include

in the present Budget. The Government was undoubtedly in the grip of the banks and financial houses, whilst Mr. Churchill's statement regarding the silk duties was sheer humbug.

The ex-Chancellor (Mr. Philip Snowden) scathingly criticised the betting tax, which he alleged was an outrage on the most sacred feelings of a vast number of people and would lead to collusion between backers and book-

makers. He recalled that he described last year's Budget as the "rich man's Budget." This year it was the Budget of the profile and bankrupt." (Loud Labour cheers).

The general impression of the Germano-Soviet Treaty in official circles in London is that many phrases are vague, indefinite, and capable of another interpretation. There does not appear at first sight to be anything objectionable.

The newspapers agree that the Treaty does not create a new situation and that the general lines of German foreign policy are unchanged, which fact is regretted by some of the more violent Nationalist journals.

Somma che League. Paris Anvill 276

The “Homme Libre” argues that the Soviet will thus enter the League in Germany's baggage, as once Germany is a member of the League she will be unable to associate herself with any League decision without being sure of agreeing with Moscow.

The paper concludes that the Soviet thus joins the League without any commitments or responsibilities.

Concern Not Dispelled.

The publication of the text of the Russo-German Treaty has not dispelled the concern in French political circles in regard to its possible "effects on" the fabric of Geneva and Locarno.

An active exchange of views is proceeding between London and Paris, but it is premature to talk of representations being made to Berlin.

The "Temps" says that Germany wants to reserve the option to choose between the Western Powers and Soviet Russia when the fateful hour strikes, but it is hardly conceivable that such an attitude can be compatible with Germany's unconditional entry to the League of Nations.

headline: U.S. INDUSTRIES.
text:
RODUCTION GREATEST FOR OVER A YEAR.

ACTIVITY IN MILLIS

The Federal Reserve Board's monthly index of production in the basic industries shows that the increases in March reached the highest level for more than a year. The increases were marked in "steel" ingots, pig iron, anthracite coal, copper, and news-print.

There was also great activity in textile mills, and the output of motor cars was the largest since October.

headline: RUSSIAN FLOODS.
text:
SEVERAL VILLAGES UNDER WATER.

EIGHT LIVES: LOST:

The Volga and its upper tribu- tinies have overflowed their banks.

The River Klazma has flooded the town of Orekhovo 45 miles east of Moscow.

Eight persons were drowned. Eleven bridges were destroyed. Many textile mills are idle. Loss of life is also reported at Rybinsk where the Volga is 50 feet

Scores of villages are flooded. The inhabitants have taken refuge on the roofs.

Detachments of the Red Army are blowing up ice jams on the rivers in order that the waters can flow to their natural course

headline: SOVIET FINANCE.
text:
REVENUE AND EXPENDITURE GREATER

Moscow, April 27. The Soviet Central Executive Committee concluded the fortnight's session by unanimously adopting a resolution on Military-Innoff's report fully approving the Government's foreign policy. They also adopted a law reforming agricultural taxation, and the ratification of the Soviet budget which showed estimated revenue 4,809,000,000 roubles, being an increase of 37,000 compared with the original estimates, and estimated expenditure 8,922,000,000 roubles being an increase of 20,000. (Reuter's Service.)

headline: 1916 MASSACRE.
text:
AMERICA NOT ENTITLED TO DAMAGES

The neutral Chairman of the Mexican delegates on the American Claims Commission has signed and issued their decision to the effect that the United States is not entitled to damages for the massacre of Americans at Santay Safe, Mexico, in 1916.

The American delegate declared the decision was illegal and did not bind the United States.

Theft of a diamond ring and a ruby ring set in platinum, the property of Mr. C. A. S. Russ, was one of many charges preferred against two Chinese at the Central Magistracy this morning. The first accused, defended by Mr. A. E. Hall, pleaded not guilty. The other only admitted a charge of giving a false name and address when pledging clothing at pawn-shops.

Giving evidence from the witness box, Mr. Russ said that the rings were left by his wife on a shelf at a tailor's shop in D'Aguilar Street at 5:30 one afternoon and she forgot all about them until 8 p.m. when he heard of it while away at Fanling. On returning the next morning he carried out investigations at the shop, but without result. Referring to compensation to the pawn-broker in respect of the diamond ring which had been pledged for $50 and for which he originally paid £280, Mr. Russ strongly opposed any payment, stating that the article was traced owing to the ticket being found. Prosecuting in a case of theft of copper plates from the Hongkong Electric Company, Mr. L. R. Andrewes pressed for severe punishment against a Chinese, as he said that thefts of this nature were continually taking place without being detected.

Accused, pleading guilty was sentenced to one month's hard labour.

headline: WAR DEBTS:
text:
The "New York Times" expresses the opinion that the war debt settlements cannot endure. It adds:—

"Nothing can be more certain than that two generations of Europe will not, without protest, continue paying vast sums to the United States. It is equally certain that it would be good Business for us to accept virtually for cash in hand the present value of the debts as soon as any sound and skillful plan for funding them can be elaborated and agreed to"

The coal outlook is admittedly dark, but there is some hope in this darkest hour before the dawn. The miners' leaders were early this morning discussing the policy with the General Council of the Trade Union Congress, and it is learned that the whole Trade Union movement will solidly support the miners' demands. Simultaneously, the owners conferred separately, and their Committee later saw Mr. Baldwin. All negotiations are most secret, but much depends on the latest attitude of the owners.

The Trade Union Conference has adopted a resolution in favour of general support of the miners. No decision regarding a gen.

Though the coal negotiations are still continuing, late in the evening the gravity situation was indicated by Mr. J. H. Thomas (Labourite, Derby), expressing the opinion that it was 1,000 to one on a stoppage, adding that if they were inch apart last night they were separated by an arm's length to night.

The coal discussions continued till after midnight when the Prime Minister, after a discussion, lasting 2½ hours, with the owners' representatives, met the Committees of the miners and the Trade Union Congress, and after a brief sitting the latter conference was adjourned till later in the morning.

It is stated that the owners will submit specific proposals to the Prime Minister after which he will again confer with the joint Committee of the Trade Union Congress and the Miners' Executive.

It is understood that the Miners' Executive have definitely rejected the eight-hour day proposal and that the question which the Prime Minister discussed with the owners as the immediate issue was the suspension of the employers' notices. It is reported that the Prime Minister indicated that he is prepared to consider an extension of State financial assistance for a few days in order to give further time for negotiation, provided that the owners suspended their notices.

It is understood that Mr. Baldwin is convinced that there will not be a con&stoppage.

headline: SUGAR RESTRICTION.
text:
CUBAN PARLIAMENT ADOPTS

HEAVY PENALTIES:

Both Houses of Congress have approved of the Bill for the restriction of the sugar crop and the establishment of a sugar intelligence Committee.

The Bill provides a fine for every bag of sugar milled over each planter's quota and a fine of £2,000 a day on mills violating the decree fixing the date for the commencement of the sugar harvest.

headline: PEKING COMMUNISTS
text: Peking, April 21. The activities of Communists in Peking have been restricted to some extent. It is learned that they have decided to keep a few moderate members in Peking exclusively to enlist and train new members, and to send skillful workers to conduct propaganda among the employees of the Government railways. The majority of Communists leaving Peking will proceed to Chengchow, Kaifong, and Talyuanfu, the rest will travel along the Peking-Mukden and Tiantsin-Pukow lines with the exception of a few who will start work on the Peking-Sulyuan line. Most of the comrades now remaining in Peking have removed their residences in order to escape the attention of the police.—"Kuo Wen New Agency."

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
An official statement issued from No. 10, Downing Street before the meeting stated that the Prime Minister had received a letter from the General Council of the Trades Union Congress advising him that the conduct of the dispute and negotiations would be undertaken by the General Council, and that the General Council would hold itself available at any moment should the Government desire to discuss the matter further. The Prime Minister had thereupon invited representatives of the Trades Union Congress to meet him.

After the meeting, Mr. J. H. Thomas, Mr. P., one of the Negotiating Committee of the Frudes Union Congress, said: "The Prime Minister, having received a communication from the Trades Union Congress, invited the Congress Committee to explain it. After a long discussion, it was found necessary that further explanations should be given, while it was done by a small Committee of that body. The matter is adjourned with the hope that further negotiations will take place today." Sunday."

At noon, to-day a Cabinet Council was held. In the afternoon the General Council of the Trades Union Congress met. It adjourned, whilst its Negotiating Committee visited the office of the Labour Party. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, leader of the Labour Party, was there, and subsequently reached a decision, which was not disclosed.

The Negotiating Committee then joined the General Council, whose deliberations continued.

At seven o'clock the Negotiating Committee proceeded to Downing Street and again met the Prime Minister and numbers of the Cabinet.

headline: Significant
text:
Some significance attaches to the fact that the members of the Miners' Executive, most of whom had returned to their districts after the breakdown of the conglomerations of Friday, have been recalled to London by a telegram sent out this morning by the headquarters of the Miners' Federation.

In view of the could stoppage the Government has taken steps to conserve the available could supplied in this country. It has notified foreign Governments that as there is no reserve of bunker could at British ports and no prospects of replenishment of current stocks, it will not be possible to provide bunker coal in this country for vessels other than those performing Services essential to the national interest.

The Government has added to this notification that every effort will be made to minimise delay or inconvenience to foreign shipping. Farefull Meeting

The Negotiating Committee of the Tendes Union Congress arrived at nine o'clock this evening at 10. Downing Street, where it appears the Committee assembled in one room and the members of the Cabinet in another, Mr. J. H. Thomas and Mrs Arthur Pugh acting as intermediaries.

Mr. Herbert Smith, Mr. A. J. Cook, and other members of the Miners' Executive who were recalled from country districts arrived in Downing Street in taxieabs at 11:45 pm. This development is considered hopeful.

Preparing the Country:

The Home Secretary, Sir W. Joynson Hicks, issued a notification late yesterday evening stating that the country must be prepared for a general strike to night.

The Government is taking all possible steps to maintain the supply of food, fuel, and light, and to ensure protection to all engaged in these industries and the preservation of law and order.

Recruiting stations for volunteers will be opened to-day.

headline: HOPE GONE.
text:
It is officially announced that the negotiations to avert a general strike have been broken off. Official Statement

An official statement issued from 10, Downing Street at one o'clock this morning says:

"The following decision of His Majesty's Government has been conveyed to-night to Mr. Pugh, Chairman of the Trade Unions Congress Committee: "The Government believes that no solution of the difficulties of the coal industry which would be both practicable and honourable to all concerned can be reached except by a sincere acceptance of the report of the Commission. In the expression acceptance of the report is included both the re-organisation of the industry, which should be put in hand immediately, and pending the results of reorganisation being at-

tained, such an interim adjustment of wages or hours of work as would make it economically possible to carry on the industry meantime. "If the miners, or the Trade Union Committee on their behalf were prepared to say plainly that they would accept this proposal, the Government would have been ready to resume negotiations and continue the subsidy for a fortnight, but since the discussions which occurred between the Ministers and the members of the Trade Union Committee it has come to the knowledge of the Government not only, but specific instructions had been sent under the authority of the Executives of the Trade Union represented it the conference convened by the General Council of the Trade Union Congress asking their members in several of the most vital industries and services of the country to carry out a general strike on Tuesday next, but that overt acts have already occurred, including gross interference with the freedom of the Press.

"Such a nation involves a challenge to the constitutional rights and freedom of the nation."

"This Majesty's Government, therefore, before it can continue" the negotiations, must require form the Trade Union Committee both repudiation of the actions referred to that have already occurred and the immediate unconditional withdrawal of the instructions for a general strike.

headline: War Declared
text:
"War" has been declared" was the statement made by Mr. J. H. Thomas to a Pressman after the breaking off off the negotiations.

It is learned that the Government's proliminality arrangements for the distribution of supplies are already operating.

It is stated on behalf of the Government that food conditions are normal and there need be no anxiety on the part of the public, still less anything in the nature of a panic. If they loyally carry out the Government regulations, in regard to food, could, petrol, and other essential supplies, and do not indulge in hoarding, their comfort and convenience will be safeguarded.

In the event of the newspapers ceasing publication the Government will keep the public informed by means of wireless, and bulletins posted outside Town Halls and Post Offices.

headline: EARLIER NEWS.
text:
"The Government enquired whether, if the ecalowners suspended the notices, the miners would accept the recommendation of the Royal Commission that while re-organisation should proceed the miners should consent to a reduction in wages in the meantime."

The miners replied they were not prepared to accept a reduction of wages as a preliminary to reorganisation of the industry, but were prepared fully to consider all the difficulties of the industry when the Government initiated schemes of re-organisation. The Government finally offered if the miners accepted the report of the Commission, including wages, to establish an Advisory Committee on which the miners and owners would be represented, to advise the Minister of Mines in regard to the re-organisation of the industry.

The miners' leader, in his reply, made it perfectly clear that he could not accept any reduction in wages, so the negotiations terminated at 11.30.

"Keep steady and remember that peace on earth comes to men of goodwill" was the message of Mr. Stanley Baldwin to the nation which was wirelessly broadcast this evening. The Premier's use of this medium of communication is interesting in view of the reported intention of the Government to commandeer the British Broadcasting Company in the event of the closing down of the Press. Referring to this suggested possibility, an official statement issued at the close of a long sitting of the Trade Union Congress this afternoon says the General Council of the Congress are arranging direct communication with the offices of the Trade Unions to which all authoritative reports and announcements will be made directly. The General Council warns Trade Unionists to "Take no notice of any statement that may be broadcast wirelessly or circulated in any other form."

Vital Services.

The Trade Union Conference has decided to call a general strike of vital services, including transport, on Tuesday if there is no settlement of the minera's dispute.

Control of Coal.

Orders have been received at South Wales ports to suspend export of coal. Ships which have already sailed have been ordered by wireless to return, which is an indication that all the coal in the country is under the control of the Government.

The Trade Unions offer to maintain the distribution of essential foodstuffs.

A conference of the Executives of the Unions affiliated to the Trade Union Congress met in London secretly, to discuss their policy to support the miners. A resolution submitted provides for an embargo on handling coal, especially imported at docks. It is not contemplated there will be a general strike at this stage. The delegates believed negotiations would be re-opened.

The miners' delegates previously sat for one hour and fifty minutes, and decided to leave the conduct of matters in the hands of the Council of the Trade Union Congress. Mr. Herbert Smith urged the miners in the districts to refrain from action giving the authorities the excuse of interference with the people.

Reports from the coal-fields indicate a general cessation of work. Everything is orderly. The miners are gloomy, but determined.

Position in Manchester:

Big industrial concerns in Manchester and neighbourhood are well prepared to meet emergencies and there is little likelihood of curtailed production for some time. Most of the cotton mills now use electricity, and depend on Manleipul supplies, which are not likely to be curtailed yet. Others have the biggest stocks of coal. The commendations of the Short Time Committee that the American Spinning Section should cease working temporarily next week will ease matters. The opinion is generally expressed that the coal stoppage will only slightly interfere with work.

The Government, as a precaution, have moved detachments of troops into South Wales, Lancashire and Scotland.

A, memorandum of the Trade Union Congress says the trades involved in the strike call include all forms of transport, printing trades including the Press), iron and steel, chemical and building workers except those employed in housing or hospital work; electricity and gas, but the sanitary services are to be continued.

There will be no interference with health and food services.

Regulations of Trade Union discipline, and declares that any found inequity the workers to riot must be dealt with immediately. Later. The Chairman of the Trade Unions' Conference said the Trade Unionists fully supporting the Council's policy numbered 3,653,527, and the Trade Unionists who negatived the policy 49,911. Mr. Ernest Bevin expressed the Council's appreciation of the magnificent response of the various executives to its proposals. The Council did not submit proposals for action until it was learned that the Emergency Powers Act had been signed and propaganda had been started, which was considered as proof that the Government were behind the scenes immobilising the forces of war. "We have not declared war on the community. War has been declared by the Government." We are selecting certain vital trades to bear the first brunt of the contest, and there must be no argument as to who shall remain in, and who shall come out. You must take and obey orders. Members told to operate the voluntary services must not be interfered with.

Mr. Ramsay Macdonald said the Government had decided to fight the people's standard of living. He believed they had got peace at ten o'clock last night, and the decision of the Government to break off negotiations last night was a crime against society and was an unnecessary wicked and criminal fight. They would raise the whole question in the House of Commons on Monday by standing by the miners, but he was still hoping something would happen before then to enable the workers to continue at their posts.

Mr. Cook, the Miners' Secretary, said "We shall urge the men to keep the peace and protect the mines and carrying on safety work. I personally appeal to the men to observe instructions, so as to avoid any untoward incident that possibly might lead to bloodshed.

There may possibly be an important development in the crisis this evening, as, on the invitation of the Premier the Trade Union Congress Negotiating Committee held a long conference with the Premier and the Cabinet at No. 10, Downing Street. It is understood that in the course of the meeting the Trade Union Congress representatives stated that if resumed negotiations were immediate there was the prospect of the general strike, due to begin at mid-night on Monday not being carried out. The Trade Union Congress representatives, it is understood, contend that owing to the lateness of the owners' offer, presented to them

on Friday evening, there was no time for real negotiations on this.

The meeting of the Premier and the Trade Unionists at Downing Street adjourned at 1:30 this morning, after a five hour sitting.

Mr. J. H. Thomas, in an official announcement to the Press, does not reveal the subject matter of the discussions, but concludes by saying "The matter was adjourned with the hope that further negotiations will occur to-day."

The "Sunday Times" learns that the Council of the Trade Union Congress at last night's conference with Mr. Baldwin expressed willingness to delay the operation of notices for a general stoppage if the Government will grant temporarily continuance of the subsidy and owners withdraw their notices.

The British strike decision was held responsible for the irregular opening of the Stock Market. Recent bullish enthusiasm was dampened by the selling of sterling, demand rate dropping 3 1/6 cent. Other markets are also adversely influenced, but the coal-market is buoyant in expectation of higher prices and better demand in the American market. Shipping circles foresee a rise in charter rates.

headline: What Did the Chancellor Mean?
text:
A significant incident occurred when Mr. Winston Churchill sat down.

Mr. Thomas asked the Prime Minister whether the Chancellor's statement meant that, if the general strike notices were withdrawn, the Government would see that the employees' notices were withdrawn. Mr. Thomas intimated that he did not expect an immediate answer.

The House melted following Mr. Thomas's query, and immediately thereafter Mr. Baldwin was in contact with individual Trade Unionists, whilst the Miners' Executive held a special meeting in the House. No Uncompromising Spirit.

The main speeches were Hated to try almost unbroken silence and the complete absence of any uncompromising spirit on any side. Clearly the House was anxious for a last minute accommodation and indisposed to abandon hope.

headline: ONE OBJECTIVE
text: The debity on the war crisis was opened in the House of Commons this afternoon by Mr. S. Baldwin. Prime Minister in a speech dwelling upon the many difficulties besetting the coal industry which, he said, had been considerably increased for many years past by the organisation of the industry itself and its intricate machinery for wages adjustments. The coal trade had not been wholly happy or settled since the war, and the difficulties which were already showing symptoms about four years ago, were only masked and delayed by the French occupation of the Ruhr which, whilst, it lasted, gave what was really a fetitious value to coal. When the Ruhr occupation was removed the world's supply increased so fast that the world's prices tumbled fast.

headline: Position Summarised.
text:
After reviewing the terms of the report of the Coal Commission the Prime Minister said that the single attempt of the Government had been to obtain the assent of both parties to the recommendations of the report with a view to placing the industry on an efficient and self-governing basis.

He related the course of the negotiations, and said that last Friday night the position was that the miners' representatives were not prepared to consider any immediate reduction of wages or an increase of hours, which meant that the industry could not be carried on without a continuation of the subsidy. The Government could not agree to continue paying indefinitely wages to miners and profits to mine owners at the expense of the taxpayers. The negotiations broke down on Friday night. On Saturday the General Council of the Trades Union Congress expressed its willingness to discuss matters with him, and he invited its committee to come and see him that night. He did so in spite of the threat of a general strike which he ignored for the moment, so anxious was he to see if even at the last moment a way might be found out of the position which had become almost insoluble.

He paid a tribute to the efforts which all had made to reach a settlement, and said that "they had endeavoured to reach a position where the Trades Union Council, on behalf of the miners, would give an assurance to the effect that they felt confident that, given another fortnight, a settlement would be reached on the basis of the Coal Commission's report.

If the Government had been able to get that assurance, it would have risked another fortnight of negotiation.

The discussions were resumed on Sunday evening, and another effort was made to obtain that assurance. Meanwhile, he had learned that certain overt acts had already taken place in anticipation of a general strike. They were acts interfering with the freedom of the Press, and the Government found it impossible to pursue negotiations further. The Government found itself challenged by an alternative body, which was incapable of arresting disobedience to its commands.

headline: Wrong to Continue.
text: He became convinced last night that the General Council of the Trades Unions was not in control of the situation, and that it would be wrong for him and the Government to continue negotiating unless they got an immediate and unconditional withdrawal of the order for a general strike.

headline: SITUATION DEPLORED
text:
Mr. J. H. Thomas, Labourite, who was one of the Negotiating Committee of the General Council of Trades Unions, deplored the situation. He emphasised that this was a purely economic dispute, and that there was nothing revolutionary in it. If a ballot were taken in this country he did not believe that two per cent. of the balloters would vote for anything revolutionary.

The responsibility to try to improve the situation rested upon all; and it was for Parliament, as representing the people of the country, to try to avert it. A last effort ought to be made.

headline: THREAT A MISTAKE
text:
Mr. D. Lloyd George, the Liberal leader, appealed to Parliament to see whether something could be done even now to avert a catastrophe. He thought that the threat of a general strike was a mistake. But he pointed out that the men responsible were men who had fought hard against the subversion of the Constitution. He had seen many strikes, and the House of Commons had always kept its head, and in the end it was the intervention of the House of Commons that had brought about peace. He was certain that that was what would happen here.

He asked whether it would not be possible to resume negotiations? He did not believe that the House would object to a continuance of the subsidy during the fortnight that would be necessary to conclude the negotiations. He begged the Prime Minister to make another effort for peace.

headline: T.U.C. CONDEMNED.
text: Sir Robert Horne (Conservative, Hillhead): strongly condemned the action of the Trades Union Council in threatening a general strike. The Council had taken action, he said, without consulting its constituents.

headline: MINERS' WAGES.
text:
Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, Labour leader, emphasised how much the Trades Union Congress had worked for peace. He claimed that the miners' wages could not be reduced except in relation to the reorganisation of the coal industry. The Coal Commission, in its report, expressed the opinion that any sacrifices by the men should be contingent upon a final agreement for improving the organisation.

In conclusion, he said that if a general strike developed, whatever their views and differences might be, let them enter into it not with hot heads but rather with cool minds, determined to give fair play and justice every time.

headline: GOVERNMENT'S POWERS
text:
The Proclamation of a state of emergency empowers the Government to take all measures deemed necessary for the maintenance of public order and an assurance of essential supplies, transport, etc., under the 1920 Act, which enacted that the declaration of a state of emergency may be proclaimed if any action is taken or immediately threatened which is calculated, by interfering with the supply and distribution of food, water, fuel, light, and means of locomotion, to deprive the community of the essentials of life.

The Council of (the Q.M.S announced to-day that its whole organization would be handed over to the Government.

[From Whitaker's Affirmation for 1928] we take the following: A non-political and non-party organization has been established under the title of "Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies" in time of big trade disputes or at other times when the ordinary means of distribution appear to be breaking down. The lesson of the court crisis was too evident. Though Governments have appointed a Minister as a Civil Commissioner to keep organised the machinery for such distribution, it was apparent in July and August that the nucleus would be far from sufficient should the general strike be declared. As a means of protection in the event of a repetition of the threat of stoppage the O.M.S. was established, and it has quite an unofficial nature at the moment. Lord Hardinge of Penhurst is President, whilst the Council consists mainly of retired naval and military commanders who have been accustomed to organisation and discipline on a huge scale. Registers are open for names of volunteers, and separate though allied organizations are being established in all centres. The Labour Organisations place their faith in the Cooperative Movement for supplies for trade unionists during the big strike.

headline: REACTION IN U.S.A.
text:
A sharp decline in stock prices, a drop of over half a cent in sterling exchange, and a new low record in French and Belgian currencies were Wall Street's reaction of the British labour crisis.

The German Miners' Federation has issued a manifesto adhering to the Brussels Agreement and recommends the miners not to work overtime.

The Transportation Workers Federation has exhorted its members not to assist coal loading for Britain and not to work vessels

headline: 1914 Scenes Recalled.
text:
"They failed! A general strike is on to-morrow." In these words the miner's Secretary, Mr. A. J. Cook, told Reuter of the fateful failure of the negotiations between the Cabinet and the Trade Unionists soon after eleven o'clock last night.

Meanwhile, around the Houses of Parliament, the scenes recalled those of 1914 at the beginning of the war. Thousands completely blocked parliament Square, whilst Downing Street was impassable. Throughout the evening dozens of extra police with the greatest difficulty cleared the way for taxis and motor cars leaving the Palace yard section.

The crowd repeatedly sang "The Red Flag" and raised cheers for the miners. Another section sang "God save the king" and there was a rush at their direction. The police however controlled the crowd and there was no disorder.

headline: Orderly and Deliberate.
text:
Orderly and deliberate was the manner of the general strike of workers in transport, printing, building, and various other industries, which became effective at midnight.

Men whose shifts began before midnight finished their turns of duty. Thus the night omnibus and railway services concluded, the vehicles being taken to the depots. The men did not book on after midnight.

headline: EARLIER NEWS.
text:
The General Council of the Trades Union Congress has sent a long letter to Mr. Baldwin expressing surprise and regret at the Government's decision to terminate the discussions, and declaring the public will judge the nature of the Government's intention by its "precipitate and calamitous decision," and deploring that "the sincere work in which the Council has been engaged to obtain an honourable settlement has been wrecked by the Government's unprecedented ultimatum."

As regards the Government's first reason for breaking off the negotiations, namely, that specific instructions were sent to trade unionists in several industries and services to cease work, the letter says it is not unusual for workmen to cease work in defence of their interests as wage-earners, and the specific reason for the decision in this case was to secure for the workers the same right as employers insist on with their workers, namely, that negotiations shall be

namely, that negotiations shall be conducted free from an atmosphere of strike or lock-out.

The Council disclaims any knowledge of overt acts including interference with the liberty of the Press mentioned in the Government statement, and says the decisions of the Council definitely forbid any such independent and unauthorised action. It regrets it was not given an opportunity of investigating and dealing with the alleged incidents before the Government made them an excuse for breaking off the peace discussions.

The magnitude of the threatened general strike can be gauged by the fact that already a million miners are idle, and the general strike will involve 1,500,000 workers in the transport and allied trades. Meanwhile thousands of volunteers have already enrolled at the temporary recruiting office—a wooden hut in the court yard of the Foreign Office.

The Electrical Power Engineers Association representing technicals employed at the electrical status, have sent a letter to the Premier declaring they have resolved to help to maintain essential public services is connection with the supply of electricity.

Hyde Park was closed to the public at midnight, and is to be used as a milk distributing centre for London. Arrangements have been made to call up special costables.

The "Dilly Mail" leader to which the, printers objected was headed. "For King and Country," and said inter alia: "The general strike is not an industrial dispute. It is a revolutionary moment intended to inflict suffering on the great mass of innocent persons of the community and, therefore, put forcible constraint on the Government. It cannot be tolerated by any civilised Government. We call 'on all law-abiding men and women to hold themselves for the service of King and country.'"

Mr. Churchill while walking from Downing Street to Whitehall was rushed by a crowd which the police were keeping back on the opposite side of Whitehall. They rushed across and hemmed in the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

A number of police had to be brought from Downing Street to clear a way for him, and eventually Mr. Churchill was compelled to take refuge in the Home Office.

Meanwhile a "queue of a thousand strong was Hining up in the Foreign Office quadrangle, waiting to sign on as volunteers to help the Government.

The mobbing incident is minimised by spectators, who declare that the crowd blocked the Chancellor's path through force of numbers, but little hostility was displayed.

It is reported that after a special meeting this afternoon the Japan Transport Union have cabled to the British Transport Union "Our comrades will fight to the last."

The Japanese miners are expected to send similar messages to-morrow, whilst it is reported the leading labour organisations are discussing the question of supporting the British strikers in all ways possible.

headline: GROPING ITS WAY.
text:
The Government had introduced Naval ratings and volunteers to assist loyal workers. He referred in this connection to the cessation of the generation of electrical power and light in the day time at five stations, which had affected the London Hospital, a number of bakeries worked by electricity and the cold storage stations in the docks, as a result of which the meat would likely go bad.

The food supply of London was proceeding quite satisfactorily. Referring to the question of the protection of willing workers, he said that he proposed to ask the community as a whole to enroll as special constables in much larger numbers. There were 7,500 original special constables already on duty and over 3,000 were sworn in during the last two days.

He had directed the Police not to allow the proposed mass meeting in the heart of London to night, which was organised by the Dept-ford Brenneil of the Communist Party and kindred associations.

Sir W. Joynson-Hicks appealed to the people not to notice the alarmist rumours, many of which had already been circulated. The only riot had been a small one at Poplar. The country was steady at the moment, and he enjoined it to stand, just.

headline: Mr. Henderson Desires a Formula
text:
Mr. Anthony Henderson, the ex-Home Secretary, emphasised that the Trades Union Congress had offered to maintain the essential services. He criticised the bitter attack in a leading article in the "British Gazette" on men whose praises the Government was singing loud a few days ago.

He appealed to the House to strive to get a formula for a settlement of the dispute on which they were working before the final break which, he believed, would not have occurred if the news had not come through that a certain paper had been interfered with.

Mr. Lloyd George condemned the precipitancy in "breaking off the negotiations. He agreed with Mr. Henderson that the nation had a deal of sympathy with the miners, but the general strike had obscured the merits of the minors' ease and alienated sympathy.

The Government had public opinion behind it in the present steps, but he agreed with the condemnation of the "British Gazette" article.

Published in a Hurry. Sir W. Joynson-Hicks, intervening, said that he had not read the article until that moment, but he would convey the Opposition views to the Editor. The paper was published in a great hurry, and the Government did not desire to use it for propaganda purposes.

Mr. Lloyd George accepted this, but he asked for complete impartiality on the views of all Parties. I could not be for the absence of space, because a whole paragraph to day was devoted to monkeys and bearded lizards. Stopping the Press was a most foolish thing, and the Liberals would not oppose the emergency regulations.

headline: NO CHALLENGE
text:
Mr. Thomas Repudiates

Mr. J. H. Thomas (Labourite, Derby) stated that the General Council in its counter news bulletin repudiated emphatically that the Government was being challenged and instructed a. repudiation of anyone inlting or suggesting in subordination or mutiny by the troops or sailors. Labour desired to make it an industrial dispute.

headline: LABOURITE'S FEARS
text:
Resumption of Negotiations $ ^{1} $ $ ^{1} $ Urged.

Dr. L. Hayden Guest (Labourite, North Southwark) in urging the resumption of the negotiations, said he feared that some rash and ill-considered action by the hot-heads might precipitate a catastrophe.

But Not This Week or Next.

Mr. John Bromley, the engineers' leader, admitted that if all the Government resources were brought to bear they were bound to be defeated, but it would not be this week or next or the week after. He paid a tribute to the peace efforts of the Prime Minister who at the last moment had swayed "sinister hands."

headline: NEWSPAPER OFFER
text: Sir E. M. Wilfer (Conservative, Timworth), on behalf of a group of newspapers with a circulation of ten millions weekly, offered to print two columns of matter supplied by the Labour Party provided that the matter conformed with the law. He was confident that other editors would take the same line.

headline: "INVINCIBLE"
text: Mr. J. R. Clynes, (Labourite, Plathing) emphasise the ultimate invincibility of the Labourites, claimed that the strike call was not merely successful, but that hundreds and thousands of men had come out who were not required to strike.

headline: NO PERSONALITIES.
text:
The studied absence of anything in the nature of embittered personal references was strongly evidenced by all Parties earnestly seeking a solution.

There was an eager chorus of demands to know the nature of “the formula” which Mr. Thomas declared that the Labourites were ready to present to the Prime Minister when the negotiations were broken off.

The labourites opposed a number of individual clauses in the regulations, especially that empowering the Postmaster to refuse to accept certain classes of telegrams. The amendment was defeated on a division, the voting being:— For..... 301 Against..... 92

A similar fate overtook a motion to delete the clause prohibiting the possession of firearms, explosives, weapons, stones, and dangerous missiles.

Debate Adjourned: The debate was adjourned till to-morrow.

H.R.H. the Prince of Wales and H. R. H. the Duke of York were present in the Gallery during the sitting.

The "British Gazette" appears in two editions, the later of which contains four instead of two pages. Both issues appeal to loyal citizens to support His Majesty's Government and Parliament to defeat the general strike. "Either the country break the general strike or the general strike will break the country."

headline: ON THE CONTINENT.
text:
Exporters Losses in Fruit and Potatoes. Pat's, May 5 The fall of the franc is attributed to sales by British Banks to boater up sterling, and also to the fact that the strike is bound

seriously to affect French exporters and ultimately Continental trade generally.

It is reported from Boulogne that a number of British cargo ships laden with fruit and new potatoes from Spain are held up. The export of cherries, strawberries, and other early fruit from Provence, has entirely ceased. The growers are likely to be involved in heavy losses.

Two thousand workmen in a motor car factory at Saint Ouen have struck in sympathy with the strikers in Great Britain.

headline: German Unionists
text:
Berlin: May 5.

The conference of the General Federation of Trade Unions, miners, transport workers, and railwaymen adopted a resolution to support to the utmost the British Unions. There will be no bunkering of British vessels, and all measures are being taken to prevent coal reaching Great Britain.

'Difficult to Refuse.'

Copenhagen, May 5. The Danish General Workers' Union has stated that if a request for support is received from the British it will be difficult to refuse in view of the help which British labour afforded the Danish strikers in the Spring.

Soviet Labour Support.

The Soviet labour organisations are organising financial support for the British strikers.

headline: IN AMERICA.
text:
Strike Deplored As a Tragedy.

The British strike news monopolises the front pages of all the morning and evening newspapers. Editorials deplore the event as a tragedy, though the talk of a Revolution is received with incredulity as a contradiction of the calmness of the British character. The "Tribune" says that a Revolution in Great Britain is as absurd as Arctic weather in Cuba or Cairo.

The "New York Times" defends Mr. Baldwin, who, it declares, incurred the reproaches of the more Conservative Tories on account of his efforts in the past two years to promote the interests of the working class, but when the Labourites adopted the attitude that the Trades Union Congress was mightier than Parliament "even the long-suffering. Mr. Baldwin could not be down before that."

headline: EARLIER NEWS.
text:
Good tramway services are operating in Glasgow, Liverpool and Bournemouth.

The publication of newspapers has been resumed in a number of country towns, including Newcastle, Cardiff and Glasgow, photographic plates of typescript being utilised in many cases. London financial papers are published with stock and share movements.

Broadensting was extensively used last night for the distribution of Government information and other news relating to public arrangements. The service was operated every half hour from 9.30 to midnight.

All the newspapers comment on the remarkable coolness of the British public in the present crisis.

"Le Petit Parisien" says the man in the street in Britain has set his face resolutely against revolution.

The “Gaulois” says that all civilised peoples should stand together in such a time.

The "Echo de Paris" does not doubt but that Constitutional Government will ultimately triumph. The "Oeuvre" is of the opinion that the strike is due to the re-adoption of the gold standard.

headline: Emigrant Traité.
text:
Emigrants from Amoy to both the Straits and the South Sea Islands are estimated to number about 250,000 since February of this year. The present unrest in the interior, together with better business conditions in the South, is the chief cause of so great a number of people leaving this district.

The submarines of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet, under the command of Captain Marquart, are spending a few days in Amoy, en route to North China from the Philippine Islands. Major Burton Young Read, aide-de-camp to the Governor-General of the Philippines, and Mr. Leroy Webber, American Consul in Amoy (recently transferred to Chefoo), are accompanying the Fleet to Tsingtao and proceeding thence to Peking where Mr. Webber will have medical treatment at the Rockefeller Hospital before undertaking his new work in Chefoo.

headline: IN THE COMMONS.
text:
Warm Discussion on Emergency Regulations.

Their Royal Highnesses the Prince of Wales and the Duke of York were again present in the Gallery of the House of Commons when the debate on the motion authorising the continuance of the Emergency Regulations was resumed.

"A warm discussion ensued over a Labourite objection to the regulation dealing with the protection of property."

Mr. J. Batey (Labourite, Spenny-moor) saw in the regulation an attempt to enable the coal owners to fill the pits with blacklegs. He warned the Government that this would lead to trouble.

Sir Douglas Hogg (Conservative, South Marylebone) in replying said that the suggestion that the people should not be allowed to carry on their business because a body of Trade Unionists had forbidden it was the best justification for this regulation. (Loud Ministerial cheers and angry Labour cries.)

Mr. T. I. Murdy Jones, (Labourite, Pontypridd) hotly said that the Miners' Federation took up Sir Douglas Hogg's challenge. He declared that every miners' member would do his utmost to prevent the mine owners working blackleg labour. The regulations were a scrap of paper as far as the miners were concerned.

Mr. Jack Jones (Labourite, Silvertown) likewise warmly condemned the regulation, saying "Do your damnedest, we are prepared to fight."

The Labourite amendment to the regulation was rejected on a division:—

For..... 307 Aguinst...... 95

vative..... H. A. Briggs, Liberal...

Majority..... 3:004

headline: Obstruction Policy.
text:
The Labourites adhered to their policy of moving the rejection of successive emergency clauses, but the amendments were rejected by overwhelming majorities.

Following a short debate on each clause Mr. G. Lansbury (Labourite, Bow and Bromley) moved the deletion of 'the regulation prohibiting acts likely to cause dissatisfaction among His Majesty's Force', Police, Fire Brigades, and the civilian population or to impede the distribution of food and other vital supplies, also the essential transit by locomotion. He provoked irational Ministerial laughter by declaring that already men were being interfered with because they were acting as pickets.

headline: Dark Threats.
text:
Mr. E. Thurtle (Labourite, Shoreditch) sought the erasure of Regulation 22 empowering the Home Secretary to prohibit meetings and processions where there was reason to apprehend that they would provoke disorder. Mr. Thurtle indulged in dark threats. He said that the West-end was now in the ascendant. When the East was in the ascendant "for every turn of the thumb-screw you give to-day we will give ten" Sir Douglas Hogg paid a tribute to the exemplary patience and tact of the Police in difficult circumstances. It would be unfair unavoidably to increase their burdens. Nobody could doubt that scenes of disorder could easily be produced by irresponsible processions. The House signified its agreement by voting for the regulation as follows:—
For299
Against89
Majority210
The same fate befall further cluses, notably that authorising the entry on premises suspected of being used for producing seditious publications, after which the Labourites left the House. The House confirmed the regulations without a division, only one Labourite being present.

headline: STERN WARNING.
text:
Government and the Pickets.

An official communique issued this evening says that abundant food and ample transport are available, but the strikers' pickets are interfering with their distribution. "This aspect will require increasing attention during the next few days, and all attempts to impede the free movement of the public or its food'shall be methodically and firmly repressed." The Navy has rendered prompt and effectual civil assistance at several seaports. No use for the display of armed force has been required.

It adds that the Government's policy to refuse co-operation from the organisers of the general strike should be maintained by all the authorities.

Insurance Agalnet Damage.

The market insurance against damage by rioters and strikers remains steady.

The British "Gazette" states that a considerable amount of business is doing at rates that do not show a panic tendency, though they are naturally higher than on May 3. At present they approximate from 2/6 to 4/2 per £100 for retail shops, according to the nature of the trade, whilst those dealing exclusively in foodstuffs and provisions are quoted at from 4/- to 7/0.

headline: SAKEATVALA IN COURT
text:
Intenced To Two Months.

Mr. St. Saklatvala, Communist M.P. for North Battensen, against appeared in Bow Street Police Court. He refused to find two surities and was sentenced to two months' imprisonment.

His counsel told the Magistrate that accused had decided to conduct his own defence.

Saklatvala admitted the fairness and accuracy of the Police report of his speech. He said that his trial was intended for the public good. He did not regard it as a personal prosecution. He considered that in view of the present political outlook he should not be bound over any more than the Premier for the Premier's speech against a section of the community.

The Magistrate declared that no reasonable man could doubt that Saklatvalu's speech was most seditious.

headline: ARCTIC FLIGHT.
text:
MISHAP TO WILKINS'S

STRUCK A HUMMOCK

The single-engined aeroplane in which George Wilkins proposed to make his 1,000-mile Arctic flight had its right wing torn to shreds, the landing gear smashed, and the propeller shattered in striking a hummock of earth on attempting to rise.

This was the second attempt to hop off, the aeroplane's load having been lightened after the first unsuccessful run to field.

headline: THE ONLY DETERRENT.
text:
A trap set, to catch a Sikh Police constable who had been demanding bribes from a hawker with a threat to have him arrested for obstruction was described by Captain H. F. Bloxham before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning when the man was charged with accepting a bribe and misconduct as a police officer.

Three marked ten-cent pieces changed hands at Ice House Street and when searched before an inspector the coins, together with another 15 cents were found inside the pugarree.

The record produced by Captain Bloxham showed that the man had four year's service and twelve reports against him during this period.

Mr. Leo D'Almada, defending, said that accused had frankly admitted his guilt. He made a strong plea for a fine which would serve as a deterrent.

In imposing sentence of four months' hard labour, His Worship remarked that imprisonment was the only deterrent in cases of this kind.

headline: ASSAULT CASE.
text:
COOLIE PUNCHES.NAVAL POLICEMAN.

RESCUED BY SAILOR.

The assault on an Indian Naval Yard policeman by a Chinese old job coolie who resented interference with his smoking was, witnessed by a bluejacket who came to the rescue.

When the coolie was charged with the offence before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning, Stoker Howe (H.M.S. "Tamar") said that he heard a police whistle being blown and looking in that direction he saw the accused striking the policeman with his fist. The policeman was in difficulties and witness assisted in placing accused under arrest.

Accused denied the charge of assault. He was sent to prison for fourteen days.

A dog, identified as the animal which bit Mr. Chanson a few days ago at Wong-Nel Chong Road, was run over by a motor car and killed. The carcase has been sent to the Bacteriologist.

headline: "PUG" SAMPANS LOSE.
text:
Another chapter has been recorded in the petty warfare waged continually on the 'Canton River' as a result of activities by the boycott pickets.

Columbia New process RECORDS

Native craft have got together crews who describe themselves as the "pugilistic sampana," their business being to convoy fast moving boats with passengers for the steamers bound for Hongkong.

headline: CELLO SOLOS
text:
L1007 {LE CYNE BERCHUSE DE JOCHLYN

Several fights between the strike breakers and the pickets have taken place recently. "Allies" of the "pugs" are the fish coolies who succeeded in beating off armed pickets and capturing even a number of firearms from the strikers.

headline: L1028 { ALSATIAN MHODY POPPER'S GAVOTTE
text:
L1032 ANDANTE IN E FLAT RONDO

On Wednesday night, two such sampans put off from Fongchuen, acting as guard to small passenger boats. When the pickets' motor boats have within range and gave an order to swing to, the sampans answered with a volley. After a running duel, the "pugs" were captured, together with their passengers, who numbered between ten and twenty. These, it is presumed, will have to undergo trial at the strike headquarters.

text:

May 10—At Lammert Bros. Sales Room, Duddell Street, miscellaneous goods, at 11 a.m.

headline: MORE INTENSE.
text:
(Continued from Page 4.)

The Civil Commissioner in London announces that no further volunteers are required for mounted-ed Police

to-day's "Yorkshire Post" was on sale in London at an early hour. The continental "Daily Mail" was distributed to London and Suburb. The most noteworthy development is the withdrawal by workers of the Union facilities for distribution of food and supplies from well-known caterers such as Lyons, but an army of volunteers are carrying on the distribution. At Edinburgh the Police, with batons drawn, repeatedly cleared the thoroughfares, but order was not restored until Mounted Police were called out. Many windows were smashed, including those of many business premises.

Twenty-two arrests were made, and it is stunted the disorders were entirely due to rowdies and not by strikers, who resent the disturbances.

Tram-cars and buses are running and the railway services are increased. OFFICIALS INDICTED.

British Newspapers. The Press situation continues to improve following the London papers publishing emergency editions to-day by the “Times,” “Daily Telegraph,” “Daily Express,” “Daily Mirror and “Daily Mail.”

headline: Trouble at Hull
text:
Further trouble occurred at Hull to-dry. The police charged the strikers with their batons in the City Square. Several were injured, seven being treated in the infirm.

Troops Not Called Up. The War Office states that no troops have yet been called up to aid the civil power except as guards at vulnerable points.

Attention a full conference of the Christian Churches of Great

Britain, the Archbishop of Canterbury issued an appeal to all parties in the present crisis to resume negotiations, urging simultaneously and concurrently, firstly, that the Trade Union Congress cancel the general strike; secondly, that the Government renew its offer of assistance to the coal industry for a short period; and, thirdly, that the coal owners withdraw their new wares scale recently issued.

Interference With Hospitals.

The British Worker appears half of yesterday's size. It declares that the Cabinet has stopped the supply of news print.

Three important London hospitals lack electricity owing to the Stepney power-station cutting off the supply: The British "Gazette" in this connection says that it shows the "incompetence of the Trade Union Congress, who promised that there would be no interference with the hospitals."

headline: Strikers Jailed
text:
Numerous strikens have been sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour for interfering with the Police.

A Moscow report says that the Soviet General Council of Trade Unions has transferred two million roubles to the Trade Union Congress as a second instalment of the collection among the Soviet Unions.

No. Poulton. Publicity Chairman of the Trade Unions Congress states that the Council had heard nothing about the Red International financial assistance. It was impossible to say what would be the attitude of the Council if a gift were offered.

Trouble At Cardiff.

Failing to suppress the strikers' attempt to interfere with a volunteer bus in Cardiff the police charged with their truncheons. Some women were trampled in the stampede. Two persons were injured and one arrested.

headline: ISSUE CHANGED.
text:
The "British Gazette" contends that the fact that the "British Worker" is published entirely by Trade Unionists proves that the strike is purely political and aimed at the newspapers whose opinions the Trade Union Congress disapproves.

It states that apart from the miners the strikers do not exceed a million of whom vast numbers were ordered to strike without being consulted.

The issue has ceased to be industrial and has become political and constitutional.

The chief apostle of the labour general headquarters, Mr. Ernest Bevin, of the Transport and General Workers' Union, is the real commander-in-Chief of the general strike.

Copenhagen; lator.

It is explained that the Danish sympathy strike cannot be fixed for a week and will not begin for a fortnight at the earliest.

Labour Statement.

The Trade Union Congress in an official statement states that local strike organisations have been authorised to meet employers and offer a supply of light and power for houses, streets, shops, and social services.

The statement emphasises that the Council does not challenge the Constitution and is not desirous of undermining Parliamentary institutions.

The Trade Union lenders have cancelled their continental engagement. Mr. Cook is not going to Ostend.

The General Federation of Trade Unions has decided financially to support the British戒icers as far as possible by means of voluntary contributions from workers in Germany.

headline: ON THE CONTINENT.
text:
The Executive Committee of the Danish Trade Unions' to-day gave the Employers' Association preliminary notice of a strike in support of the British strikers.

Coal Freights Reduced?

Coal freights to the Mediterranean have been reduced fifteen per cent. Freights have slumped in spite of the rush, and a vast tonnage is available.

The price of bunker coal in the New Waterway for ships in bullast has risen to $24/ and for loaded ships $26/

while the “Evening News” is publishing a special emergency edition this afternoon.

Further provincial newspapers are reappouring, and the Newspaper Society, in a statement, says the Provincial Press has vigorously replied to the attempt to muzzle it. Nearly every provincial newspaper from which information is received is publishing, and, in very many cases, editions and sizes are normal.

In several important centres it is reported that printing stuffs have refused to act unconstitutionally and have either remained at work or have returned after a brief absence.

A further indication of railway improvement was shown in the special train bringing 550 liner passengers from Plymouth to London this afternoon.

Following the refusal of the Newport (Monmouth): Corporation to discontinue the supply of electrical power to industrial concerns, the strike committee have advised the withdrawal of men from the Power Station and operatives have been notified they must cease work this afternoon.

The employees of the Newcastle Electric Supply Company struck last night, but the emergency staff are carrying on. Supply of power is uninterrupted.

A significant statement was made by the Speaker in the House of Commons, arising out of an enquiry whether arrangements will be made to enable the House to continue in session.

Notwithstanding the absence of a regular staff responsible for the ordinary services of the House, the Speaker said he regretted it was a fact that the men engaged on the staff of the principal services of the House had been withdrawn. He assured the House he would not allow the House to be disabled. If it became necessary he would conduct the House without any printing or electric light. A Japanese View. Tokyo, May 7. The Ministry of Industry and Commerce, interviewing the Press, stated he did not think the British strikes was likely to cause Labour trouble in Japan, as the conditions

with

headline: EARLIER NEWS.
text:
The Secretary for the Colonies has, wirelessly brondeasted a message stating that members of the Colonial Service on leave can place their services at the disposal of the Government or local authorities as long as such arrangements do not interfere with their return to duty oversens. In a riot at Glasgow there was injured a police sergeant who went to hospital suffering from head injuries and concussion. He was struck with a stone: A youth who dashed through a shattered window was seriously hurt.

Police baton charges were made all duty long.

Quietness was restored by midnight.

Further disturbances occurred in Edinburgh last night, the mob-stoning the Corporation bases. The Police charged the demonstrators and arrested nine.

There was rioting in Middlesbrough last night.

Official details show that heavy lorries were chained to rails in an attempt to wreck a late passenger train. A crowd prevented the closing of a level crossing, and the gates were invaded. A passenger station was wrecked and also a goods station. Serious damage was done.

In response to the Mayor's appeal Naval ratings cleared the line for traffic after several hours work. The great trek to the City and westward on the fourth morning of the strike was most disagreeable, but there is no great diminution of the number of pedestrians using the attenuated service. Trains from many districts relieved the situation. Five hundred trains ran on the Southern Railway yesterday, as indicating the improvement in long-distance railway communications.

headline: HOUSE AUCTION.
text:
No. 6, Cheung Hing Street, was put up for auction by Messrs. Hughes & Hough yesterday. The upset price was $10,000, with bids of $200 acceptable. Bidding rose to $11,600 when the property was knocked down to Mr. Ho Cheung-chee. The attendance was poor. In spite of the strike the British delegation, headed by Lord Cecil, is leaving, for Geneva to-morrow, travelling by air to Paris to attend the meeting of the Committee on the composition of the Council of the League on Monday and thereafter the preliminary Disarmament Committee and the ordinary Council meeting in June at which Sir Austen Chamberlain will preside.
