headline: COAL STRIKE
text:
AIMING AT LONG PEACE.

The Government's proposals for a settlement of the coal strike were examined this afternoon by the full Executive of the Miners' Federation, and at the conclusion of the meeting the members had an interview with the Prime Minister, Mr. S. Baldwin, at the House of Commons.

The Prime Minister was accompanied by Sir Arthur Steel Maitland, Minister of Labour, Lord Hirkenhead, Mr. Neville Chamberlain, and Colonel Lane Fox, Secretary for Mines.

A general discussion took place in explanation of the "proposals submitted by the Government, and at the conclusion of the meeting, which listed two hours, it was stated that the Miners' Executive would meet again to-morrow morning.

Highly technical questions are involved in the proposals, and the Miners' Executive are naturally eager to be able to place a full statement of the Government's plan before their delegates' conference which is called for Thursday.

District Associations of colliery owners also are considering their policy in the light of the Government's indication of what it considers the rates of wages should be and of the possibility of a new Wages Board schedule, which would aim at ensuring a long period of peace in coal industry.

headline: Optimistic Statement
text:
Hopes that a move for the reopening of the negotiations may begin on Thursday are based on the fact that, in addition to the miners' delegate conference the Central Committee of the owners' organisation has been summoned for that day.

The newspapers anticipate that a Minister of the Crown will keep in close touch with both sides for modiation purposes when the question of the wages rate reaches the state of direct negotiation.

Shortage of Coal.

To-day is the eighteenth day of the cool strike, and large consumers are feeling the effects of shortage of stock. This factor has restricted the movement toward the restoration of normal conditions in many industrial areas and although considerable supplies of fuel are available, economy in its use is being exercised.

When at the week-end the railways were able to resume more or less normal services the companies had large stocks on hand. Representations have, however, been made to them by the Minister of Transport to conserve supplies, and it was to-day announced that on the Southern system train services will be restricted to from 30 to 50 per cent. of those normally-in operation.

The railway managers were called together this evening to consider the question of conservation of supplies, and it is reported that the restrictions to be decided upon will include the cancellation of excursion facilities during the next Whitsuntide holiday as well as a general reduction in the normal time table of passenger trains.

headline: L.C.C. Expenses.
text:
The London County Council to-day approved of a special estimate of £50,000 in respect of matters arising out of a state of emergency during the strike.

"British Gazette Losses. In the House of Commons, Mr. Winston Churchill, in reply to a question, stated that the approximate figures available indicated that the gross cost of establishing the "British Gazette" during the general strike was about £22,000 but the total net loss would probably not exceed £10,000. He said that it was a surprisingly small charge considering the difficulties that had to be overcome and the short period of publication.

headline: A SPECTACULAR INCIDENT.
text:
A scene recalling the end of the war on the return of the City Imperial Volunteers from South Africa was witnessed in the City when the First Brigade of the Guards and the First Battalion of the Middlesex Regiment, 4,000 strong, marched from Dockland, where they had safeguarded food supplies during the strike, to Waterloo Station en route to Aldershot.

Eager thousands filled the streets and cheered the mile-long procession of troops who carried their campaigning kits, with steel helmets, gas masks, and fixed hayonets. The Lord Mayor, Colonel Sir W. B. Pryke, in his robes of office, was standing on the steps of the Mansion House, and took the salute as the column passed, the Bands playing "Rule Britannia."

Further Trouble:

"Further railway trouble has arisen according to an official statement issued at the conclusion of a joint meeting of the three Railway Trade Union Executives to reinstate large numbers of employees under the terms of the settlement reached between the Companies and the Trade Unions last Friday. The Unions have received very strong complaints from the branches all over the country, particularly the Northern lines. The Unions have decided to ask the Companies for an immediate meeting to discuss the difficulties"

headline: EARLIER NEWS
text:
Sir James Martin, President of the London Chamber of Commerce, has addressed the following letter to the Premier: "On the return to normal conditions, I am impelled, one behalf of 60,000 business firms and companies represented on the Council of this Chamber, to express to you and other members of the Government, the keen appreciation and admiration which is felt by all at the manner in which the Government have functioned during the past critical days in maintaining the vital services of the country and safeguarding the food supplies of the people. I feel confident that your appeal for the spirit of goodwill in industry will not fail to meet with a send. response."

Mr. H.R. Betterton, Under Secretary for Labour, stated in the House of Commons, that it had not yet been possible to collect the material for making even an approximate estimate of the amount lost in wages in Great Britain during the general strike, but it was clear that the amount would run into many millions. Enquiries in London shopping centres to-day showed that a rapid recovery in business is anticipated. Indeed to-day, shops seemed more busy than ordinarily, although, of course, appears of buying would account partly for this.

Rugby. May 17.

Reports continue to come to hand of industries having been maintained during the general strike. In the west of England woollen industry there was no cessation of work, whilst in the Nottingham textile trade there was little modification in output. Production in the machine tool trades has been quite unaffected. Manufacturers of cast iron hollow-ware have kept their factories at work and other Birmingham Industries are resuming with the utmost rapidity. All the above industries are in a position to execute export orders without delay.

During the last few days hundreds of cablegrams have been received from overseas visitors, who are on the point of'sailing for Europe, asking if the social season was likely to be affected by the strike. They may be assured that from now onwards nearly all the season's principal events will take place. Indeed, if the coal strike is ended quickly, the season should run its normal course.

Stock markets opened to-day with a buoyant tone. There was a substantial increase in business and "services rose sharply in several sections. Following a slight reaction about mid-day, the tone became stronger.

To-day was making up day, and it is remarkable that making-up prices generally record an appreciable advance compared with the prices which ruled on the last making up-day, a fortnight ago on the eve of the general strike.

Opinion is generally expressed in financial circles that the industrial atmosphere has been cleared by the defeat of direct action and that the movement in sound British securities will come in for much more attention in consequence.

headline: RIVAL TO GENEVA?
text: Under the above heading a Home paper says:—A remarkable sign of the times is provided in the news from Egypt of a proposed Islamic League of Nations. For a long time it has been evident that Moslem is an awakening force—arousing to a sense of its power and its mission in the world. A new movement, born of the political and intellectual unrest of the last few years, aims at nothing less than the setting up of a Moslem League of Nations. A reorganised Khalifat forms part of this ideal. The President of the League would be the titular Khalif. The Daily News Cairo correspondent speaks of the activities of the Khalifat Committee in Egypt, under the direction of a well-known sheikh, Mohamed Madhdi Abud Azaim. This committee is in close touch with Moslem institutions throughout the world, and has been steadily propagating the idea of holding a representative Islamic congress at Mecca, the centre of the Islamic world, for the purpose of electing a new Khalif. The central idea is that the Khalifat should be a representative institution and not a personal office, and should function through a permanent assembly of duly accredited delegates representing the entire Moslem world. The president of this Assembly would be the titular Khalif, and its proceedings would be supported by a League of Islamic States. The consequences of this plan, if it were carried out, would be incalculable, for it would establish a Moslem League of Nations far more coherent and effective than its prototype at Geneva. For Islam is not and never has been a purely religious system. It is impossible to divorce the religious from the political factor, and a permanent representative Khalifat council at Mecca would undoubtedly introduce a factor in world politics profoundly affecting all the Great Powers with interests of any kind in the East.

headline: ITALIAN FLOODS.
text:
FATAL AVALANCHE OF SNOW

Severe floods have occurred in various parts of Italy. Three bodies have been recovered from the Adige at Verona. A considerable area is inundated. Several landslides have occurred and many roads are impassable.

The Fo overflowed its banks completely isolating three districts at Brescia. An avalanche of snow at Adamello, at a height of 6,000 feet, overwhelmed a party of workers. Only two bodies have been recovered.

headline: PIRATES BUSY.
text:
NEW FORM OF TERROR ON RIVER

DRESSED AS PICKETS

Pukkal, Kongmoon, May 16. An offshoot of the 'picket, evil' has now been developed to an extent by which it has become a real terror. Men are going about with strike-pickets' underarms and holding up vessels to robbery. Seven boats have been molested so far. The passengers have suffered heavy losses. Unlike the "professional" pirates, these outlaws do not take the passengers into captivity (for purposes of ransom).

Up-country merchants are forming small, transport companies, with boats running between Macao and the following ports: Chiu Lin, Ngol Hoi, Muk Chow, etc.

Over 2,000 (Canton, soldiers) who were sent from Shihiheng to suppress the plures (do Ho Tong) are staying and Packknid. They left for Canton at midnight last night. I learn that they are being sent to the Hunan border to join the Northern Expedition.

On heaving of the arrival of the troops, pieates in this yelnity immediately mobilised at Laki Ngok (opposite Kongmoon) and prepared to resist.

Leung She, the notorious pirate of the Ku-Tau Shen, has been making a clean sweep in the south-western part of the Canton River delta, attacking villages and river truille every day.

When the mobilisation order went out, the Kongmoon tow-boat "Lee Yuen" immediately left this port for Canton for fear of being commandeened for treop transport. Passengers had to be transferred to Kongmoon by rail, or by boats.

The employees of the Summing Rullway have now been embodied in a guild.

Native bankers at Sanhui city have refused to accept the Canton Government treasury notes.

"Airmen of the Kuomintang have established a branch nero: club at Kongmoon.

Because of alleged incompetency in collecting revenue, the district magistrate of Shuntak has been removed. He is Tang Kong's staunch supporter of General Li Fook-Iumi.

headline: STEEL HELMETSARMY REVIEW
text:
COMMUNISTS' PARADE

The German Communist Party and the extreme Nationalist organisation, the Stahlhelm or "Steel Helmets", held reviews of their respective "Armies" yesterday—the former in Berlin and the latter in Duesseldorf.

The Communists are estimated to have numbered 30,000 and the Stahlhelmites 50,000.

Large forces of police, including mounted constables, were present, but the proceedings were orderly.

The Communist review was held in a large park in Berlin in the presence of thousands of curious spectators. The "army" was arrayed in semi-military uniform and performed military evolutions with commendable celebrity, whilst the bands played revolutionary airs. Many speeches were made denouncing anything and everybody, including the British Trade Union leaders' "betrayal" of the workers. The assembly then dispersed—with bands playing and banbers flying—singing songs including the Communists' latest favourite: "Mother, the policeman killed your child."

Two police aeroplanes circled overhead during the proceedings.

headline: CONSUL INJURED.
text:
OUTRAGE BY PICKETS IN

While removing Communist posters from the walls of the Consulate on May 23 the British Consulate Swatow was assaulted by seven pickets.

The Consul defended himself with a stick and retired into the compound. The pickets, observing that other foreigners were there, did not enter.

The Consul subsequently summoned an armed guard from the British gunboat in the harbour and informed the Chinese Foreign Commissioner that the guard would remain until he received an official apology and an assurance that no more posters would be posted on the walls of the Consulate.

The Consul also demanded that the offenders should be punished and pickets prohibited from landing on that side of the harbour.

The Congul is not seriously injured.

headline: FIVE FORTS STILL HOLDING
text:
CONSTABULARY INVOLVED.

Forty Moros were killed and two forts taken by the Constabulary at Tuguya Lanao. One of the constabulary is dead and nine were wounded.

The Constabulary, wère commanded by Colonel Stevens and Provincial Governor Johnson.

Twenty-eight of the Constabulary at San Fernando, Pampagna, are involved in the killing of civilians. The Municipal Police disarmed them and lodged them in jail on a charge of murder.

A detachment of twenty constabulary from Malolos have been sent to San Fernando to preserve order.

It appears that two native officers commanding the detachment involved in the riot were absent, attending dances in other towns when the shooting began.

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
FORMER LOCAL MANAGER OF COOKS

MR. DE WIVELESLIE ABNEY.

It is with regret that we have to record the death, which took place at Home on May 22, of Mr. Evelyn Edward de Wiveleslie Abney, formerly manager of the Hongkong Branch of Thos. Cook and Son.

Mr. Abney, who had spent many years in the Far East, was formerly with the Peninsular and Oriental, Steamship Navigation Company and had been stationed at Manila where he was married. It was in 1911 that he entered the service of Thos. Cook, and Son and when he left in 1924 he was Manager of the Hongkong branch. Mr. Abney, acting on medical, advice, did not return to Hongkong but became associated with the Far Eastern Department of Cooks at Pall Mall.

The news of his death came as a great shock to his many friends in Hongkong. Much sympathy will be felt for the 'widow' and young daughter of the deceased.

headline: ABD-EL-KRIM'S VIRTUAL SURRENDER.
text:
i. (Reuten's Service.)

The Quii d'Ormai confirms Abd el Krim's letter to M. Steeg, throwing himself on the clemency of the French Government.

General, De Rivera, in an address to pressmen, said the rebellion in Morocco had collapsed sooner than was hoped.

The Cabinet has decided that Abd el Krim's letter does not justify discontinuance of the offensive.

The occupation of Targuist, Abd el Krimi's former headquarters, and the telephone centre, is the culmination of the Franco-Spanish offensive from the East which began on the 9th instant, following the breakdown of the Ujda peace negotiations.

The offensive resulted in the piercing of the Riff front from three points, the submission of many tribes, and an advance passed the Crest Mountains, dividing French Morocco from the Riff Country. Though the Riffs are now half cut-off by the Franco-Spanish front, there is the possibility of Abd el Krim holding out for some time in the mountain fastnesses of Jebel Hammam, where, it is reported, he has collected artillery, arms and ammunition, and which can be easily defended, being difficult of access.

headline: USEFUL PUBLICATION
text:
With the Armoured Car Company's compliments we have received a copy of the first edition of the Armoured Car Company Training Manual, which has been compiled by the officers, non-commissioned officers, and men. In a foreword Lieut. R. L.

"In compiling this book for issue to officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the Armoured Car Company the principal end in yellow has been the provision of information concerning the general work of the Company which will be useful and interesting to the personnel of all sections. It is also believed that there is a wish on the part of the majority of the personnel to have some ready means of learning something about the work of sections to which they themselves do not belong and to have, moreover, for ready reference information concerning the training or technical sides of their own section.

"The production of the book has been made possible by the co-operation of a number of members of the Armoured Car Company. The notes on the Vickers gun, car mechanism, and motor cycles being written by C.S.M. Hancock, Cpl. Mills, and Cpl. Spradberry, respectively. It will be noted that in some respects the technical notes go further than an exposition of principles and difficulties met with in the work of the unit, but this is in accordance with the view that, in a manual of this nature intended for members of a Volunteer unit, the presumed interest of members in the work of the section to which they have attached themselves should not be overlooked." The first portion of the Training Manual is devoted to machine gun training. There are 24 pages in armoured car training, and then follow useful hints on car mechanism, during, and maintenance.

Finally a section is devoted to "Motor Cycle Notes" with this interesting introductory:—

The Mobile Column of the Armoured Car Company was formed prior to the mobilisation of June, 1925, but it was during the "strike" period that the Column proved its usefulness as a Corps unit. “It was originally intended to confine membership to riders of solo motor cycles and sidecar combinations, but in the course of the mobilisation it became evident that car owners might usefully be enrolled as members of the Column and at the present time cars are well represented in the unit. “Since demobilisation of the Corps numbers have not shown signs of decreasing: in fact there have been and continue to be additions to the membership.

"A badge in the form of a flag suitable for display in prominent place on motor cycles and cars may be obtained from Company Headquarters, and one of these should be displayed by every member of the unit as in the event of mobilisation. It may be of importance to members to be identified as personnel of the Mobile Column." The Armoured Car Company, as a whole is to be warmly complimented on the compilation of a manual of such excellence.

text:
Further, "that they did at the same time and place incite persons to commit a breach of the peace contrary to Article 221 of the C.P.C.C. and Article 21 of the Special Police Laws."

An imposing array of counsel appeared for the defence, including Mr. H. D. Rodger, who appeared for all three editors; Mr. A. Preston, who appeared for the editor of the "Eastern Times," and Mr. A. Covey who appeared on behalf of the "Chinese Journal of Commerce." Mr. E. T. Maitland, "Police Prosecutor, appeared for the prosecution.

The alleged false functions complained of were contained in an article which appeared simultaneously in the three newspapers, under the control of the three defendants, headed, "An Echo of the Labour Troubles at the Oriental Cotton Mill." This article commenced with the announcement that the report contained therein had been received from the Kuo Wen-News Agency, a well-known Chinese news distributing agency. It went on to describe disruption which occurred in the above-named mill as a result of deductions having been made from the wages of some of the employees as fines inflicted by the staff officers. An assault upon the employees is alleged to have been committed by some of the overseers resulting in some of the former requiring hospital treatment. They resumed their duties, however, through the mediation of the General Labour Union. At the request of counsel for the prosecution the case was adjourned for a special hearing.

headline: UNION INSURANCE.
text:
With regard to what has been said about our long-standing friendly intercourse with the Cantonese, we doubtless all regret the present misunderstandings that have risen between us and look forward to a revival of the friendship and a renewal of business.

In these days it is no use/hiding one's light under a bushel, and the policy of expressing the Society's business in fine substantial buildings such as have been opened at Singapore and Sydney is, I venture to say, one of the best forms of propaganda and advertisement which can be made use of.

I feel confident that we can look forward to a continued increase in the results of the working of the Society, and I heartily endorse everything that has been said by the Chairman with reference to the ability and discrimination of the General Manager and staff in conducting the business.

I have much pleasure in second-ing the Report and Accounts.

headline: MR. ALVES' SPEECH.
text:
Mr. Chairman,—I have listened to your speech with great interest and generally wish to support the statements made by Mr. Young in the second-in-the-adoption of the report and accounts. I am in agreement with most of his remarks, but I desire to emphasize one particular point which has not been sufficiently stressed upon, and that is the prosperity of the Society is, in my opinion, solely the result of one guiding hand.

In the nature of things, undertakings large or small rise or fall by the efforts of one person, and unorthodox as it may seem to you, it is my firm belief that the larger the undertaking the greater its probability of success, where its destinies and broad questions of policy are confined to the hands of a capable single person; and in this the Union, Insurance Society of Canton, has been fortunate in the past, and if I may say so, in the present; and I hope even to a greater degree in the future, if the accounts now before you are any criterion. As a large single shareholder, and representative of a still larger shareholder closely related to me, I feel that our interests are very ably looked after by the present General Manager in the person of Mr. Paul Lauden.

Whilst commending the policy of distributing only the income from investments which, I notice, as regards the working for the year 1924 was exceeded to the extent of some £20,000, I would urge the view that when the result of the working for 1925 is better known at this time next year, the distribution to shareholders might be enlarged moderately a little further, say to the extent of a further bonus of 5% per share, which would cost about £34,000 extra.

In connection with the dividends, there is a point in the accounts which no doubt is readily explainable. If you will refer to the working account for 1924 you will find the cost of the interim dividend at the rate of 24/- at £161.994; for 1925 the cost is given in the report at £162,000 which is certainly the correct figure. I have not the Balance Sheet at December 31, 1924 before me from which to ascertain the change in the issued capital which, no doubt, took place.

headline: SERIOUS SITUATION
text:
The seriousness of the coal situation is emphasised by an announcement by the Secretary of State for Mines that householders will only be allowed a half cwt. of coal weekly from to-morrow. They must fetch it themselves, and they must have a written permit from the local authorities. This is a quarter of the amount allowed in the smallest houses in war time. It is one of many restrictions imposed owing to dwindling supplies.

Business premises are cut down to half their usual supplies. No illuminated signs are allowed, and street lighting is reduced to a safety minimum.

A Whitehall communique published under the Emergency Powers Act in this connection adds that heavy penalties are provided for non-compliance with the above orders.

The "Federation" of Master Printers and the Newspaper Society to-day agreed to a national settlement with the Printing and Kindred Trades, Federation providing for a continuance of the agreements existing prior to May 1. It contains provisions for the prevention of lightning strikes, and stipulates that there shall be no interference with the contents of newspapers and periodicals published by members of the employers' organisations.

The annual meeting of the China Fire Insurance Co., Ltd., was held to-day at Union Building, it being stated that the company was in "such a strong position."

Mr. J. A. Plummer presided, supported by the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang, Mr. T. G. Weall and Mr. W. L. Pattenden (directors) and Mr. Paul Lauder (general manager).

headline: Surrender Expected
text:
The surrender of Abd el Krim was not surprising, as it was known he was in flight, if not hiding, fearing assassination by his disappointed followers. The French had captured the greater part of Jebel Hamman, the mountain fastness which was Abd el Krim's last sanctuary.

His own tribe, the Beni Wariaghel, had submitted, and practically the whole Riff territory was in the hands of the French and Spanish.

The only two trilies intact, the Ghomara and Djebela, were apparently unaware of Abd el Krim's collapse.

End Welcomed.

France's great sigh of relief at the surrender of Abd-el-Krim rustles the pages of the newspapers which joyfully welcome the end of the Riff "venture, which, they emphasise, there must be no repetition. The Riff must henceforth be properly governed," in connection with which the continuance of Franco-Spanish co-operation "is underlined in order to exploit the wealth of Morocco.

It is suggested that Abd-el-Krim will not be permitted to reside in Moslem territory and may be compelled to apologise to the Sultan of Morocco.

headline: Bolshevist Dreams.
text: Le Matin describes Abd-el-Krim's surrender as the dissipation of a German and Bolshevik dream of France's ruin in Morocco. It adds: "For all her 1,700,000 dead France has shown once again that she can defend herself. Abd-el-Krim can rely on our clemency, but a pardon does not signify forgetfulness. We shall remember his dealings with the Bolsheviks and Pangermans."

headline: WU FOR PEKING.
text:
IMPORTANCE EMPHASISED.

Marshal Wu Pei-fu left for Peking by special train at nine o'clock this morning.

Commenting on his departure the vernacular papers state that his forthcoming meeting with Marshal Chang Tso-ling will dispel all the rumours of differences between them and enable them to arrive at a lasting understanding for the country's peace.

The local students are most active, collecting funds and otherwise encouraging a British Cigarette Company strike. The company is optimistic and hopes for a settlement in two or three days.

headline: "Wall Street's View"
text:
Mr. J. P. Morgan and Mr. Charles Steels, members of J. P. Morgan and Company, have both resigned their directorships of the International Mercantile Marine Corporation and their action is interpreted in Wall Street as intimating that the negotiations for the purchase of the White Star line have practically been completed.

It is recalled that the late J. Pierpont Morgan founded this corporation, which owns the controlling interest in the White Star line.

The J. P. Morgan Company have issued a statement saying that the resignations of Mr. J. P. Morgan and Charles Steels were prompted by the fact that their London partner might be interested in the contemplated sale of some of the properties of the International Mercantile Marine Corporation. It is reported that both the Cunard Steamship Company and Furness, Withy and Co., Ltd., have made bids for the White Star fleet, and there is a prospect of the transference of the line to the Cunard Steamship Company for a price of about $35,000,000.

Baron Kyleant's Statement. London. April 24.

In reply to an enquiry with regard to the offer of the purchase of the White Star line Baron Klyssant stated that he knew nothing at all about it.

New York, April 23. A cash offer for the White Star Line received from certain British interests will be considered at a special meeting of the Directors of the International Mercantile Marine Corporation today.

London, May 27 A Chinese seaman employed on the sea. “Fembrokeshire” charged at East Ham, with concealing 63 automatic pistols, two walking sticks, guns, and 6,700 rounds of ammunition, told the Customs that the arms were given to him at Antwerp by a Cantonese, who asked him to take them to Hongkong, promising him $3 for each gun delivered. The seaman was fined $156 or three months' imprisonment with labour. The body of a woman found floating in the harbour near the Wing Lok Street wharf yesterday was brought ashore by two Chinese firemen. Artificial respiration brought the woman round and she was sent to hospital.

headline: BRIBERS SENTENCED. / MUTING IN A KIEFF PRISON.
text:
Moscow. May 20.

The trial of 111 workers belonging to the Kief® Militia, who are charged with bribery and corruption, has resulted in four of the ringleaders being sentenced, to death, and two sentenced to ten years.

parent_headline: BRIBERS SENTENCED. / MUTING IN A KIEFF PRISON.
text:
The bulk of the remainder were sentenced to a year and seven months' hard labour.

A mutiny has broken out in the Kieff Prison, during which sixteen convicts escaped, after disarming the warders, four of whom were killed and four seriously injured by gunshot wounds.

During the pursuit two convicts were recaptured, but the others escaped.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
PRACTICAL HELP FOR THE MINERS

السعر

Practical help for the miners in coming in from many quarters, the most unexpected of which has been a donation of ten guineas to the distress fund for wives and children of Somerset miners by the Prince of Wales from the Duchy of Cornwall office. The accompanying letter says: "His Highness naturally cannot take any sides in any dispute, but we all owe a debt to the miners in the past, and every one feels sympathy for their wives and children in their hour of distress. Further it would be an undesirable end to any dispute that one side should have to give in on account of the suffering of their dependants."

The Prince of Wales's letter expresses confidence that with good will on either side there will be a happy issue out of the present difficulties. The Prince is a coal-owner in Somerset.

An extraordinary response to the collection for miners' dependants was made at a demonstration at the Albert Hall, organised by Labour interests. Sovereigns and half sovereigns were sent up to the platform, and some were sold for triple-and-quadruple-their value. Several rings and watches were given, one ring being valued at £80. The collection greatly exceeded £1,000, apart from

An official Tass agency message announced that the General Council of Soviet Trade Unions has transferred a further 400,000 troubles to the British Miners' Federation, on account of further collections from workers.

The “Sunday Times” political correspondent states that in the event of a mining deadlock continuing, the Government will arrange for the import and will distribute coal for industries now threatened with paralysis. No difficulty is expected from the Railwaymen's Unions.

Shanghai May 30.

The expected trouble in connection with the anniversary of last year has started, but there is still hope of the police being able to control the situation without resort to more serious measures.

The part of Nanking Road that was the scene of last year's firing was crowded at one o'clock, mostly with curious Chinese who were expecting something to happen. These provided good material for the agitators, who soon worked them up to a serious pitch.

From then they began stopping trams-cars and ejecting, passengers, and smashing windows.

Police parties were called out, one being stretched across the busiest part of the street and the other by the Louza Station, where the trouble started last year.

Besides the matters mentioned before, a caged motor-car with foreign police standing on top, with quick firing guns and a policeman with a megaphone warning the crowds to keep back, is "driving up and down the street.

The Fire Brigade were also called out and are lining the streets leading off Nanking and Chekiang Roads.

Crowds were throwing bricks at the firemen, who replied with hoses which kept back the crowds. One of the foreign firemen was seriously hurt, and one foreign civilian was badly injured, both with bricks.

Foreigners in ricshas were molested and ricsha coolies were beaten.

The police are handling the situation with great discretion. Several of the better class Chinese were seen in the crowds attempting to calm their compatriots, without tangible result. There has been no firing on either side.

Spasmodic Stone Throwing.

The trouble started at two this afternoon; but by 4.30 the police had the situation well in hand and had cleared a large part of Nanking Road of all Chinese.

Half the Volunteers have been called out and these are assisting the police to patrol Nanking Road, while a motor-cycle squad is patrolling the back alleys.

Crowds in other populous districts of Shanghai also indulged in spasmodic stone throwing, many trams having every window smashed.

The crowds are now apparently most good humoured and amenable to police discipline. At six this evening there was a gradually melting away.

Among the several foreigners assaulted three men and woman were sent to hospital, but their injuries are not serious.

The police throughout behaved with the utmost restraint and few arrests were made. The police are hopeful that the trouble will be only a one day affair.

Volunteers With Fixed Bayonets. Foreign Volunteers, with fixed bayonets, were patrolling the principal streets this evening. No trams or buses have been running since this afternoon.

isolated foreigners in several instances were pelted with stones, but this was mostly the work of small boys. Otherwise the situation is quiet.

headline: "FINE WORDS,"
text:
“A place in ‘the sun’ for Italy was the demand of Signor Mussolini in a speech in the Senate in the course of a debate on ‘he estimates for the Foreign Ministry’. He declared that Italian Imperialism was a demonstration of the Italian people and, above all, moral dignity, there existed a need for economic and intellectual expansion for the nation, which had “arrived” a little late.

"When a nation enters the scene where everybody else has taken his place, it causes a certain amount of uneasiness, the unexpected guest not always being welcome. One hears honeyed words about international solidarity and fraternity, people's cordiality, international relations—fine words, but in reality very different in real life. No nation follows an internationalist policy, and the policy of fraternity among all nations erects formidable barriers which for the moment are only economic and political, even nations with Liberal traditions hastily consigning them to the oblivion of the tomb."

Mussolini declared that Italian imperialism was not of an aggressive or explosive character which led to war. The Fascist Government's following could only follow a policy of peace, but the desire for peace was not connoted with disarmament.

Disarmament must be total, otherwise it would be a sorry comedy. It must be total on sea, land and air. There could be no idea of disarmament solely on land, while naval armaments were maintained or on land and sea when aerial armaments were permitted. Until all the States effectively disarmed themselves, Italy could not disarm without running the risk of losing independence and liberty. It would be suicidal.

Young Italy must find a place in the sun, he believed, and it would be able to do so gently when the time came.

He believed Italy's allies in the war would decide to meet her legitimate claim, but he emphasised that nothing could be given to anybody until Italy was satisfied. Italy had no intention of giving up her formidable weapon of veto in the League of Nations.

The second annual meeting of China Underwriters, Ltd., is to be held on April 26.

Tuesday's health return comprised a Portuguese case (imported) of scarlet fever and two causes of small-pox, both Chinese (one imported).

The second annual meeting of Shareholders of the Simplex Plaster Company. Limited is to be held at their registered offices on Thursday, April 22 at 13 p.m.

The huge matshed for the special theatrical performances at Cheung Chau has been erected; and will soon be attracting the large crowds that come from Hongkong and other centres.

Again Buick has built. a better Automobile

Shareholders are reminded that the "annual" meeting of Gundee Price and Co., Ltd. is to be held to-mornow at 12 noon, at the company's office, No. 2, Ice House Street (St. George's Building).

More than eleven hundred of the fourteen hundred registered moneylenders in Liverpool and Birkendiefer are Women. The alarming growth in their number since the war has caused grave concern to the Liverpool police authorities and social workers, for they are held directly responsible for much of the misery accentuated by unemployment on Merseyside, which has led to cases of suicide, crime, and moral degradation.

text:
The sixth and last concept in aid of the St. John's Cathedral Organ fund was held yesterday, and as a result added a further amount to this deserving fund. The programme was as follows: Pense d'Automne (Massenet), Mr. Li Chor-chi; The Jewel Song, from Faust (Gounod); Mrs. Davis; (a) Ombra mai fu (Handel); (b) When all was Young (Faust); Gounod; Mrs. Wait; Selected songs by Mr. Gardner; Phasage (Hahn), Mr. Li Chorchi; (a) Dawn (Curnan); (b) The Last Hour (Kramer); (c) Spring Sevenade (Gilberte); Mrs. Davis; (a) Like to the damask rose (Elgar); (b) My Prayer (Squire); Mrs. Watt. W

boy who on his birthday always elected to visit the dentist as a special "brunt" was referred to by Sir H. Baldwin at the Institute of Hygiene, London.

Child churchwardens and sidesmen, are on duty every Sunday afternoon at Holy Trinity Church, Richmond, at special children's services. There is also a children's church council.

Beardmore's report at Dalmuir that they have received an order for three large motor vessels for a Rio de Janeiro firm! They have also received a contract for one British light cruiser. Another such vessel will be constructed at Newcastle.

There are so many English books upon French Riviera bookstandards marked "Not to Be Sold in England;" so many periodicals (also in English) with "You Can't Buy This Kind of Magazine in England!" on the cover, that the Society of British Authors, which has an office at Nice, is inquiring just why such books should be sold upon the Riviera.

On marriage, women will be required to relinquish their positions on the staff of Barclays Bank. state the directors in announcing a new pensions scheme. They will then receive a gratuity equal to 5 per cent of their annual salary for every completed year of service. "The new scheme will come into force on January 1 next year," said an official of the bank.

British boot and shoe manufacturers have made considerable inroads into the Canadian market during the past two years, and this is stated to be due to a greater willingness to adopt themselves to Canadian styles and to deliver rational sizes. During the same period boot and shoe imports from the United States into Canada have shown a tendency to decrease. A gold watch was on March 7 found in the collection taken at St. Peter's Church, Strengham, in aid of Japanese missions.

headline: LADIES & GENTLEMEN'S HAIR DRESSERS
text:
The Oldest Hair Dressing Saloon in the Colony: Established 1876. 19, Queen's Road Central, 1st floor.

A Portuguese decree has been issued, relieving Dr. José de Bianchi of his post as delegate of the Treasury in London, as he is proceeding to Peking as Portuguese Minister to China.

CHY LOONG. New Season. Preserved Ginger. Best quality—Prompt attention to Exporters. Office:—231, Queen's Road Central, 2nd floor. Tel. Central 2530. Factory:—500-504, Canton Road, YaumatL. Tel. K869.

Madame Carl E. Smith, a well-known American vocalist and a millionaress in New York, has arrived in Tokyo on April 7, on a musical pilgrimage of the world. Madame Smith contemplates collecting the native music of all the countries with a view to organising a grand opera. She will stay in Japan for some time in order to study Japanese music such as Koto, Shomisen, and Shakuhachi. Mr. F. K. Wilson has been appointed a Coroner for Singapore

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
A movement is on foot to organise a debating society in connection with the Hongkong University.

"Don't kiss the Book—that superstition is done away with."—Murlborough Street magistrate to witness.

Fire: enused considerable damage to the Prince of Wales's stables at Tor Royal, Farm, Prineetown, in Dartmoor Forest. But all the Prince's horses were safely removed.

When at Port Tilbot it was said that the inhabitants of one street had paid neither rent nor rates for some years the magnitude remarked. "This seems to be the real Utopia."

"Don't come any further or you will be sitting on my lap soon."—Judge Furtitt to woman who failed to see the witness-box and advanced on the judge's bench at Clerkenwell.

A Chinese boatman charged at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday with participation in an armed robbery on board a junk at Deep Bay, clavigged that he was kidnapped by the other, robbers and forced to accompany them to the boat. This story was believed and the man was discharged.

One of the attractions in Japan is the Tokyo fish market. It is the longest in the country and occupies 480,000 square feet. The market is an association of 750 wholesalers and 552 brokers who operate under the supervision of municipal authorities. Two thousand fish mongers and buyers from numerous hotels and restaurants assemble at this market every morning between 5 and 10 o'clock and carry away with them from 800 to 1,200 tons of fish.

As a result of carefully planned newspaper publicity, Brighton is enjoying a "boom." During 1925-74, 327 more tickets were taken between London and Brighton, than were booked during 1924, while the number of passengers passing through the barriers of the Central Station, Brighton. During the first six weeks of 1925 was 660,000. This is an increase of 27.8 per cent, as compared with the corresponding period last year. In all no flower than 16,000,000 passengers passed in or out of the station in 1425. "I am a mere home."—Husband. at Police Court.

The four Dutch submarines visiting Manila were opened for public inspection.

Moscow is to maugurate an air post service between European Capitals on May 1.

"I know he's a har but you can't help loving him," said a woman of her husband the Bow County Court.

A. Blackpool Corporation workman, engaged on street work, stuck his pick into a cable composed of 1,600 telephone wires, and 532 subscribers were cut off from the Exchange.

Wholesale prosecution of municipal officials in Passay as a result of failure to enforce the anti-vice ordinance in force in that municipality since 1920 is expected to begin during the next few days.

A gift from Trinity House has been received by the National Lifeboat Institution, as a mark of gratitude for the saving of one of the keepers of Godrevy Lighthouse, who was dangerously ill during a gale.

France has successfully prohibited absinthe as a beverage and accomplished it in a single day. The absinthe habit was rooted in the French people. Up to the first days of the war the Paris boulevard and all France had its "hour of absinthe" or its "green hour" every afternoon at 5 o'clock.

"The University of California baseballteam's proposed tour of Japan this summer has been cancelled, say cables from America. The reason given for this action is that the University wanted a guarantee of $20,000/year for the expenses of the tour, whereas the Japanese organisers offered only a part of the receipts from the games. The California baseballers will," however, tour Hawaii for six weeks.

A new Roman Catholic Society, supported by Cardinal Bourne and many Catholic Arch-bishops and Bishops, is launching an organised campaign throughout Britain against spiritualism, which is described as a dangerous cult, aiming at the root and branch destruction of Christianity. The late Bishop of Salford (Dr. Casartelli), claimed that spiritualism was responsible for a large leakage from Roman Catholicism.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Princess Mary and Viscount Lascelles have sent £100 for the National Memorial to Queen Alexandra.

"My husband said if I didn't forgive him he'd give me a good hiding."—Woman at Willesden Police Court.

Sir Harry Lauder, when he visited Cardiff was met at the station by pipers, who conducted him to his hotel.

One of the most outstanding dresses seen at St. Patrick's Ball, Shanghai, was worn by Madame Lily formerly of Hongkong. It was made of green taffeta, trimmed with French gold lace and garlands of hand-made flowers in Louis XV style.

Jazz is degrading in that it tends to lower the white races to the level of the "lesser breeds" mentioned by Rudyard Kipling... the jazzists may take it for granted that their number is up. The above statement was made by Dr. Henry Coward, conductor of the famous Sheffield Choir, at a meeting of a Rotary Club.

Mr. Alfred Clay, of Darley Hall, Matlock, whose will has just been proved for £140,000, bought the first ticket ever issued by Thomas Cook and Son for a tour round the world. Mr. Clay was an inveterate glohe trotter, and he could say of hand where and when railway trains and steamships connected with one another in the most distant parts of the earth. He was a sort of human "Bradshaw."

A report that the personal bodyguard of the Prince of Wales has been doubled, and is now under the command of a chief inspector of the Special Branch of Scotland Yard, has been officially denied. An official of the Prince's household told a representative of "The Daily Chronicle" that the Special Branch inspector who for years has accompanied the Prince has recently been on short leave, and that a temporary arrangement had been made for other officers to perform his duties. A London telegram to the Statesman says—Diners were pande-stricken when a drunken Chinese armed with a sword entered a Paris cafe, smashed the tables and chairs, severed a dog's tail and then cut the animal in two, before he could be arrested.

Mr. A. N. Hornby, of Nantwich, Cheshire, for 20 years captain Lancashire County Cricket Club, left £6,420.

Mrs. W. T. Austen and Miss Mabel Austen for many years residents of Yokohama are on a farewell visit to Japan before leaving for their future home in England.

Mr. Louis Leon Joseph Maurice Permezel, President of the French Red Cross in Vladivostok during the war, has been decorated, for his special services to the French and Allied Soldiers, with the Legion of Honour as Knight in date of January 31, 1926.

The librarian of the Tokyo Women's Club is seeking copies of the Club Year Book previous to 1922-1923. At the time of the 1923 earthquake the records of the Club were destroyed and the files are not complete. Books may be sent to Miss Ruth Thompson, 22 Fujimi-cho, Gochome, Koji-machi.

Mr. H. A. F. B. Archer, O.B.E., who has been Acting British Consul in Chunking has arrived in Shanghai and will assume charge of the Shipping Office in H. M. Consulate-General. Mr. Mills who has been in charge of the Shipping Office recently will relieve Mr. Toller in the Land Office.

England's cricket captain is not to be selected until the season opens. This was the decision of the Test Match Selection Committee. P. F. Warner took the chair, and A. R. Gilligan, P. Perrin and J. B. Hobbs were present. A cable was sent to Rhodes, who is in Egypt, and he is in agreement with this course. A woman with a large dog dyed green was seen in Harrow Road, N.W.

The reason for the drive against western dancing is that "it is generally recognised that in the present period of great confusion in the thinking world of Japan the social dancing introduced to Japan from abroad is doing much to deteriorate the traditional manners and customs in Japan and confuse the family system of the nation".

Judged by the prosperity and peace which it should promote through opening to cultivation 3,000,000 acres in the Sudan, "Makepeace" would seem more appropriate than Makkwa as a name for the great dam recently opened on the Blue Nile.

Women pickets in a textile dispute at Kirkenton have adopted music as a “persuader.” As the non-striking operatives leave the factory the pickets “chorus” sings. “Onward, Christian Soldiers” The heads of the firm are also “serenaded” with hynns. About one hundred women are affected

Bethesda, in Curnarvonshire, is tired of its Hebrew name, but is having considerable difficulty in selecting one in Welsh. A subcommittee submitted four possible names to the urban council to-day. Glynogwen, Giltorowen. The for-wen and Naitogwen. None of them was sufficiently attractive, and the special committee was asked to meet again and try to invent a better one.

An influential delegation, representing 300 chambers of commerce: and several important national trade organisations visited Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer to make a vigorous protest against the present tax methods by which business is done by co-operative societies, which receive more favourable tax treatment than private trading. Co-operative societies have reached an enormous size in Great Britain, and it was pointed out that they are profit-making organisations and do not deserve preferential treatment as against heavily-taxed private trading.

Mr. J. A. Clarke, parish clerk at Cromer for 53 years, died, aged 82. Cromer has had but two parish clerks in 113 years.

In the Navy Estimates £55,000 is included for soap and tobacco for seamen, compared with £71,000 in 1925.

Mr. Herbert Hanson, of Kimberley, Notts, draper left to his housekeeper, Emma Kersley, £1,000 and all moneys in the names of himself and the said Emma Kersley at bank.

Mrs. Jane M. Churton, of Chester Lodge, Bournemouth, whose estate is valued at £139,948; left to her maid, Elizabeth Jamieson, one year's wages absolutely, and the income for life from a trust fund of £4,000.

Mr. Scott Skinner, the famous player of reels and strathspeys, who is 80 years of age, is to take part in the old-time fidding contest at Lewiston, Maine, U.S.A., next month, which is open to those over 60. The prize is 1,000 dolls. (£200).

Mr. C. M. Varty, who will be remembered in Japan as the manager of the Kaihin Hotel at Kamakura for many years, has been appointed assistant manager of the Hotel Plaza at San Francisco. Mr. Varty left Japan a few months before the earthquake and fire disaster of 1923.

A woman was noticed at the theatre the other night in London with her finger nails lightly tinted with jade green to match the colour of her gown. Such a fashion of coloured nails has had a certain popularity across the Channel for some time past, and at one of the most exclusive dress salons it is now possible for a woman to buy beads, shoes and nail polish to match each new evening frock. headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Miss Margaret H. Kidd, of the Scottish Bar, is the first woman barrister to be briefed to appear at the Bar of the House of Lords.

"With politics as with bootlines, patience alone will untie knots."—Lord Irwin, Viceroy-Designate of India, when entertained to lunched by the Royal Colonial Institute at the Hotel Victoria.

Mr. Charles Olive, favourably known as an actor of distinction, leaves for Home on the 22nd inst. Mr. Olive has given impersonations of characters from the works of Dickens and has appeared in such diversified plays as "R.U.R." "Waterloo" and "A Sister to assist 'Er."

An Englishman is a man who spends all his days in the open-air and who knows only one language—his own." humously said Sir St. Clair Thomson, president of the Royal Society of Medicine, at a lecture in London. "The most in-articulate animals in the world are donkeys, owls, lobsters and English-mén," he added.

Before he left Tokyo for Hongkong, Mr. George E. Costello, for several years general agent of the Passenger department for the Canadian Pacific in Japan, was host to Communications officials, Railway department officials, Japan Tourist Bureau attaches and members of the Press, at a dinner given in a private dining room of the Imperial Hotel.

The Siam Observer of March 31 says:—Yesterday we recorded the opening of the handsome business premises of the Borneo Company, Limited, by H. R. H. Prince Chandaburi, "Minister of Commerce: To-day Mr. M. T. Cooke-Collis, the manager of the Company, hands over the ruins to Mr. A. R. Malcolm, prior to retirement from the country. He leaves on Saturday for Singapore by the Valaya, and will sail from the Southern Settlement towards the middle of April for Home. To-day he severs his active association with the Borneo Company after twenty-five years service. During the whole of that time he has been stationed in Bangkok, with the exception of a few months at Sriracha. And he was left fermenting.

The eight-hour day is to be gradually reintroduced for members of the British civil service, who now work only seven. The world's largest tyres—for the new giant air liners—are being manufactured by Messrs. Dunlop. The tyres will have a diameter of ninety inches and weigh two hundredweight. The tubes, each weighing 38 lbs., will be able to withstand a breaking load of 36 tons.

In anticipation of an interesting event towards the end of April, an up-to-date nursery is being installed at 40. Grosvenor-square, which for a time is to be the town house of the Duke and Duchess of York. Some relics of early Sydney came to light the other week when an electrician was renewing the electric wires beneath the floor of the old barracks facing King Street, now used as law courts. A quantity of old-fashioned clay pipes and bowls, some containing tobacco, large spoons, forks, and pieces of crockery were uncovered. Many of the pipes were just lying on the earth, while others were buried beneath it. It is considered that these relics are over a century old, and that they were at one time used by the soldiers who occupied the building. The structure was built by Governor Macquarie in 1817.

A. correspondent writes to the "Straits Echo": --A well-known local Chinese millionaire, it is rumoured, had some time ago about. $2,000,000 to let out on loan, but there was no one ready to take up this money or part of it even at the low interest of 4 per cent. He finally decided to invest $1,500,000 in Government Bonds, carrying interest at 5 per cent.

Penang is now represented by two lawyers in the Legislative Council, and local mercantile interests have no spokesman directly connected with trade or shipping, says the "Straits Echo." But that is the fault of the Chamber of Commerce, which preferred to send a member of the legal fraternity rather than a merchant to represent it in Singapore.

The surviving members of the Russian Imperial Family have decided to fight in the Courts the attempt at the sale of the Russian Crown Jewels, valued at £50,000,000, by the Bolsheviks. They are sending a lawyer to New York to arrange for the seizure of the jewels if they appear in the American market, and are also ready for an action in the French or other Courts against the Soviet.

Benito Mussolini, Facist leader and Premier of Italy, is revealed as the owner of an heroic sized bust of himself displayed in the Grand Central Galleries in an exhibition sponsored by the Italian Government. The statue is 10 times normal size, and on the dictator's brow is curved a wreath of a Roman emperor. The bust was packed and sent to Boston for display following the close of the exhibition. Later it will be shown in other cities.

The Prince of Wales is nothing if not democratic. Recently he mingled with the "down-and-cuts" at the East End Labour Exchange in London, and talked sympathetically with the unemployed. Apparently the Prince appreciates a fact, not yet generally understood, that a man, though lowly, is not necessarily low.

Private Robert Yeates, a survivor of the Charge of the Light Brigade, in which he was wounded in the leg, and lay bleeding alf night beside his dead horse, died on March 25 in Belfast Workhouse, aged 103. Until his death he vainly fought the War Office who had stopped his pension of 18.3d, a day when his Army papers were destroyed in a fire in 1900.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Dr. C. N. Abraham, second son of the late Rev. S. Abraham, has been appointed Assistant Health Officer for Kinta.

Me. G. J. Dickson has been appointed hon. secretary of the Malacca Branch of the Malayan Agri-Horticultural Association.

Mr. Charles Christian Heidsieck, of the well-known firm of Charles Heidsieck, Rheims, champagne growers is at present in Penang on a short visit.

Will the provisional title "Queen Mary as Working Woman," a remarkable and unconventional book by a new authoress will be published this spring.

Seventy thousand children were entertained by the Salvation Army at banquets in various parts of the country in celebration of General Booth's seventieth birthday.

At Belmont Parish, Church, Glasgow, on the 4th instant, the marriage took place of Mr. James Whyte, of Singapore, eldest son of Mr. and Mrs. Whyte, Friarscroft, Renfrew, to Miss Mona Hardie Macnie, M.B., Ch. B., only daughter of the Rev. R. L. Macnie and Mrs. Macnie, Loth. Sutherland.

H.S.H. Princess Phorn, a daughter of H.R.H. Prince Damrong, who has received a Siamese Red Cross scholarship, left for Manila on the 5th instant with Dr. and Mrs. Lowell to take up a course of medical studies. This will be the first occasion on which a princess has left Siam to prosecute her studies.

Doubleday, Page & Company, are strongly opposed to Mrs. Conrad's book about her distinguished husband, which is regarded as too intimate and too trivial and not calculated to do Mr. Conrad's reputation any good. Among other things, Mrs. Conrad told how her husband would monopolise the bathroom, splashing in the tub, to the exclusion of their guests.

There is to be another attempt to show that Shakespeare derived from factors other than rustic and common. The Cambridge University Press will publish "A Chapter in the Early Life of Shakespeare," by Arthur Gray, in which the author will endavour to show that Shakespeare did not spend all his youth at Stratford, but passed part of it at Polesworth, Warwickshire, a literary resort of the period.

The Earl of Craven, for whom a deportation warrant was issued in Washington, in connection with the immigration trouble.

Dr. S. W. Eveson is appointed to officute as "Health Officer, Malacca, with effect from March 25.

Colonel Russell Brown leaves the Colony to-morrow for Peking. This will mean his withdrawal from the tennis tournament.

Lady Gregory, who was one of the founders of the Abbey Theatre, is writing her reminiscences. Two new plays by her are to be published shortly. Lady Gregory's "Hyacinth Hvaley" was one of the plays performed at the recent celebration of the coming of age of the Abbey Theatre.

Baroness Clifton is not the only society girl "to take up the law, The Hon. Sylvia Moulton, the 23-years-old daughter of the late Lord Moulton, the famous judge, has taken her law degree at Cambridge, and has even eaten her dinners at the Temple, though few of her associates, reallsed who she was.

Still another Hamlet, this time an Italian version of the great English classic, will be seen this season in London where John Barrymore's interpretation and the plus four rendition already have been applauded. Ruggero Ruggeri, one of the best actors in Italy, will give "Amloto" at the St. James Theatre and later at Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and Glass.

Claiming to be the tallest people in England, Mr. and Mrs. L. G. Murray are starting from Plymouth on two years' cycling tour of the world.

Mrs. Henry Allhusen is the donor of £4,000 for a National Home of Health as headquarters of the New Health Society, as a memorial to her husband and children.

Sight has been given to three sisters and their brother, all born blind and all grown up, by Dr. C. M. Hawes, of the Hawes-Marple Hospital at Huntington, West Virginia.

Students of the Labour College protest against the project to convert Easton Lodge, the gift of the Countess of Warwick, into a Labour University, and suggest a convalescent home.

Tolstoy's centenary falls in 1928 and the Bolshevik authorities in Moscow are preparing a complete and uncensored edition of his works in twenty volumes. A million copies will be printed.

The Beverly Hills estate of Douglas Fairbanks and Mary Pickford is to be sold. They plan to build a Spanish hacienda farther back in the hills. The couple will leave soon on a tour of Europe.

"She called me a teetotaller, and I look upon that as an insult."—Man at Tottenham Police Court.

No youths at Meashum, Leicestershire, are applying for apprenticeships to tradesmen, although they may under a charity to this village.

Building trade rates to apply to the erection of all houses was the gist of a resolution passed by a Scottish Labour conference at Glasgow.

Post Office savings deposits on December 31, were £285,400,-000, Government stock sold £314,-918,471, and holders' credit £188,775,460.

In an attempt to lift South Wales from "iniquity," magistrates who consider ordinary dancing as "dangerous" excitement," barbaric" and "sensuous," have forbidden this. "indiscreet" pastime late at night.

It is reported from Mysore that at a village, a few miles from that city, some unknown person has poisoned 25 wild monkeys. Orthodox Hindus who venerate the monkey, dressed the bodies in funeral garments and took them in religious procession through the streets of the city to the denomination ground and disposed of them with Shastrie ceremonially. The outraged Hinds are looking for the poisoner.

"Let who will make the laws of a country, if I may control the cinemas." Mr. Snowden, ex-Chancellor of the Exchequer, thus modernised the old adage at the annual dinner of the Citizen-tograph Exhibitors Association at the Hotel Victoria. Tax oil entertainments was bad, anid violated all sound financial policy, he said. It discouraged a legitimate and very useful form of enjoyment. Thirty million people went to the cinema, and he believed that it did more than any other agency to promote temperance and sobriety.

headline: WHEN BETTER AUTOMOBILES ARE BUILT, BUICK WILL BUILD THEM
text:
One of the latest novels—"The Uncharted Sea"—has Hongkong for its scene. There is a loveless marriage with a Taiwan of Hongkong's "machine-like, business-loving Englishman." We are told that "a great strike breaks out," in which the husband plays a die-hard part, being killed by the strikers.

Last year the time ball at the Royal Observatory (Kowloon) was dropped successfully 664 times. There was one failure, on December 16 at 10 a.m., owing to an injury sustained by the coolie, when hoisting the ball. It was dropped successfully at 11 a.m. The ball was not raised on June 26 at 10 a.m. owing to high wind, and on July 14 at 4 p.m., during a severe thunderstorm.

Referring to the “strike,” the Hongkong Observatory’s annual report says:→On “leaving the Observatory on June 26, the printer and his assistant, were assaulted by intimidators, so failed to attend on June 27 and 28. In consequence the weather reports for these days were not issued until June 29 when the printers returned to duty. This was the only interruption caused by the strike, so far as the routine work of the Observatory was concerned.

The "Soul Press" announces that a Japanese "birdman" has invented "a safe, practical aeroplane." The machine is a combination of an aeroplane and a helicopter, has sixteen wings, and is warranted to fly in any direction.

In connection with the alleged leasing of land in Mexico by Japanese the Tokyo Foreign Office states that it has received no information whatever. No Japanese residents in San Pedro, it is stated, are rich enough to undertake such a big enterprise and the truth of the story is doubted.

On the 31st ultimo, as the Hamburg-Amerika liner Oldenburg was passing the Akashi strait on her way to Kobe, she sighted a motor boat in distress, the men on board the boat, which was not under control and had a heavy list, waving their arms to attract attention. Captain Lueck slowed down, and took the men on board, tiving the motor boat also to safety.

A large-size submarine (2,000 tons), which was built at the Kawasaki Dockyard, Kobé, and taken to the Yokosuka Naval Port in the latter part of last month, is claimed by the Japanese Navy to be unique, embodying all the lessons of the European War, and her fighting efficiency is a match for ten submarines of the existing types. Submarines to be laid on the blocks are to be designed to this type in future. Admiral Kato, Commander-in-chief of the Naval Station, has inspected the submarine.

The Chinese Legation building in Seoul has been sold reports the "Osaka Jiji," which vouches for a price of ¥750,000. The building stands at Meji-cho on a lot covering an area of 7,500 tsubo an attempt was made several years ago by the Mukden Army to realise the estate it more than two million yen to supplement its chest, but the plan failed. Since then a large number of estate brokers have been interested in the property, which has now been sold. The proceeds will not be utilised for war purposes, it is understood, but go to reinforce the depleted treasury of the Peking Government.

text:
LAIDIES HAIR SINGLE A SP CIALITY. ALSO MANICURE AND MARCEL WAVING.

Mr. W. E. Gooch defeated Mr. R. J. Graciani in the final match of the Kobe Club Handicap Billiard Tournament, the play being witnessed by a large number of the members. Mr. Graciani, with a handicap of minus 150, had scored 128 points when his opponent, with a handicap of minus 250, had scored 250 points.

Prince Chichibu of Japan has presented the Kandahar Ski Club, of Murren, with a challenge cup to be known as The Prince Chichibu Challenge Cup. In accordance with the express desire of the Prince, who is a member of the Club, the cup will be awarded to the winner of a straight race open to all members of the Club.

Osaka Chauffure, dissatisfied with their treatment, recently went on strike.

Since the Armistice 2340,000,-000 has been spent, without service rendered, on unemployment.

Five thousand settlers are expected in Canada this year under the scheme for establishing families on the land.

The Gaumont Graphic at the Queen's Theatre shows pictures of the recent golf-archery contest with victory going to the Archers.

"What Happened to Jones" at the Queens is a first rate comedy which convulsed big audiences yesterday. The picture is being screened to-day and to-morrow.

From his London residence: Sir Evelyn Murray, secretary of the G.P.O., has spoken to America by telephone, but it is not certain whether it is commercially practicable.

On March 1 the cost of living, says the "Ministry of Labour Gazette" was about 72 per cent. above that of July, 1914, as compared with 73 per cent. a month ago and 79 per cent. a year ago.

The Government of Quebec is preparing to tax the heavy eater. A Bill introduced into the Legislature provides that a restaurant meal costing more than 4s. 2d is taxable at five per cent.

Twenty guineas (8 offered by the National Farmers' Union) for the best pound lond of bread made entirely with flour milled from wheat grown in England and Wales, at the Bakers' Exhibition this year.

A well-dressed man coming out of a tea shop near the Temple pulled a banker chief out of his pocket, and at the same time dropped a sixpence. He walked on unaware of this, but a little girl standing near by picked up the coin, ran after him, and handed it to him. He rewarded her with half a crown.
