The Spring issue of St. Andrew's Young Men's Club magazine is a bright and interesting production on which those concerned deserve congratulations.

A record snowfall for April is reported from Takayama and other towns in Hida province, Japan, where the depth is said to be over five inches. The snow and cold weather marred the festival of the Hiya Shripe in Takayama.

A plan for harnessing the electrical energy believed to be possessed by the Nitherto: lifeless lake known as the Dead Sea is announced. It properly exploited, it is declared, the lake can produce a maximum of 350,000 horse power.

Mr. Charles Talbot, of the Union Oil Company organisation in Japan with headquarters in Kebe, says that recent flows in California in which millions of dollars worth of oil in tanks was burned would not affect the distribution of the company. "In the least."

Japanese labour leaders are making arrangements for the celebration of May Day, which, according to present plans, will be observed by a gathering in Shix park, and a parade from there to Uyeno park, Tokyo. D'tails of the programme will be arranged at a meeting of representatives of labour organisations which are to participate in the celebration.

Two of the oldest saloons in England are shortly too pass out of existence. The "Two Brewers" saloon at Perry Mill, Catford, near London which was in operation before Columbus discovered America and which has been dispensing drinks ever since is shortly to be demolished to make way for a modern hotel. Here, Dick Turpin, the famous highwayman who was hanged at York in 1739, used frequently to step in for a drink, to the consternation of the "bar-flies." "Ye Older Whittington" near Kinver, Staffordshire, which dates from early in the sixteenth Century and where King Charles stayed in his flight from Worcester, is shortly to go under the auctioneer's hammer.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Mr. A. K. McDonnell's Dodge Roadster has been won by ticket No. 34.

All being well, the Bishop of London is likely to be in Hong Kong on Christmas Day.

Mr. Harry Tobias, of N. Lazarus, is due in the Colony next month on his return to Shanghai from Home leave.

The engagement is announced of Dr. Herbert Manchester, pastor of Yokohama Union Church, to Miss Mary B. Gersbacher of Syracuse, N. Y.

Capt. Daniel J. Keating, M.C., who has been promoted to that rank in the East Yorkshire Regiment, is with the 1st Battalion at Tientsin, North China. He was commissioned in the Leinster Regiment in April, 1916, and in 1922 was transferred to the Sappers on the disbandment of the Liensters. Capt. Keating was mentioned in despatches in 1917, was given the Military Cross in recognition of his conspicuous courage in action, and also wears the two-war medals. Mrs. Douglas Robinson, a sister of the late President Roosevelt, underwent an operation, seeking restoration of her sight. She has been blind for some time in one eye, and recently discovered that the sight of the other had dimmed to a point where she could scarcely see.

Mr. Frank Booth, of Tokyo, representative in Japan for the Baker-Perkins Company, suffered a broken leg in the driveway of the Imperial Hotel, "Tokyo" when his lower limb struck a projection as he was driving out on his motorcycle. Mr. Booth was leaving the driveway at low speed and placed a foot on the ground to aid in guiding the machine. The motorcycle was driven too close to the wall and his limb struck the brick. The bone snapped. Mr. Booth was taken to hospital and is resting easily.

The death occurred on March 20, in Osaka, of Mr. P. Paterson Fox, after a serious internal operation. Mr. Paterson Fox was a scholar of singular merit and had previously followed a distinguished teaching career in England, having taught at St. Peter's Court, Broadstairs (patronised by the British Royal Family) and at Uppingham. He went to Japan about a year ago to fill a Government appointment in a school at Shizuoka, but relinquished this in December last to occupy a better one at the Maizuru Naval College, when the first symptoms of his final illness appeared, and prevented his ever fully occupying his new position.

Bolton Wanderers who have won the English Cup final are popularly known as "the Trotters."

Mr. John Fitzpatrick, of Eckett Street, Bermondsey, has just celebrated his 100th birthday. He has lived in Bermondsey all his life. His chief pastime is walking, and he attributes his long life to hard work.

Mr. F. S. Brockman, of New York, associate general secretary of the international committee of Y.M.C.A., who has been touring the Orient has arrived in Tokyo. Mr. H. S. Sheyd, secretary of the Yokohama Y.M.C.A., is to confer with Mr. Brockman at Tokyo on various matters concerning the association works.

Mr. Mitsugu Hara, adopted son of the late Premier Hara, accompanied by his wife will soon leave Japan to study in England again. He recently married the daughter of the late Dr. Tokichi Masao, former Japanese Minister to Siam. Mr. Hara will continue to write from England for a literary magazine started in Tokyo by his friends. Mrs. Hara will continue her study of oil painting.

The announcement of the engagement of Miss Diana de Warzee, the daughter of the Belgian Minister to China, and Baroness de Warzee d'Hermalle, has created much interest in Tokyo where the family lived for nine years. M: de Warzee was Secretary and for a time Charged Affairs of the Belgian Embassy. After leaving Japan about five years ago, Baron de Warzee served as Belgian Minister at Havana, Cuba, and afterward as Charge d'Affaires at Washington. He inherited the family title of Baron after leaving Japan.

Mr. Hou Tsung-line, a Chinese medical student, has won a doctor's degree at the age of 23. As a special honour, the degree will be conferred by the Japanese Minister of Education. He recently graduated, from the South Manchurian University medical college and has been made assistant professor at that college. His degrees was won by his research work into the blood circulation and amount of oxygen needed in the brain of a dog, which was finally approved only a few days ago by a board of professors of the Medical Faculty of Kyoto University.

headline: AND GENERAL.
text:
The Water Authority announces that a constant supply of water will be turned on in all rider main districts until further notice.

The Yokohama Municipality is to build a five-storeyed steel frame, fire and earthquake building designed for the hotel business.

A cash box containing about $30 was stolen by an armed robber early yesterday morning from a Chinese widow, living at Taipo Old Market. The woman was struck on the head when she made an endeavour to recover her property.

"I do not believe," says Lord Hugh Cecil "that there is in the whole of Christian history any settled part of the Christian Church which is less remote from the Kingdom of Heaven as sketched in the New Testament than is the Church of England today."

The Union of Chinese Chambers of Commerce, with headquarters in Peking, has submitted a memorandum to the Peking Government urging the immediate opening of formal negotiations with Soviet Russia for redemption of "ruble notes" in possession of the Chinese people.

China's capital is one of the few walled cities in the world the gates of which really close every night and remain closed until daylight. The time for opening and closing the city gates has now undergone another change. For some time past they have opened at 5 in the morning and closed at 6 at night. But now they are open at 6:30 a.m. and close at 6 p.m.

Washington policemen are wondering just how one can hit a prisoner and still be courteous about it. In a lecture cautioning policemen to dispense with "hard-boiled" tactics, Edwin B. Hesse, Superintendent of Police, said there was "no excuse for gruffiness or discourtesy" in dealing with law offenders, and added: "Even when a prisoner becomes violent, there is no reason for it. If you must hit him, hit him in courteous way."

Residents of New York City give up Ten Million Dollars a year to "charities" which are questionable or completely fraudulent.

The Home Secretary, Sir William Joynson Hicks, M.P., has informed the Lord's Day Observance Society who wrote to the Home Office regarding the battling on girls' races on Sunday mornings at the North Walthamstow Athletic Grounds that these races have now been discontinued.

Aerial tours of Great Britain are to be offered American visitors this summer. An English aircraft company is building a fleet of four and eight-seater planes to meet the American demand for speed. Three, four and seven-day tours of England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales, with landings at the principal places of interest are to be offered. Some of the machines will be seaplanes, equipped to descend on lakes and rivers, designed especially for tours of the lake country and the coastal towns.

A, tempest, in a teapot has been raised in Stratford-on-Avon. The Town Councillors, some of whom are also trustees of the Shakespeare Memorial, have changed the historic if not exactly magnificent names of some of the streets. For instance, Skinner's lane, leading to Anne Hathaway's Cottage, is to be Anne Hathaway Road; Back Lane is to be dressed up as Grove Road and Swine Street is to be changed into Ely Street. A protesting letter to the "Times" from one Shakespeare trustee will probably be followed by others.

"Rose Marie," the first production which has ever run for a year at Drury Lane Theatre, has celebrated its birthday. The theatre was opened in 1663, so "Rose Marie" establishes a record for 263 years. Over a million people have seen the play in London and the provinces, and a wealthy Indian merchant, who has now returned to the East, bought a box for every Wednesday matinee of his six months stay in London. So far the members of the company have worn 1,400 costumes, 1,600 pairs of shoes, and 2,000 pairs of stockings.

To "boost" England, Mr. Gilbert Frankau, the novelist, has left on a lecture tour in America.

King Alfonso was returning from a drive on the outskirts of the city, when his car was pulled up for a minor adjustment to be made. At that moment a tired-looking workman, walking citywards, not recognising the King, asked for a lift, as he was overcoming with fatigue. With a smile, the King bade him jump in, and the car conveyed him swiftly to his humble dwelling in the alums of Madrid.

Dr. Henry Coward, addressing the members of the Leeds Rotary Club, remarked that only those who had been brought up in a musical atmosphere knew how it sweetened life. "A man's business is more likely to go west if he shuts music out of his life," said Dr. Coward. "The subtle, stimulating, wit-sharpening, spirrit-rousing, nerve-soothing influence of music is Nature's pleasant medicine. The most thriving business districts of Britain are the most musical. In sleepy, dead-alive places, music is always at a low ebb. That is not an accident; Musical people are the brightest, and most alert."

General Managers HONGKONG

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:
Professor James Iarnell, one of Germany's most distinguished and successful surgeons, died recently in Berlin at the age of 78. Professor Israel was a specialist on kidney troubles.

Mr. Bucknell, Senior American Assessor at the Mixed Court, said goodbye to the Court on April 27, this being his last day in attendance officially. Mr. Bucknell is leaving for America shortly.

A report comes from London that the principal English yachting association has repealed the decision according to which nationals of the Central Powers shall be excluded from participating in English pegattas for a period of 10 years after the conclusion of peace.

Mr. Carl Ray Sadler, Cavalier of the Texas Company, Shanghai met his death as the result of a collision with a motor car driver by Hong Ah-sen, a coroner's jury in the American Court decided on April 21, but no charges were brought against the Chinese. Action, if any is taken, is up to the Municipal Police.

Word has been received in Tsingtao from a party of Germans, that they arrived in Berlin exactly twelve days after leaving Tsingtao. So far as is known this is the quickest time ever made since the war via the Siberian Railway between Tsingtao and Berlin. Ordinarily this trip has taken at least fifteen days in the past and now takes three weeks.

There was a fair attendance at the opening of the Spring Exhibition of the China Society of Science and Arts on April 24. The exhibition which is being held in the old British Post Office building in Peking Road is being held in conjunction with the British Women's Association and the American Women's Club art departments.

A series of boxing matches in which Japanese champions will take part will be held at the compound of the Yasukuni Shrine on the occasion of the semi-annual shrine festival early in May. The Japan Boxing Club is promoting the meeting. Due to the growing popularity of boxing in Japan, the War Office, which sponsored Japanese wrestling matches at the semi-annual festival for three days, has spared one day for the boxing matches. The French Fire Brigado held an inter-company competition in the use of the fire fighting equipment at the French Park last Saturday.

One case of diphtheria was notified on Tuesday from the district of Victoria (city), the patient being Chinese. We are officially informed that the King's Birthday parade will take place this year on June 8, at Happy Valley. Time and details will be communicated later.

At the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday, a cook brought a claim against Mrs. R. El Matthison for 16 days' wages at $18 per month and one month's wages in lieu of notice. After hearing both sides, the Magistrate held there had been a misunderstanding between the parties and recommended the payment of $10 to the complainant.

A conductor employed by the Kowloon Motor Bus Company told the Magistrate yesterday when he was charged with absconding with a sum of $10.95 that he was obliged to run away owing to his inability to replace some one-dollar notes which were blown away by the wind. He was sentenced to six weeks' hard labour.

Colonel Yen Chung-yang, Chief of the Chinese Police, has definitely made his intention known regarding Wong Ching-yuin, chairman of the Shanghai General Labour Union, who was arrested recently. According to the Chinese Press, Colonel Yen will release Wong from custody only if the labourers and students cause no trouble during next month and its many anniversaries.

Construction of the four torpedo destroyers called for in the recent Japan Diet session, is to be started soon by the Navy Department, to be completed within three years at a cost of ¥26,110,400. The Diet approved an ¥8,000,000 appropriation for the current year, ¥10,274,160 for next year and ¥7,836,240 for the following year for these destroyers, as a part of the auxiliary fleet.

For what was held to be the balance due for wines and refreshments supplied to the Stonemason's Guild, the Wing Shing Company claimed $535.60 in the Summary Court yesterday but were awarded $35.60 only, as plaintiffs admitted in the course of the case that $500 had been received. Mr. H. S. Fitzroy (Instructed by Messrs. Lee and Ruas) appeared for plaintiffs and Mr. A. J. O'Donoghue for defendants.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
To-morrow, the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps smoking concert (and prize-distribution) will take place at headquarters at 9.15 p.m.

The retirement of still another old Shanghai resident has to be recorded, Mr. Tom Wallace, after 43 years of continuous service with the Waterworks Co., having decided to retire into private life.

The funeral took place last evening at Happy Valley of Vera Gertrudes Xavier, the fifteen months old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. R. G. Xavier, No. 25, Jordan Road, Kowloon, whose death occurred on Tuesday.

The death took place at the Severance Hospital, Seoul, on the morning of April 21 of the Rev. C. H. I. Hodges, who in June last succeeded the Rev. Eustace M. Strong as chaplain of Christ Church, Yokohama.

Bishop Trollope, the Anglican diocesan in Korea, is shortly leaving for England, owing to a breakdown in health, due to heart trouble. During his residence in Korea Bishop Trollope took a keen interest in the construction of the Anglican Cathedral at Seoul.

Sir Henry Gollan, Chief Justice, has granted probate to Mr. W. E. L. Shenton of the will of the late Capt. James Henry Woollacott, master mariner. Capt. Woollacott, who died in the Government-Civil Hospital here in December 1924, left $10,000, and died in state.

Dora Chappell, daughter of the Rey James and Mrs. Chappell, well-known missionaries in Japan, was married at St Andrew's Church, Shiba, Tokyo on April 21, to James Coster Lloyd Edwards. The young couple are to reside in Wales, the home of the bridegroom.

Mr. C. J. Spiker arrived in Shanghai on May 1 for temporary duty at the American Consulate-General where he will take up the work of the Senior American Assessor during the absence of Mr. Howard Bucknell. In this work will not be new to him as he was in Shanghai in 1916-19

Miss Dorothy Gish, the famous film star has arrived in London. She is to make three British films during her visit.

The First Lord of the Admiralty, Mr. W. C. Bridgeman, spent part of the Easter recess on an official visit of inspection to Gibraltar.

Sir Hedley Le Bas, governing director of the Caxton Publishing Co., Ltd., died in a nursing home at Reigate, Surrey, on March 26 in his 58th year.

Mr. Hsu Lan-tsu, industrial commissioner of Kiangsu, and Mr. Ma Wen-chih, staff officer to Marshal Sun Chuan-fang, have arrived in Shanghai from Nanking.

Captain D. Margesson (rec. 6) beat the Prince of Wales (sor.) in the fourth round of the Houses of Parliament squash racquets, handicap at the Bath Club on March 25 by 2 games to love (18-17, 18-15). Mr. W. J. Bellerby, part-owner of King of Clubs, which won the Lincolnshire Handicap at odds of 100 to 1 against had odds of 200 to 1 to win £2,000. He also has a "double" of 2,000 to 1 about the horse coupled with Sprig for the Grand National. The Duke and Duchess of York have given their patronage to the ball which Lady Airlie and Mrs Gerard Leigh are organising at Claridge's Hotel, for the Prince of Wales Sea Training Hostel at Limehouse. Among those on the committee are Lady Ancaster Lady Beatty, Lady Carlisla, Lady Pembroke, Lady Chaplin, Lady Stanley, Lady Mary Kenyon-Slaney, Lady Moira Lyttelton, and Lady Kathleen Rollo. Miss Violette Cordery, 16 25 years old, woman racing motorist, arrived in London after breaking 57 records on the Monza track near Milan, taking turns at the wheel with five other drivers day and night. Miss Cordery is of slight build with small hands and a fresh complexion and half buried boneless bouquets of flowers heaped on her in the Pulitan car of her train. It seemed difficult to assist her with the endurance records and news about

A hundred thousand people lined the route taken by the funeral procession of the Dowager Queen of Denmark from Amalienborg Castle to the Central Station. The coffin was there transferred to a special train and taken to Roskilde, the burial place of the Danish kings, for interment. Prince Arthur of Connaught represented Britain at the funeral.

For the first time in history, the Sultan of Morocco is to break the laws of the Korean to visit Paris. Escorted by a brilliant delegation of the great Caids of Morocco, and Islamic leaders from Algeria, Egypt, Palestine, and Arabia, he will visit the French capital in July to inaugurate the largest mosque constructed in the Western world.

The Rev. James Sibree, F.R.G.S., now of Bombley, who celebrated his 90th birthday last month has a most interesting history. It is said that he learned his Greek Testament in waiting-rooms and trains; travelled to Madagascar in a sailing ship in 1868 to build four churches for the London Missionary Society; he was shipwrecked once, and was once nearly drowned in a twobass

Mrs. Mary Wilkin, of Summerhill, Tenterden, Kent, has left estate of the value of £81,518, with net personality £75,979. She left £2,000 each to her housemaid, Eessie Willis, and her parlourmaid, Ellen Short, £1,000 to her coachman, Charles Masters, £800 each to her cowman, George Harris, and her cock, Margaret Mallion; and one year's wages to each of her servants. Mr. Edmund Fowler, who won the V.C. for bravery in March 1879, during the Zulu campaign in an assault on the Onliobane Mountain, died at Colchester on March 27. Some delay occurred in the execution of orders for the dislodgment of Zulu's from a cave but Private Fowler dashed for war and, with his subtler cleared the cave after Captain Campbell their leader had been killed. Fowler later became a BEST PORTLAND CEMENT

Wish I'd sent it to the Cold Stores. Goods for storage now being received at our Depot and Branches for transfer to Cold Storage works. Pamphlets on application.

The Dairy Farm Ice & Cold Storage Co., Ltd.

A magnificent monument to Saint Francis is to be erected in the Piazza of St. John the Lateran in Rome in honour of the seventh centenary of the death of the saint of Assisi which occurs this year.

In future all meetings of the Shanghai Philatelic Society will be held in the Kalee Hotel, as the manager has kindly arranged for a room to be at the disposal of members from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. on alternate. Wednesdays.

The "Secul Press" announces that a Japanese "birdman" has invented "a safe, practical aeroplane." The machine is a combination of an aeroplane and a helicopter, has sixteen wings and is warranted to fly in any direction.

There are more than 180 rubber factories in Japan. The growth of the industry has been remarkable since the end of the Great War. In 1913 there were but six rubber plants. In 1917 there were 18. By 1922 this number had been increased to 152 and in 1922 the total stood at 180, where it probably remains. Few new businesses have been started in the slump which has prevailed in Japan since 1922.

Two Loke Yew Scholarships, which provide free board and tuition, and one Donor Scholarship, which provides free tuition, at the University of Hongkong, fall vacant in January, 1927. They are open to Chinese students' indigenous to British Malaya who have good school records and who are in poor circumstances. Applications for them should reach the local Inspector of Schools on or before July 31, 1926.

A large-size submarine (2,000 tons), which was built at the Kawasaki Dockyard, Kobe, and taken to the Yokosuka Naval Port in the latter past of March, is claimed by the Japanese Navy to be unique, embodying all the lessons of the European War, and her fighting efficiency is a match for ten submarines of the existing types. Submarine to be laid on the blocks are to be designed to this type in future Admiral Kato, Commander-in-Chief of the Naval Station, has inspected the submarine.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:
An extraordinary general meeting of the Hongkong Philharmonic Society will take place at the Cathedral Hall, on Monday. June 7 at 5.30 pm.

Fines of $5 were imposed at the Central Magistracy yesterday on several Chinese for firing crackers in the vicinity of the Government Civil Hospital.

Captain Lorign (the Spanish aviator) is unlikely to fly his machine from Macao to Manila, because of the uncertainty of when his new motor will arrive in Macao from California.

A police report states that a Chinese escaped from the charge room at the Taipo police station while under arrest. The man's name is Lee Yuen, 21 years old and he was dressed in blue cotton clothes.

Evidence was taken at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday in a charge of theft of about $400 in money and jewellery against a Chinese servant girl from a house at Woo Sung Street. The case was adjourned.

Three property sales are advertised to take place at the auction rooms of Messrs. Lammert Bros. on June 3 at 3 p.m. The properties that are being put up are: The Ming-Yuen Gardens, Leasehold Property, situate at 40, Bonham Road and Leasehold Property situate at Nos. 21, 22, 23 and 24 Hill Road.

For allowing his dog to be abroad without being muzzled or on a lead, Mr. Reid, of Broadwood Road, was fined $10 at the Magistracy yesterday. The caretaker of the Japanese Crematorium, Sookumpoo, was fined $40 for keeping four dogs without licences. Fines of from $5 to $10 were imposed on other offenders.

There were 314 deaths in Singapore during the week ending May 8, according to the statement of the Registrar of Births and Deaths. Pneumonia accounted for 44 of these, convulsion of 38, phthisis for 33, fever not specified for 21, and malnial fever for 21. Under nationalities there were one European two Eurasian 249 Chinese, 45 Malay, and 16 Indian deaths One death from bubon'e plague occurred. A ratio per mille of the population of 32.0 was returned.

The annual meeting of the Pauk Tramways Co., Ltd. is to be held at the Hongkong Hotel at 11 a.m. to morrow

Shareholders are reminded of the annual meeting to tomorrow, at Union-Building, of the Union Insurance Society of Canton, Ltd. (11 a.m.); British Traders' Insurance Co., Ltd. (11.15 a.m.); and China Fibre Insurance Co., Ltd. (11.20 a.m.).

The tenth Congress of the International Women's Suffrage Alliance is to be held in Paris, May 30 to June 6. Although Chinese Woman Suffrage has not yet affiliated itself with this international woman's organisation, it has decided to send a fraternal delegate to the conference to carry greetings from the women of the Orient.

"Mr. Chow" Shing-ting, the chairman of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, Hankow, has sent in a long petition to General Headquarters complaining that in spite of the transport companies' advancing $300,000 to the railway company as transportation fees the military along the line are still freely detaining cars. Mr. Chow voices the hope that Headquarters will take the necessary measures towards protecting the cars in future.

Peking, May 13.—The Panshen Lama has circulated a telegram joining those in the demand that Dr. W. W. Yen assume office without further loss of time as Regency Premiers. The Tibetan dignitary dwelt upon the 'dangers which would ensure to the country if the present state of affairs in Peking were allowed to continue and voiced the hope that all civilian and military leaders throughout the country would co-operate with one another so that the country may settle down at an early date.

Billards enthusiasts are reminded of the exhibition by Mr. Claud Falkiner at 9 p.m. tomorrow at the South China A.A. headquarters in China Building. The famous British professional will meet Mr. S. C. Kwok, one of the best of Chinese cueists in the Colony. Mr. Kwok has been a finalist in the Hongkong championships. When not playing for any trophy, as he will be tomorrow night, he is likely to give of his best, his style being of the free and easy, and three figure breaks are not out of his reach.

The Netherland Indian Government has declared Amoy to be an infected place or account of plague. Ipon, May 18.—A mail bag from Ipon to Malacca was lost in transit to the local station last night and is still untraced.

Peking, May 8.—Evacuation of troops from Peking's historical centres is said to have been effected by General Wang Hual-ching. The places from which the military are being moved include the Confucian Temple, Lama Temple, Coal Hill Temple, Temple of Heaven and Temple of Agriculture.

By the terms of a resolution adopted at the recent annual general meeting of the Shanghai Medical Society no longer will any account be taken of the nationality of those who may join the organisation. This means that after a lapse of years German and Australian physicians again will be admitted to the membership of the Society.

The long reported issuance of funds to the employees of the Peking-Hankow Railway Administration materialised recently, when all the officials received their pay for April, and were promised the arrears for January/February and March by instalments within ten months. It is said that Mr. Lao Chif-chang, the new Director of the Bureau is preparing to pay all the arrears of salaries to the dismissed employees shortly.

Peking, May 8.—The British Minister called on Dr. W. W. Yen this morning in connection with the liquidation of loans owing Great Britain by China. At the request of Sir Ronald, it is reported that Dr. Yen promised to present the question to the authorities, when a discussion of the liquidation of domestic and foreign loans as regard the use of the increased Customs revenues came up.

On May 18 a fire broke out in a shop in Kampong Djawa at Padang. The flames soon spread to the adjacent buildings and it was not long before the whole of the market was one sheet of flame. All houses and shops were a prey to the flames. Lack of water was the reason for the rapid spreading of the fire. No casualties are reported. More than 100 shops have been burnt down. The damage is estimated at roughly 200 to 300 thousand guilders of which only a small amount is covered by insurance.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Lt.-Com. G. W. Hoare Smith has been appointed to H.M.S. "Moth," in command.

The appointment of Mr. E. T. Williams as a police magistrate at Penang, and also a member of the Board of Examiners in Malay, has been notified.

Peking, May 8.—It is announced that the Italian Minister will soon be transferred, and will return to his country at the beginning of June.

The Annual Ball of the Russian Benevolent Society took place at the Majestic Hotel on May 18, and proved an unqualified success. The ball room was thronged with dancers, close on seven hundred at least being present.

The engagement is announced of Joseph W. Brouwer, the Singapore Y.M.C.A. cricketer, and Edith Joan, younger daughter of Mr. E. V. Xavier, retired Kuala Lumpur postmaster, and Mrs. Xavier—M. M.

On arrival here from Haiphong, Madame. Herriot (wife of the ex-French Premier and President of the Chamber of Deputies) was entertained at the French Consulate. Madame. Herriot was accompanied by Madame Wilden (wife of the French diplomat). It is reported that arrangements are being made by a number of leading Shanghai educators and merchants for the establishment of a commercial college in Hankow. Mr. Y. S. Wei, Mr. L. S. Tong and several other prominent businessmen are reported to have made contribution of funds and the college is expected to be ready to open sometime this September. Past and present members of the Middlesex Regiment were entertained by past and present Officers of the Regiment on May 15 at the Europe Hotel Singapore. Colonel R. H. Haseldine, D.S.O., presided and made an impressive speech at the end of the dinner recalling that wherever Middlesex men were to be found the world over some effort

A telegram from Moscow states that Marshal Feng has been busy since his arrival there attending official functions arranged in his honour. He is quoted as planning to go to Germany very shortly to visit industrial centres.

At a recent meeting the Board of Directors of the Shanghai Chinese Y.M.C.A. accepted with regret the resignation of Mr. C. G. Hoh, for several years the General Secretary of this Association, who has been detained in Honolulu by family responsibilities. Mr. Z. H. Tong succeeds him.

Tokyo, May 21.—Seventeen Chinese connected with "electric enterprises" arrived from Peking, this morning, at the invitation of Baron Den, President of the Japan Electric Association. The party is remaining till May 27 inspecting the general condition of electric enterprises in Japan. Nearly 400 people representing all the Volunteer organisations in the French Concession Shanghai were present at the dinner given on May 21 at the French Club by M. Naggar, French Consul-General, and members of the French Municipal Council, when high tributes to their services to the municipality were paid.

San Francisco, April 21, Liu Yu-ching 8½ feet high, arrived here to day from China. He is the tallest Chinese that ever came out of the Far East. A special bunk had to be arranged for him aboard the "Dollar Liner." President Lincoln. His weight is near 400 pounds. He is 38 years old and at one time was a member of the Imperial Guard at Peking. He expects to go into the movies. Mr. Sllas H. Strawn, the American Commissioner and Chairman of the Extrateritorial Commission, is remaining in Peking to finish up what can be done at this time in the work of the Customs Conference. He hopes to make the trip north with the other Commissioner and to get away from Peking for the summer in time to meet his wife and daughter.

Madrid, May 20.—Archbishop Ventura Martin Garcia, the last Spanish Archbishop of the Philippines, is seriously ill and physicians feel that his recovery is doubtful.

John R. Freeman, Jr., of the Bureau of Standards of the United States Government, arrived in Shanghai recently accompanied by Mrs. Freeman. Mr. Freeman is the son of J.R. Freeman, Sr., who was formerly connected with the Whangpoo Conservancy Board here.

Mr. J. Merle Davis, general secretary of the Institute of Pacific Relations, Honolulu, was the guest of honour at a tiffin given by the Pan-Pacific Association of Shanghai at the Union Club on Monday, May 17. Mr. S. U. Zau presided and in addition to the address by Mr. Davis there was a talk by Mr. L. T. Chen of Shanghai. Washington, May 20—Vice Governor Gilmore called at the White House to day for a final conference with the president before leaving Washington. He plans to sail for the Philippines on June 27. Subjects touched upon at their conference to day included the auditor bill educational and health questions.

Rev. Father Jose das Neves, Vicnr-General of Portuguese Timor, and Father Alberto Goncalves, arrived in Malacca on May 11, en route to Portugal. Father Jose has laboured in Timor as a missionary for 29 years without a break, and has held the office of vicar-general for the 1st 25 years. He is now going home on leave. The fathers left Malacca on May 14. Washington, May 20 — Mr. Carmil A. Thompson, special envoy of President Coolidge, who is going to the Philippines to investigate economic conditions, will sell on the steamer President Grant from Seattle on June 15, carrying here on July 9. headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:
Washington, May 20.—After fifteen years exclusion gum has been readmitted to good standing in the navy and will be sold to the men aboard ship.

The Tientsin Grammar School Committee has decided, with the approval of the B.M.C., to inform parents that it is not considered desirable that pupils of the school should attend the Races. In no case will pupils be permitted to absent themselves from school for this purpose.

A Chinese chauffeur who caused the death of a coolie with the car in which he was driving, was sentenced to one year imprisonment by the Shanghai Mixed Court authorities. The accused was charged with causing death through inattention to his duty as a driver of a motor vehicle.

"Tokyo, May 20.—Opinion is growing in Japan that the Geneva disarmament conference is abortive.—The government also reiterates its intention of approving any reasonable and equitable proposition agreed upon. The government expressed its willingness to consider naval disarmament separately from the land forces or jointly."

In his annual report the British Resident of Pahang records that a discovery of considerable historical interest was made at Pahang Tua in 1925. This was the finding of the tomb of Muhammad Shah, the first Sultan of, Pahang. The inscription on the tombstones marking his grave gives the date of his death as the 16th Jamed Al Awal, 1880 A.H. which corresponds with September 17, 1475 A.D.

Sentence of death was on May 20 passed upon four armed robbers found guilty of being concerned in a number of armed robberies within the International Settlement during March last. A quantity of arms and ammunition was seized by the police at the time of the arrest of the condemned men whose most lucrative robbery was the theft of 2,000 coppers, 132 10-cent pieces and $6 Mex, on March 19 last from a shop-situated at No. 328 Penang Road.

Tokyo, May 20.—A Japanese passenger arriving at Yokohama to-day by the R.M.S. "Empress of Canada" from Shanghai committed suicide by jumping overboard. In a letter addressed to the captain of the vessel he stated that his action was meant as a protest against the Canadian "attempt to exclude yellow peoples."

Batavia, May 18.—The town of Sourabaya, Samarang and this city have been practically under martial law for several months as a result of the activities of the Sareka Rayat, a popular revolutionary party. The eastern and western coasts of Sumatra are in a similar situation. They have the appearance of a country ruled under martial law. For this reason, the agents of the Sarekat Rayat are compelled to carry their work in a very secret manner.

Vienna, May 16.—Following disturbances in the Apollo Theatre, the police ordered the suppression of a comedian's lines wherein the dish "pork's head" is as a "head" with the mouth wide open. It is understood that the head of the local Fascist club instigated the disturbance which broke up the show. The Italian minister thereupon made an official visit to the foreign office and requested that the lines be suppressed.

Another example of popular legend without much foundation is that in connection with "The Cheshire Cheese," an ancient and famous inn which stands in Wine Office "Court, Fleet Street. In this inn on the wall behind "a certain seat is a grease-patch, and, according to tradition, this mark was made by Dr. Johnson, who, allegedly, habitually sat there resting his bewigged head on the wall behind him. There is no proof, however, of this; there is no proof even that Johnson ever entered the establishment, and the only evidence in its favour is that Dr. Johnson's house in Gough Square is only a very short distance from the inn. But the story lives, and although many do not give it credence doubtless the landlords of "The Cheshire Cheese" have profited by it for years.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Rev. W. T. Austen, for 26 years Missions to Seamen's chaplain at Yokohama, has been appointed vicar of North Shoebury, Essex. A 10-months-old Great Dan'epuppy exhibited at the Championship Dog Show held by the Kensington Canine Society at the Crystal Palace was priced in the catalogue at £1,500,000. Mrs. F. Hornsby, its owner, said that although no one was likely to offer so large a sum, that was its actual value to her. A "beauty parlour" for dogs was a feature of the show. The "parlour" was a large room set aside especially for the grooming of the various exhibits.

Lieutenant E. A. A. Glbbon, R.N., H.M.S. "Hermes," and Marjorie Duce Kiddle, of Amberley, Stroud, were, to be married early this month at Malta.

In something between ten and twenty years' time, it seems, there is to be another war, and the rebuilding of a new world will begin in London. Such is the theme of Lord Halsbury's "1944," a strange romance. The thunder starts in a conflict between China and Russia, at a time when Britain is once more dimly unconscious of the horror at its gates. The Duke of Connaught, K.G., president, presided at the annual Empire Day dinner of the Royal Colonial Institute on May 20.

A British ju-jutsu expert writing to the "Daily News," offers to go to Nottingham at his own expense, and revive a girl who has been in a trance. A well-known Japanese ju-jutsu exponent says it is possible by the Katsu method to apply a slight physical shock to the nerve centres which would revive the action of the heart, but it is not intended to cure bodily ills and diseases.

Johnstone, late Treasurer of the Institution, as a small appreciation of his work as Hon. Treasurer to the Institution and as a token of osteem. The presentation was made by Mr. J. Ormiston, President, who spoke in eulogistic terms of Mr. Johnstone's work, Mr. B. L. Frost andorsed Mr. Ormiston's remarks.

During April the Calcutta Fire Brigade had to attend to 227 aforalarms, the highest number ever recorded in a month. The majority of the calls were due to incendialism in connection with the recent riots.

Wireless has brought a child into the world. Out of the air in mid-Atlantic the Canadian Pacific liner "Montclare" picked up an urgent appeal from the "s. Nagoyn" asking for a surgeon to attend a passenger at the birth of a child. From a distance of 100 miles the "Montclare's surgeon" wirelessed directions and within two hours the message came: "Mother and child-doing well."

Nauen, May 5.—Political circles are discussing the possibility of the Vatican renewing diplomatic relations with the Soviet Government, following the return of the Vatican's delegate, Jesuit Herbigny from Moscow where he negotiated with the Soviets according to a dispatch from Rome. Unquestionably, it is said, this would strengthen decidedly the international position of the Soviet Government.

Washington, May 22.—A summary of Governor Wood's annual report to the President describes conditions in the Philippines as greatly "improved commercially and socially." The governor states that he has visited in all parts of the archipelago and made a special effort to maintain personal contact with the people. He says that he found them everywhere happy and contented, "living under steadily improving conditions, undisturbed by political propaganda from Manila."

By playing "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star," an entertainer at a children's tea party distracted their attention from a terrific thunderstorm in North London, and probably averted a panic. There were nearly 1,000 children in the building, and many became terrified at the vivid flashes of lightning and peals of thunder. Some jumped out of their seats and one fainted. The entertainer, Mr. Arthur Hyde, ran to the piano and calmed the children's fears by amusing them with popular choruses and songs.

headline: SHANGHAI MILL SUIT
text:
ANDERSEN, MEYER & CO. SUED BY CHINESE SPINNING CO.

First testimony in the suit of the Heng. Dah Cotton Mill against Andersen, Meyer and Co., Ltd.; for Tls. 378,777,72 for alleged breach of contract, was taken on May 7 in the United States Court for China.

Major C. P. Holcomb, counsel for the, Heng Dah Cotton Mill, outlined the case to the Court, stating that the mill entered into a contract with Andersen, Meyer and Co. on July 21, 1919, for the purchase of certain cotton spinning machinery. Delivery was not made within the time limit set by the contract, Major Holcomb, said, and the defendant firm is alleged to have breached the contract still further by failing to deliver certain castings, beltings and accessories enumerated in the contract.

Attorney W. Chalaire, who appeared in court with Judge C. S. Franklin, defending the case for Andersen, Meyer and Co., stated that the delayed shipments of machinery were accepted by the mill upon delivery without complaint, thus putting the mill in the position of having waived any breaches. He also explained that the materials and machinery were delivered late because of labour strikes and embargo and other disturbed conditions, for which Andersen, Meyer and Co., were in no way responsible.

Moh Shu-tsai, manager of the dotton mill, was the first witness put upon the stand. Moh testified that the machinery was not delivered in the time noted in the contract, and that certain of the accessories were found to be defective and were replaced by purchases from other firms.

The mill claims not only damaged of Tls. 269,777.72 from the alleged breach of contract, but an additional loss of Tls. 110,000, due to the varying value of the exchange—"CP."

The Spanish avilators left Macao yesterday at 7.25 a.m. on the last stage of their flight from Madrid to Manila.

A message received by the Spanish Procuration in Hongkong yesterday afternoon announced the safe arrival of the flyers at Apart Northern Philippines.

The two alrmen. Captain Gallarza and Captain Loriga, are flying in the former's plane, the two mechanics being left behind at Macao. The French gunboat Algol left Hongkong yesterday morning and escorted the aviators for some distance in the direction of the Philippines.

headline: REPORT ON JOSEPHUS' "JEWISH WAR."
text:
ALLUSIONS TO CHRISTIANITY AND THE TRIAL BEFORE PILATE

Dr. Vacher Burch calls attention in an article published in the Diocese of "Liverpool Review" to the striking additional evidence these references afford to the authenticity of the New Testament record. Josephus, he says, tells us he knew about the "trial before Pilate," that "many were slaves of the wonder-worker Jesus," that these "preached that their 'Rabbi' who had died and risen from the dead... taught a new law which is in opposition to the old Jewish law," and that these very early messengers were "teaching others by the help of the primitive 'documentary' mode, which he had inspired."

Continuing Dr. Burch says: "It means very much that Josephus knew about the trial of Jesus. It means even more that he should touch on the facts and believe concerning him, as risen from the dead. It is of surpassing value that he should indicate 'documentary' resources, of the preaching of these'slaves.'" Charles H. Box, professor of King's College, London, criticizing Dr. Burch's article in the "Observer," agrees that "the subject 'imperatively demands a thorough study.'" Mr. Box adds: "If the authentic character of the Slavonic version can be established, its importance is obvious."

headline: JAPANESE PRESS ON BRITISH COAL STRIKE.
text:
Tokyo, May. 4.—The leading Japanese papers this morning publish editorials on the British coal strike. The general tone is neutral and sympathetic to both parties, though reflecting a realisation of the seriousness of the situation.

The "Hochl" considers that a permanent settlement is impossible till the question of the nationalisation of mines has been definitely decided.

The "Kokumih" likens the recurring coal strike to a canoe in the British system of domestic administration which necessitates a very drastic surgical operation before a permanent settlement is possible.

The "Hochi" advocates mutual sacrifices for a compromise. The "Chugai" recommends continuing the subsidy till a permanent solution has been reached.

The Asam Publones Inc. ions of leading Japanese statemen and publicists, including Mr. Inouye, a former President of the Bank of Japan, and Viscount Takahashi, the former Premier.

Mr. Inouye thinks that the situation is serious for other nations as well as Great Britain and considers that it may lead to the nationalisation of the mines.

Viscount Takahashi and others anticipate a reasonable solution of the crisis without disorders.

Mr. Snakal, the veteran Socialist is reported to have expressed the opinion that the outcome of the present crisis is likely to decide whether the world's Labour movement will develop towards the Left or Right. It is stated that the Japanese Foreign Office fears that the Baldwin Ministry will "receive some mortal wounds" unless the situation is handled very carefully.

headline: SHANTUNG COLLEGE.
text:
Toronto, April 10.—That the past year has proved the best in the history of Shantung Christian University, despite prevailing conditions and the anti-foreign movement in China, is the report submitted to the Board of Governors at their meeting here. The enrollment of students has been the largest in the history of the University.

Mr. F. H. Hawkins, secretary of the London Missionary society was elected chairman of the board for the following year. Mrs. William McDowell of Washington is the first vice-chairman, and Principal Alfred Gandler of Knox College, Toronto, is second vice-chairman.

Reference was made during the meeting to the fraternity between the fifteen mission boards operating in governing the University.

headline: College Changes.
text:
The editorial states, in part:—In June, 1924, was started our school magazine under the able-editorship of Mr. Lim Hoy Lan, who we very much regret has had to vacate his honorary post owing to pressure of new duties as our Headmaster.

Director, we would assure our good-will and loyal support, for we are certain that when the history of Wah Yan College comes to be written, in it will not be forgotten the great debt parents and boys owe to him. We are glad that we shall still be able to avail ourselves of his kindly help, sympathy, and experience. Mr. Tsui relinquished his post as he lives in New Territory and finds that he cannot be at the School before 9 a.m. "Secondly, by delegating part of his duties—those relating to studies—to Mr. Lim, Mr. Tsui is able to supervise the work of the Branch School at Yaumati.

We, the Staff, extend to Mr. Lim our good wishes that under his government Wah Yan will go on prospering. With us, we are sure every Wahyanite concurs and will so strive to play the game that when they go out they may "fling the torch" that has been lit with no uncertain hand to those who succeed, to be borne aloft by them.

Mr. Lim in his work with us has shown himself to be conscientious and ever ready to sacrifice himself for the benefit of the boys. Which boy of Classes 1, 2 and 3 does "not know" the neat and painstaking red ink corrections in his exercise books signed with the initials L.H.L.?

pute have been proceeding actively from, an early hour this morning. The Premier was in conference with Sir Arthur Steel-Maitland, Minister of Labour, and Colonel Lane Fox, Secretary for Mines, at eight o'clock this morning.

At noon the Premier and his two colleagues received the representatives of the coal owners, who submitted details of new proposals. It is understood that these proposals consisted of new wages terms and a national minimum, which the coal owners were prepared to offer in return for a revision on hours, and that it was explained that this did not necessarily mean a week of 48 hours.

The coal owners' new offer was conveyed to the miners and to the Industrial Committee of the Trades Union Congress.

The miners' representatives considered the proposals at a lengthy meeting and consulted the Trades Union Congress Committee.

The result of their deliberations is stated to have been unfavourable to the proposals.

The miners' leaders then took the step of instructing the National Conference of the miners' delegates to join the conference of the Executives of other Trades Unions with a view to a discussion of the whole position by the Trades Union movement generally.

During the afternoon and evening negotiations have continued, the Premier taking the leading part, and a joint meeting of miners delegates and Executives of other Trades Unions has been postponed from hour to hour.

Little time now remains for a settlement as the notices to the miners expire to-night. But the prolonged discussions which have taken place are regarded in political circles as indicating that there is still hope of an eleventh-hour development which may avert a stoppage in the coal industry.

headline: EARLIER NEWS
text:
The con controlations have continued throughout the day.

The Premier has received all the House of Commons in turn, the sub-Committee of coal owners, the Industrial Committee of the Trades Union Congress, and the sub-Committee of the Miners' Executive. He had made certain proposals to the coal owners last night, and it is understood that to-day he received the reply of the coal owners to these proposals and communicated it to the Industrial Committee of the Trades Union Congress and to the Miners' sub-Committee. It is reported to night that the coal owners have made a new offer to the miners based on an eight-hour day. It is stated to be a better minimum wage than they would be prepared to give on a seven-hour day, which was worked under the old agreement. The miners, however, have so far resisted any change of hours and are supported in this by the Trades Union Congress.

In the course of the day, the Executives of every Trades Union affiliated to the Trades Union Congress met in London to consider the situation.

Mr. J. H. Thomas, ex-Colonial Secretary, moved a resolution which was adopted endorsing the effort of the Industrial Committee of the Trades Union Congress to secure a honourable settlement and favouring the continuance of negotiations "provided that the impending lockout of mine workers is not forced". This provision indicates that an attempt is being made to obtain an extension of the notices to miners, which expire tomorrow night.

writing in the British Australian and New Zealand describes a new industry for Western Australia which may in future affect for good the British and other settlers in that region. It appears that sharks, those dreaded denizens of the ocean, infest those coasts in great numbers, and according to Dr Alfred Ehrenraith this fact may have great commercial importance. This research worker has found that the hides of sharks can be successfully tanned, an average of ten square feet being generally obtainable from this part of a shark. The leather is durable and suitable for soles of boots; a material from which soft leather for boot uppers is obtainable can also be produced from the shark's stomach. Besides this, from the shark's liver and intestines medical and other oils can be expressed glue can be made from its head; its teeth can be utilised by jewellers from its secretion of pancreatic acid, insulin a cure for diabetes can be manufactured, and its flesh and fine are edible. The shark is, in fact, now declared to be more valuable to man than a pig. The new venture in catching these monsters of the deep is to be launched states this writer, at Shark's Bay, about 800 miles from Fremantle.

headline: LABOUR LEADERS LEAVE / CANTON SHORT OF CASH.
text: In order to attend the Second Chinese National Labour Mass Meeting to be held in Canton for ten days, starting from May 1, 1926, representatives (including ten employees of the Japanese owned mills) from the local labour organisations "have left secretly during the past few days. When the first mass meeting was convened last year, each representative from various cities was paid his travelling expenses to and from Canton by the Communist Headquarters in that city. But this year, in view of the shortage of funds by Canton Communists, representatives from local labour organisations were given $30 each as travelling expenses by their respective Workers' Union. It is feared that after the representatives return here from Canton, they will cause agitation among local labourers. Apart from anything of a political nature, a new movement aiming at improving living conditions of workers in general is expected to be promoted by them, thus appealing to public sympathy, according to the "Shanghai Mainichi."

It is in the supplemental statement, says the "Christian Science Monitor" of Boston, informally issued by the "spokesman for the President," rather than in the communication bearing the official stamp of the White House, that one discovers the actuating motive which prompted Mr. Coolidge to authorise a friendly survey of the Philippines by his special, emissary, Carmi A. Thompson of Cleveland, There are in both the official and semi-official statements the announcement, apparently purposely emphasised, that the mission is designed to reassure Gov. Gen. Leonard Wood, who has remained uninterruptedly an his post for more than five years, of the continuing support of his policies by the Administration in Washington. There is included, likewise, an implied pledge of the continuance of the present political relations between the Philippines and the United States. It is thus, no doubt, that it is hoped to reassure American capitalists who have made investments in the Islands, and to encourage those who may have held alooff. It is agreed, apparently, that the industrial and economic development which is possible will tend to solve many heretofore unsolved problems. The programme as outlined in advance of the survey which Mr. Thompson will conduct or supervise offers little for the encouragement of the agitators who are insisting upon political independence in the archipelago.

fore prohibition: There is no restriction whatever as to the sale of alcohol in any form and quantity. to anyone in any stage of intoxication. at any hour of the day or night. At the hotel where I had been ill-advised enough to put up for a few days, a place operated by Americans, there was a drunken, orgy practically all night, the participants being sailors from the ships, in the harbour, the degenerate Americans—of whom there are a number here—half-castes, and natives. The same thing goes on in a number of places every night, only varying in degree with the number of ships in port.

There is no check of any sort, despite the fact that this is American territory, and that the Eighteenth Amendment certainly applies her morally, and in spirit, even though it appears that no competent authority has yet decided that it applies legally or in letter. But the main point is, it seems to me that we, as the Nation which long ago assumed a moral as well as a physical and political guardianship over these Eastern peoples, are very delinquent in the exercise of that guardianship when we permit such examples of the white man's moral obliquity as this to exist under the eyes of the natives. It lowers America's prestige among them, and breeds additional disrespect and scorn for the entire white race.

Moreover, such conditions are so strikingly opposed to the careful, beneficent English colonial rule in the same regard as to make one wonder if America, after all, is properly intrusted with the guardianship of an alien people. Nothing like the state of affairs here exists in any South Sea group, not even in French Tahiti. No such degenerate white men as hang about the saloons here would be permitted to remain in Samoa, Fiji, the Cook Group, or elsewhere in the British Pacific Island possessions. Does it not logically follow that England inculcates into the native mind a deeper respect for her ways and her people than can America, so long as such a disgraceful state of affairs as the unrestricted sale of liquor to the natives in the Philippines continues?

Here is a condition known to exist. The mere recital of these facts would seem to indicate, at least in part, what the United States can do to better conditions in the Islands.

Peking, April 27.—According to a despatch from Canton, the National Government has, at the request of the Executive Council of the Kuomintang at Canton, sent a protest to the French Government through the French Consul-General against the persecution and deportation of the members of the Kuomintang in Indo-China. headline: CANTON COUP DETAT DENIED.
text:
There has been no coup d'état in Canton, in spite of asseverations to the contrary in the cables from China and the reports in the Japanese press.

This authoritative information was given to a representative of the "Japan Chronicle" by Sir James Jamieson, British-Consul-General in Canton, who left Kobe for Home on April 28 by the "Empress of Australia."

According to reports that have been current for over a fortnight, the Red regime was recently ousted, and a new administration took its place. At the time of receipt of the first news, the authenticity of the report was doubted, and when subsequently no confirmation was received from other quarters, it became evident that propagandists had been at work. This theory was substantiated when news was received, from Hongkong that the Kwangtung Foreign Minister, the famous Dr. C. C. Wu, son of the late Dr. Wu Ting-fung, had taken steps to bring about a rapprochement between Hongkong and Canton. Dr. Wu is one of the Red section of the Kuomintang, the party in power in Canton. Sir James Jamieson, who stated that he preferred not to make any public announcement on the political situation in China, said that a conference between Hongkong and Canton was still in progress, and though Hongkong hoped that a settlement of the boycott would be effected, yet up to the time that he left Canton the situation was in practically the same position as it had been for the past few months. Sir James's declaration that he is merely going home on furlough and that he will be returning to Canton, belies the reports current in the Chinese Press that he had been recalled by his Home Government.

Sir James Jamieson came considerably into prominence during the anti-British agitation in South China last year, though his famous warning to the Canton Government, which was broadcast throughout the world the day before the students, supported by Russian officers, attempted to take the Shammen foreign concession by storm. On that occasion Sir James informed C. C. Wu that he had received information that the students had drawn lots as to who should have the honour of sacrificing their lives in taking the Shammen. Sir James solemnly warned the Foreign Minister that in the event of the threatened assault eventuating, the foreign authorities on the concession would use whatever force they considered necessary to protect it. The following day the collision occurred, and the French and British soldiers and marines fired, killing a number of the demonstrators. Shortly afterwards Sir Austen Chamberlain cabled to Sir James Jamieson, stating that he had the support of the British Government behind him in any action which he took to protect foreign interests in Canton.

Sir James is expected to be away for about six months.
